Name: Göttingen
Alternative_Name: Gutingi; Guthingen; Guthinge; Gutinge; Gutingen; Guttingen; Gudingin; Gotinge; Gotingen; Ghotingen; Gothinge; Gottinghe; Gottingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 953 in a donation charter of Emperor Otto I to the monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg.
Town_Description: It is unknown when exactly the town rights were acquired, probably in the early 13th century. First mention as "civitas" around 1230.
Fair_Description: In Göttingen trade regulations of the year 1398, four fairs are mentioned, taking place on St Walpurga, Corpus Christi, St James and St Simon and Juda. The Corpus Christi fair was founded in 1380.
Toll_Description: Fee for safe conduct for commodities moved through town, owned by the Duke of Brunswick, and toll for all commodities sold and bought in Göttingen, except those intended for the nobility and clerics, perishables and retail. Already in 1380, the height of the toll was defined by the civic council. Extensive toll registers exist from the first half of the 15th century. The toll was levied at the town gates.

Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the time of Emperor Conrad II (1024-1039) as "predium" (estate) of count Udo of Katlenburg. The monastery of St Alexander was founded before 1085. South of it, a market settlement developed in the late 12th century.
Town_Description: Einbeck was mentioned as "civitas" in 1203 und 1239. A council is first mentioned in 1252, a town wall in 1264, and a "new" market in 1266. Braunschweig town privileges were granted in 1279.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct in Einbeck was changed into a road and bridge fee in 1417.

Name: Aachen
Alternative_Name: Aquis; Aquisgrani; Ahha; Ais em ma chapelle; Aix-la-Chapelle; Aken
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 769, Aachen was the primary residence of the Carolingians and place of coronation for over 30 German kings.
Town_Description: Aachen was granted town rights, as well as market and mint rights, as "caput civitatum" (head of towns) and as "caput et sedes regni Theutonici" (head and seat of the German kings) on 8 January 1166 by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The document became known as the "Karlsprivileg" and made the town to a free imperial city.
Fair_Description: Emperor Frederick granted two fairs in 1166 (Jan. 9): Sunday Invocavit (Sunday before Eastern) during 15 days and eight days before St. Michael (Sept. 29) till 8 days after that.

Name: Aalborg
Alternative_Name: Alaburg; Aleburgh; Aleburgensis; Alæburgh; Alburgis; Aalebwrgh; Olborg; Albergia; Aaleborgh; Alæburgh
Settlement_Description: Archeological excavations have revealed a viking age seasonal market. Around 1000 AD a church was built, and Aalborg now seems to have been a permanent settlement with an urban character.
Town_Description: Around 1040 the Danish king Hardeknud (1035-1042) minted coins in Aalborg. Characterized as a town (“civitas”) by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen around 1075 . According to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231, Aalborg was royal property (Danish: Kongelev). The royal castle of Aalborghus was mentioned for the first time in 1340, but probably established in the 13th century. The king’s bailiff (Danish: Foged) is documented in 1293. Existing town privileges were confirmed and expanded in 1342 by king Valdemar IV Atterdag (1340-1375). Mayors, a town council and citizens (villani) are known from the middle of the 14th century onwards. At the beginning of the 13th century the medieval town square (Danish: Gammeltorv), where well-established, and in 1232 a Franciscan convent was founded. Also in the 13th century Aalborg was fortified with a palisade, moats and earthworks. Before 1431 a town hall was built at the medieval town square. A new town hall was built shortly before 1499, but burned down in 1530, and was not rebuilt before after the Count's Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536. The medieval castle of Aalborghus was also destroyed during the war, and a new castle was built closer to the harbour. Aalborg benefited from its central role in trading networks between Norway and Germany. From the 13th century onwards German merchants played an important role in the network. The trade with herring caught in Limfjorden was particularly important to Aalborg, and during the late medieval period the town competed with smaller urban settlements in the region such as Nibe to control the herring trade. Around 1600 Aalborg almost had a monopoly on the trade with fish from Limfjorden, and the town experienced growth until the Dano-Swedish wars around the middle of the 17th century. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era Aalborg was one of the most important towns in Jutland.
Fair_Description: From around 1400 onwards the rich herring fishing in Limfjorden became more important. The fishing trade generated economic activities and several fairs were established. In general, the town of Aalborg tried to dominate and even monopolize the trade in the regions around Limfjorden, something which can be illustrated with the ongoing conflicts between the small urban settlement of Nibe and Aalborg. Already in the early medieval period at least one annual fair must have been held in Aalborg, but the age, character and date of this fair is unknown. In the later medieval period Aalborg had at least two annual fairs, but shortly after 1650 only one annual fair took place in Aalborg.
Toll_Description: At least from the middle of the 14th century onwards Aalborg was one of the most important royal tolls in Denmark. The origin of the toll is, however, unclear. In the middle of the 14th century toll was collected on herring, horses and oxen and other commodities exported from Aalborg. Toll lists from the years 1517-1519 have been preserved, and at this time German merchants had to pay a higher toll than the local Danes. During one of the Dano-Swedish wars, the Torstenson War 1643-1645, a toll building in Aalborg was destroyed. It was rebuilt already in 1651.
Ferry_Description: Aalborg was founded at the most narrow part of Limfjorden; an obvious place to cross the fjord by boat. When the first ferry connecting the region of Vendsyssel with Aalborg was established is, however, not known. Presumably, a royal privileged ferry between Aalborg and Vendsyssel was in place in the 13th century. The ferry is, however, not documented before the 15th century. On the northern side of Limfjord opposite Aalborg the ferry landed near the settlement of Sundby.
Harbour_Description: Aalborg benefited from a good natural harbour due to the town locality at a river estuary and beach meadows. The knowledge of the medieval port is, however, limited. It was placed in the small river, Østerå. Bulwarks were constructed in the 13th century. Smaller vessels could be loaded at a bridge across the river, Ladebro, while larger ships had to anchor in the fjord outside the harbour. In the late medieval period the port was expanded. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era Aalborg was one of the most important ports in Jutland. From the early 14th century onwards, German ships often used to port, for example from Lubeck in 1366 and 1399.

Town_Description: Around 1040 the Danish king Hardeknud (1035-1042) minted coins in Aalborg. Characterized as a town (“civitas”) by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen around 1075 . According to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231, Aalborg was royal property (Danish: Kongelev). The royal castle of Aalborghus was mentioned for the first time in 1340, but probably established in the 13th century. The king’s bailiff (Danish: Foged) is documented in 1293. Existing town privileges were confirmed and expanded in 1342 by king Valdemar IV Atterdag (1340-1375). Mayors, a town council and citizens (villani) are known from the middle of the 14th century onwards. At the beginning of the 13th century the medieval town square (Danish: Gammeltorv), where well-established, and in 1232 a Franciscan convent was founded. Also in the 13th century Aalborg was fortified with a palisade, moats and earthworks. Before 1431 a town hall was built at the medieval town square. A new town hall was built shortly before 1499, but burned down in 1530, and was not rebuilt before after the Count's Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536. The medieval castle of Aalborghus was also destroyed during the war, and a new castle was built closer to the harbour. Aalborg benefited from its central role in trading networks between Norway and Germany. From the 13th century onwards German merchants played an important role in the network. The trade with herring caught in Limfjorden was particularly important to Aalborg, and during the late medieval period the town competed with smaller urban settlements in the region such as Nibe to control the herring trade. Around 1600 Aalborg almost had a monopoly on the trade with fish from Limfjorden, and the town experienced growth until the Dano-Swedish wars around the middle of the 17th century. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era Aalborg was one of the most important towns in Jutland.
Fair_Description: From around 1400 onwards the rich herring fishing in Limfjorden became more important. The fishing trade generated economic activities and several fairs were established. In general, the town of Aalborg tried to dominate and even monopolize the trade in the regions around Limfjorden, something which can be illustrated with the ongoing conflicts between the small urban settlement of Nibe and Aalborg. Already in the early medieval period at least one annual fair must have been held in Aalborg, but the age, character and date of this fair is unknown. In the later medieval period Aalborg had at least two annual fairs, but shortly after 1650 only one annual fair took place in Aalborg.
Toll_Description: At least from the middle of the 14th century onwards Aalborg was one of the most important royal tolls in Denmark. The origin of the toll is, however, unclear. In the middle of the 14th century toll was collected on herring, horses and oxen and other commodities exported from Aalborg. Toll lists from the years 1517-1519 have been preserved, and at this time German merchants had to pay a higher toll than the local Danes. During one of the Dano-Swedish wars, the Torstenson War 1643-1645, a toll building in Aalborg was destroyed. It was rebuilt already in 1651.
Ferry_Description: Aalborg was founded at the most narrow part of Limfjorden; an obvious place to cross the fjord by boat. When the first ferry connecting the region of Vendsyssel with Aalborg was established is, however, not known. Presumably, a royal privileged ferry between Aalborg and Vendsyssel was in place in the 13th century. The ferry is, however, not documented before the 15th century. On the northern side of Limfjord opposite Aalborg the ferry landed near the settlement of Sundby.

It was placed in the small river, Østerå. Bulwarks were constructed in the 13th century. Smaller vessels could be loaded at a bridge across the river, Ladebro, while larger ships had to anchor in the fjord outside the harbour. In the late medieval period the port was expanded. From the early 14th century onwards, German ships often used to port, for example from Lubeck in 1366 and 1399.

Name: Aalst (Vlaanderen)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 866, in an 18th-century copy, as "villa" in possession of the abbey of Lobbes. Situated on the left bank of the river Dender and on the medieval road Bruges-Cologne (possibly earlier the Roman road Boulogne-Cologne). The lords of Aalst built a castle in the 11th century.
Town_Description: The settlement was fortified in the late 11th century. At the end of the 12th century it was acquired by the counts of Flanders. A new town wall was built in c. 1200. A town hall ('schepenhuis') was built in the first quarter of the 13th century.
Fair_Description: In 1351 (Sept. 26) the count of Flanders granted two free fairs, both during 14 nights. The first starting 8 days before Sacramentsday and 8 days after that. The second on (8 days before?) St. Bavo (Oct. 1) and 8 days after that.

Name: Aarhus
Alternative_Name: Aros; Arus; Arusuensis; Arosei; Arusia; Arhvs; Arws; Aars; Arhws; Arusie; Aarhwss; Aarhuus; Århus
Settlement_Description: Aarhus is one of the oldest urban settlements of Denmark. Archeological excavations have shown how Aarhus was a permanent settlement with an urban character from around the year 800.
Town_Description: From the second half of the 10th century onwards Aarhus was a diocese, and one of the most significant towns of Denmark. Throughout the middle ages and early modern period Aarhus remained the clerical center of Eastern Jutland. At the turn of the 12th century at least three churches were built in Aarhus, and work on a new cathedral in the town center had begun. Soon after a town square, Store Torv, was established in front of the cathedral. A Dominican monastery was founded c. 1239. Around the middle of the 11th century the king issued coins in Aarhus, and later in the century the chronicler Adam of Bremen described Aarhus as “civitas”. Around 1300 Aarhus was given a town law by the king and a town hall was built at Store Torv. As in other towns in Jutland the town law was a copy of the law of Schleswig. The oldest preserved town privileges were granted by king Christoffer the Bavarian (1440-1448) in 1441, but the town was probably granted its first royal privileges in the 13th century. Already in the 10th century a rampart was built around most of the town, and the town continued to be fortified throughout the medieval period. Significant parts of the settlement, however, were located outside the fortification, especially from the 13th century onwards. During the late medieval period and early modern era Aarhus kept its status as one of the most important Danish towns. The town benefited from its central location in Jutland, and as an important junction for both land based and maritime transportation. The town was at its economic peak in the late 16th century, but in the following 17th century Aarhus stagnated, and the town was also damaged heavily during the Dano-Swedish wars.
Fair_Description: Market activities were essential already in the late 8th century, when craftsmen and traders gathered near the estuary of the river of Aarhus Å. During the medieval period at least one annual fair, the fair of Saint Olav, was held in Aarhus. Aarhus also held other annual fairs in the later middle ages and early-modern period. The age and character of these fairs is, however, uncertain. In the second half of the 17th century Aarhus only had one fair.
Toll_Description: The age and character of the toll in Aarhus is not known. Presumably, a royal toll was collected already in the Viking Age, and most certainly also in the early medieval period. In the 17th century a toll station was constructed, probably on the southern side of the river. But an even older toll station was presumably constructed on a piece of land owned by the king near the river in 1477. During the reign of king Hans (1481-1513) a specific toll on beer, wine and other goods was introduced in Aarhus as well as other Danish towns, the so-called ‘accise/sise’. This toll was collected by the town and on a regular basis handed over to the king. From Aarhus, registers of the sise-toll from the years around 1500 have been preserved.
Bridge_Description: The age and character of the first bridge in Aarhus across Aarhus Å is uncertain. In the 13th century a watermill and dam was mentioned for the first time, and in the middle of the 13th century a bridge was probably also built at Immervad, where there previously had been a ford across the river. The bridge at Immervad was first mentioned in 1477 and again in 1512. Another bridge (‘Mindebro’) further downstream was first mentioned in 1634.
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the sea of Kattegat between Aarhus and Kalundborg on the island of Zealand was one of the most important ferry routes in Denmark throughout the middle ages and early-modern period. The ferry connection between Aarhus and Kalundborg was apparently first mentioned by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen c. 1075. According to Adam it was also possible to take a ferry to Norway from Aarhus. The ferry to Zealand often went via the island of Samsø. Ferry accounts from the 1640ties have been preserved. The registry reveals that 10-15 smaller vessels were used as ferries between Aarhus and Kalundborg, and that these ferries annually transported between 700 and 1400 passengers across Kattegat.
Harbour_Description: In the viking age and early medieval period the harbour was placed by the town fortification on the northern bank of the river, Aarhus Å, and near the river’s outlet into the sea. In the 15th century a new harbour was built on the opposite southern side of the river. Throughout the middle ages and the early-modern era the port was one of the most important in Jutland.

Name: Altenburg
Alternative_Name: Altenburc; Aldenburch; Plisna; Plysn; Plisne; Aldenburg; Pauritz; Podegrodici
Settlement_Description: From approximately 800 centre of the Slavic area called Plisni (Pleißenland). A fortification was referred to as Altenburg, first mentioned in 976. A small village named Pauritz developed close to the castle's ramparts. From the 11th to the 13th century the castle was used as an imperial palace ('Kaiserpfalz') so that the village developed early urban structures in the 11th century.
Town_Description: From 1165 Altenburg consisted of an old and new town. In 1205 it was referred to as civitas. First record of town rights in 1256.
Fair_Description: Altenburg received the right to hold an eight-day fair from Sunday Rogate until Exaudi from margrave Wilhelm in 1419. A second fair on the Nativity of Mary is mentioned in 1437.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct in Altenburg is first mentioned in 1504. The regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') and accounts ('Geleitsrechnungen') for Altenburg from 1515 regulated the fees for several wares.

Name: Amersfoort
Alternative_Name: Amersfoirde; Amersfoorde; Amersforden; Amervoirde; Amersfordia; Amersfort;
Settlement_Description: Amersfoort is first mentioned in 1028. It developed from a bishop's court that is first mentioned in 1203. A hospital is first mentioned in 1378.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted before 12 June 1259 by Henry I van Vianden, bishop of Utrecht.
Fair_Description: In 1331 the town obtained permission from the bishop of Utrecht for another two fairs next to the existing one with St. Gallen (Oct. 16): 1) with Eastern, 2) with St. Bartholomeus (August 24). In 1432 merchants from Amersfoort are first found on the fairs at Frankfurt. In 1478 (Febr. 22) a free fair for horned cattle with safe-conduct for the visitors was obtained from the bishop. Regular income from the market and year-toll and from the toll on the road outside the Rode poort (gate) and Slijkpoort and from the year-toll and toll on the road at the Kamp- and Bloemendaalse poort are found in the town-accounts dated 1464-'72. In 1562 the king collected 90 pounds at the   Kamp- and Bloemendaalse gates and 80 pound at the Slijk- and Utrechtse gates.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Utrecht in Amersfoort is first mentioned in accounts from 1325/26, but must have existed since the 13th century. It was a fair toll as well as a transit toll for land transport.

Regular income from the market and year-toll and from the toll on the road outside the Rode poort (gate) and Slijkpoort and from the year-toll and toll on the road at the Kamp- and Bloemendaalse poort are found in the town-accounts dated 1464-'72. In 1562 the king collected 90 pounds at the   Kamp- and Bloemendaalse gates and 80 pound at the Slijk- and Utrechtse gates.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Utrecht in Amersfoort is first mentioned in accounts from 1325/26, but must have existed since the 13th century. It was a fair toll as well as a transit toll for land transport.

Name: Amsterdam
Alternative_Name: Amstelledamme; Amstelredamme; Amstelodanum; Amestelredam; Amestelredamme; Aemstelredamme
Settlement_Description: Amsterdam is first mentioned in 1275.
Town_Description:
Town privileges were officially granted after 21 May 1300 and before 5 August 1301. Extended town privileges were granted on 9 December 1342. In 1368 Amsterdam received from the king of Sweden the privilege for a 'vitte' (trading-post) on Schonen (southern point of Sweden) with its own guardian. 
The largest of six 'Kamers' (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, the Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Amsterdam.
Fair_Description: It is unknown when Amsterdam obtained market rights. In 1304, the market rights were withdrawn by William III of Holland, the eldest son of the count of Holland. It is unknown when market rights were regained, but this happened definitely in the fourteenth century. A weigh-house is first mentioned in 1392. In the fifteenth century, there were at least two fairs. In 1422 the first merchants from Amsterdam visited the fairs of Frankfurt. Until the beginning of the seventeenth century, the fairs took place on the Dam and the Damrak.
Toll_Description:
In 1275 the people who lived at the Amestelledamme (dam in the river Amstel) obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. Probably shortly before 1323 a toll on all imported beer from Hamburg and the Baltic via the Zuiderzee was located by the count of Holland in Amsterdam at the entrance of the 'rout binnendunen' through Holland. Accounts ('particulen') of the beertoll are preserved and edited for the years 1352-1354 and 1364-1366. Yields are preserved and edited for the years 1343-'69. From 1469/70 the accounts of the stewards of Amstelland mention a toll on 'vreemd bier' (imported beer). In an unedited account dated 1531/2 it is said that inhabitants of Amsterdam were free of this toll as those exempted from the toll at the Spaarndam. In 1557 Amsterdam purchased this right from the count (king) of Holland, Philip II. 
In the 14th century Kampen took care of buoying the Zuiderzee and the tidal inlets. In the course of the 15th century Amsterdam took over this role more and more. 'Bakengeld' (buoy-money) is first found in 1413 after duke Albrecht situated a new toll in the Zuiderzee or the Marsdiep. The Hanse opposed this toll. In 1452 duke Philip of Burgundy granted the raising of the harbour-money or 'paalgeld'. In 1474 an ordinance stated the levying of 'paalgeld' from goods of the Hansa for two years. In 1527 Kampen renounced the right to place the buoys in the Vlie, Marsdiep and other tidal inlets where paalgeld was levied, to Amsterdam. Goods of Kampen however would be free of this tax (this was the case already in 1514). Yields of the paalgeld are edited and analysed for the 1530-'72 and show a considerable increase of the shipping in the periode circa 1545-1565. Around 1550 there are 'paalmeesters' (collectors of the paalgeld) for Amsterdam in Hoorn and Enkhuizen. This caused opposition. Tariffs of the paalgeld dated 1514 (especially for England), 1556 and 1560 are almost corresponding. In 1573 king Philip II granted after advice of William of Orange and the Estates the right of the paalgeld to Enkhuizen.
Staple_Description: The count of Holland ordained shortly(?) before 1323 that all beer imported via the Zuiderzee from Hamburg and the Baltic had to be traded in the ports of Amsterdam and Medemblik. Afterwards Medemblik is never mentioned again. The staple was important both for the early development of Amsterdam as for the utilisation of the 'route binnendunen' through Holland. The famous worldstaple-market which Amsterdam supposedly was during the Golden Age, is altered by Lesger in a gateway to the Dutch hinterland with moreover a news- and information-staple then a staple for goods.

Name: Andernach
Settlement_Description: Mentioned at the end of the 3rd century on the stone of Tongeren. Originally a Roman fortress next to a settlement on the Rhine street. In the Middle Ages it became a Frankish royal farm, donated to the Archbishop of Cologne in 1167.
Town_Description: NULL
Toll_Description:
(1) The Archbishop of Cologne levied a river toll on the Rhine from 1147 to 1190, in 1235, from 1277 to 1282, from 1287 to 1302 and from 1306 to 1365. In 1365, the toll was relocated to Linz until it was reestablished in Andernach in 1475. Between 1475 and 1485, the annual return amounted to 3000 Gulden. The amount to pay for wine was relatively low, but salt, fish and grains are similar to the tariffs in Bonn. The tariffs can bee seen under the following source below. 
(2) In 1302 and from 1312, together with the river toll, an escort fee was levied by the Archbishop of Cologne.
(3) This unknown toll, probably a transit toll, was levied from 1389 and concerned millstones. The tariff per millstone was 6 Pfennig/Denar. The annual yield amounted to 12 Mark in 1390-95 and 1433.

Name: Antwerpen
Alternative_Name: Andouerpenses; Andouerpis; Antwerpo; Andouerpis castro; Antwerpia; Antwerpensis;  Antwerp; Anvers; Antorff
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the eighth century in a tenth-century copy. Next mention from 692-726, in a copy dating from 1191.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: In 1298 (April 24) a horsefair on Saterday for all Brabant is granted by the duke of Brabant. In 1325 two fairs are found: with Pentecost (May 26) and St. Bavo (Oct. 1). Salt and fish market, which was moved to Malines. Emperor Henry VII moves it back to Antwerp in 1309, but moved to Malines again in 1369. A comital cloth-hall is first found in 1226, in 1250 half of the revenues are donated to the town. In 1317 all of the revenues and the building were given to the town and it was rebuild in 1324.
Staple_Description: In 1259 several towns (Brussel, Tienen, Aarschot, Herentals, Turnhout, Oisterwijk, Den Bosch, Breda, Hoogstraten, Lier, Zierikzee and Leuven) declared that the saltstaple had been in Antwerp forever. Malines citizens were freed from staple obligations for fish, salt and oats in Antwerp in 1356, which led to decades of conflict between both cities, ended in favour of Antwerp in 1415. Staple of fatty products for Holland in 1358. 1407: Staple of English cloth merchants. 1409: Privileges of the Hanse, partial relocation of Hanseatic activities from Bruges to Antwerp. In 1416 the staple for herring was relocated from the St. Jansvliet to the Holenvliet. 1444 Staple of Middelburg trading guilds. 1452: Hanseatic staple of Rhenish wines, together with Dordrecht. 1491: Staple for alum from Tolfa. 1540: Agreement with Scotland for a staple of Scottish salt and fishes. An agreement with the Hanse made the city the principal Hanseatic residency in the Netherlands in 1563.

Name: Arnhem
Alternative_Name: Arnheim; Arneym; Arnem; Arnheym; Arem; Aerhem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 893. Before the 13th century domains in Arnhem were in possession of the monasteries of Prüm and Elten and the count of Guelders.
Town_Description: Shortly before 1200 a merchant settlement developed on the shore of the Rhine, which acquired town privileges on 13 July 1233 from Otto II, count of Guelders. A town council is mentioned in 1291, a burgomaster in 1339.
Fair_Description:
Three fairs are mentioned in 1240, their dates are known from 1294/95. In 1459, and additional cattle fair was granted. Since the middle of the fourteenth century or even earlier, the dukes of Guelders had been pawning or leasing out the cashing of all three Arnhem fairs to private persons, and since 1372 to the town of Arnhem itself. Around the middle of the fourtheenth century, town accounts of Deventer mention a fair in Arnhem 'in festo Palmarum' or '(in) Palmis', which could refer to the Mid-Fast fair.
Fairs took place on the 'Nieuwe Markt' (New Market), the present-day 'Korenmarkt', which was in function from the second quarter of the thirteenth century, whereas the weekly market took place on the old market. Cloth was the most important commodity traded on the fairs in Arnhem, followed by wine and salt.
Toll_Description: A land toll ('weggeld'), owned by the landlord, the duke of Guelders, was levied at all four mayor town gates: the Sabelspoort, Rijnpoort, Velperpoort, and Sint-Janspoort. The toll at the Rijnpoort (Rhine gate) linked up with the ferry, which stimulated trade-related traffic coming from the ferry to enter Arnhem. Most traffic used the Rijnpoort; profit from the Sint-Janspoort was quite low.
Staple_Description: Officially, Arnhem had no grain staple, but around the mid-fifteenth century, from 1437-1439 onward, the town de facto forced people to offer their load of grain for sale in Arnhem when passing by on the river Rhine. The grain market was located outside the Rhine gate, near the harbour.

Three fairs are mentioned in 1240, their dates are known from 1294/95. In 1459, and additional cattle fair was granted. Since the middle of the fourteenth century or even earlier, the dukes of Guelders had been pawning or leasing out the cashing of all three Arnhem fairs to private persons, and since 1372 to the town of Arnhem itself. Around the middle of the fourtheenth century, town accounts of Deventer mention a fair in Arnhem 'in festo Palmarum' or '(in) Palmis', which could refer to the Mid-Fast fair.
Fairs took place on the 'Nieuwe Markt' (New Market), the present-day 'Korenmarkt', which was in function from the second quarter of the thirteenth century, whereas the weekly market took place on the old market. Cloth was the most important commodity traded on the fairs in Arnhem, followed by wine and salt.
Toll_Description: A land toll ('weggeld'), owned by the landlord, the duke of Guelders, was levied at all four mayor town gates: the Sabelspoort, Rijnpoort, Velperpoort, and Sint-Janspoort. The toll at the Rijnpoort (Rhine gate) linked up with the ferry, which stimulated trade-related traffic coming from the ferry to enter Arnhem. Name: Bergen op Zoom
Alternative_Name: Bergon; Berga; Bergen supra Zoom; Bergen super Zoem; Berghen super Zoem; Bergen vp den Zoem; Berghen anden Some; Berghen opten Zoem; Bergen op ten Zoom; Bergh... svper Zome
Settlement_Description: Bergen op Zoom is first mentioned in 966.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted between ca. 1198 and 25 February 1212 by Godfried II, lord of Breda and Schoten. A hospital is first mentioned in 1246.
Fair_Description: In 1314 a cloth-hall and a weekly market on Monday are found and a weighhouse is built in 1355. Before 1337 there were already two fairs. In 1338 a cloth-fair is mentioned. In 1365 two fairs were arranged by the lord of the town: the famous free Eastern- and 'Koude'(Cold/Winter)-fairs (although named like this already in 1359) during 6 weeks, including 2 weeks for the journey there and back. The Koude-fair started 2 weeks after All Saints (Nov. 1), the Eastern fair 2 weeks after Maundy Thursday. In 1349 and 1356 the German emperor and the duke of Brabant granted free traffic through Brabant and Limburg, which afterwards was confirmed. In 1486 the emperor granted free travel to the fairs of Bergen in all his empire. In 1490 the period in which the merchants were protected on the way back of the Koudefair in the seigniory was enlengthened till Jan. 24 and in 1495 even during the whole year. This caused many protests from the towns in Flanders and was thus raised in 1498. In 1501 the freedom of the Eastern-fair was enlengthened 1 week and for the Koude-fair 3 weeks. This two fairs made a cycle with those in Antwerp with Pentecost and St. Bavo (Oct. 1). Origins and numbers of merchants from the Netherlands are visualised on a map for the period 1432-89. Socalled 'Craam' (market-stalls)-accounts are preserved and analysed for the years 1481-1542. In it are found the names and origin of the merchants and their goods and taxes. After 1530 the fairs were in decline as a result of the floods of 1530 and 1532 which hampered access of the harbour. As a result of the floods the Honte was better navigable, which was profitable for Antwerp. The important market for madder was relocated to Zierikzee.
Toll_Description: The landtoll in Brabant was partly collected in Bergen op Zoom. Yields of this comital landtoll are published for the years 1531-'85.
Staple_Description: Between 1388 and 1392, the Hanseatic wool staple was moved from Bruges to Bergen op Zoom. In 1474/'5 the staple of the English cloths is here.

Name: Berlin
Alternative_Name: Berlin-Kölln; Berlin-Cölln, Cölln, Kölln; Perlyn; Berlyn; Berlinum; Berlinensis; Berolinum
Settlement_Description: A Slavic settlement is attested from the 6th to 8th century, but it was not necessarily the immediate predecessor of the German settlement that was first mentioned in 1244, then already a town.
Town_Description: The first indication of Berlin is given in the mention of its provost in 1244, who was already mentioned as provost of Cölln in 1237; both towns were closely associated. Since its first mention, Berlin can be seen as a town, it is referred to as civitas in 1251. The exact date of the acquisition of town rights has not survived. Participation at the Hanseatic Diets in 1359, 1430 and lastly 1443; in 1518 they were forced by their territorial lord to quit the alliance.
Fair_Description: The date of the awarding of the fairs in Berlin is not mentioned.
Toll_Description: In 1298 Berlin acquired the river toll of Köpenick. The privileges referred to as "Nedderlage" (entrepot / staple) were tolls for merchants who travelled through the town; they were transferred to the prince electorate in 1448.
Staple_Description: A record, in which Berlin was granted staple rights in 1297, turned out to be a forgery. Especially the mention of the staple therein is insecure. The first secure confirmation of the staple right in Berlin is granted in 1337, even though a fee was probably already collected in the 13th century.

Name: Bernburg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the castle Brandanburg in a donation charter of Emperor Otto I to the Monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg in 961. Archaeological evidence shows early medieval fortifications on the castle hill. A civic settlement developed in the valley along the main street that crossed the Saale with one or more fords.
Town_Description: The town consisted of the old and new town in the valley (Talstadt), which received town privileges after Magdeburg model in 1278, but were formally united only in 1561. The Bergstadt around the castle hill was raised into a town between 1442 and 1457 and was merged with the Talstadt in 1825.
Toll_Description: A toll in Bernburg is first mentioned in 1239, but it could refer to the bridge toll only. In 1537 the toll from Neundorf (Anhalt) is moved to the district of Bernburg. A regulation of safe conduct of 1563 settles the bridge and road toll.

Name: Bingen
Alternative_Name: Bingen am Rhein; Bingium; Bingum; Pinger marca; Bingam; castello Pinge; castello Pingua
Settlement_Description: A copy of the 11th century suggests a first mention of the settlement around 107. A castle called Klopp was built in the 13th century.
Town_Description: NULL
Toll_Description:
There were two land tolls in Bingen owned by the Archbishop of Mainz: 
1) A toll for cattle was probably levied from 1190 or 1194/98. In 1368 this was leased out for 200 guilders.

2) The 'Gaupfortenzoll' was first mentioned in 1247. In 1390, 50 pounds Heller were collected.

In addition, a river toll was probably levied around 1250. A transit toll on the Rhine in the 14th and 15th centuries, however, can be ruled out. It was probably only a fee for the ferry.

Name: Bonn
Alternative_Name: Bonnam; cum castris Bonnensibus; Bunna; Bonna; cisalpinae Veronae; Bunno; acta Verona
Settlement_Description: Before the Romans could establish their military camps, the Ubii settled in the area of today's Bonn. In the 1st century Bonn served as a legionary suburb, a so-called 'civil vicus' ('Zivilvicus'). Under Frankish rule, Bonn rose to become an important marketplace and after 1288 became the residence of the Cologne electors.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: In 1166 a May-market was granted for 3 days. Of old a fair was organised here at the Joh's cross near Dietkirchen on June 23-29.
Toll_Description:
Three tolls were levied in Bonn by the Archbishop of Cologne:
1) The river toll on the Rhine was levied 1244-1254, before 1282, 1293-1302 and from 1306. The tariff was 12 pfennigs in 1293. In 1367 the customs were leased for 4 years for 30600 guilders a year. In 1371/74 the revenues added up to an average of about 16839 guilders a year. In 1473, the toll was moved to Remagen for a few weeks.
2) From 1302 onwards, the escort fee was probably levied together with the Rhine toll.
3) A land toll was established before 1282, but was not attested again until the beginning of the 15th century. In 1454/60, 70 marks were estimated for the cattle fee.

Name: Brandenburg (Havel)
Alternative_Name: Brandenburg an der Havel; Brendanburg; Brennaburg; Brandenborch; Brandenborg; Brandenburgensis; Brandeneburg; Parduin; Parduwin; Brennabor
Settlement_Description: A Slavic settlement is first mentioned in 928. Foundation of a bishopric in 948 under Otto I, but lost to the Slavs afterwards. Premonstratensian Canons settled in Parduin (the current old town) around 1147. Reconquered by the margrave of Brandenburg and the archbishop of Magdeburg in 1157. They resided on the cathedral island.
Town_Description: The old town (formerly the village Parduin) developed into a town after 1157. Toll privileges are granted in 1170 for the 'cives nostri Brandenburgensis'. The new town is first mentioned in 1196. In the middle of the 13th century, Magdeburg town rights are attested, although it is unknown when they were granted. In 1263 council members are mentioned in the old and new town; both parts were were formally merged in 1718.
Fair_Description: At the end of the 15th century two fairs in old and new town, one additional fair in the new town. At the end of the 16th century 6 fairs in the old town and 5 in the new town.
Toll_Description: In 1424, 1446 and 1458 the margravial toll in both towns Brandenburg (old town and new town), as well as the toll on the streets between Plaue, Pritzerbe and Wustermark and between Brandenburg and Werder was pawned to the town of Brandenburg.
Staple_Description: In a treaty of the Elector Frederick with the Neustadt in Brandenburg from 1455, a three-day staple is mentioned for merchants who wanted to travel through the "Arche". Since 1564 there was also an entrepot in the old town.

Settlement_Description: Most likely used to be an old prussic settlement, a castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1240 and destroyed by the Old Prussians in 1242, a new german settlement was founded in 1250 and destroyed in 1260, what is now known as the historic district was built in 1276
Town_Description: Town law was granted in 1254 by the first Warmian Bishop, Anselm, the now historic town district was granted a handfast of Lübeck town law in 1284 by Bishop Heinrich Fleming from Lübeck, the new town district was founded on Lübeck town law in 1342 by Bishop Hermann of Prag

Name: Braunschweig
Alternative_Name: Brunswick; Brunesguik; Brunswik; Brunswijk; Brunßwig; Brunßwik; Brunßwigk
Settlement_Description: Braunschweig is first mentioned in the dedication charter of the St Magnus church from 1031.
Town_Description: The town consisted of the five initially independent boroughs ('weichbilde') Altstadt, Hagen, Neustadt, Altewiek and Sack, which merged with each other and appeared as the single town Braunschweig in the course of the 14th century. The oldest town rights of Altstadt were granted in 1204.
Fair_Description: The three most important fairs in Braunschweig, on St Walpurga, New Year's Day and St Giles, were first attested in 1385. Three smaller fairs are attested in 1439, on Sunday Jubilate (the dedication day of the church of the Paulinian fathers), Sunday Rogate (dedication day of the Franciscans) and the day of St John. In the late 15th century, the town tried to raise its markets to large international fairs after the example of Leipzig. A privilege was granted in 1497; the New Year's market was moved to the period between 9 and 19 December and the Walpurga market to Friday after Ascension Day. Further extensions came with the market privilege of emperor Maximilian in 1505, when both fairs were extended to 10 days and the New Year's market moved to the day after the Immaculate Conception. However, the great ambitions were never realised, and the three large fairs were reduced to 6 days again in 1521, with the Ascension Day market being moved to two weeks after Easter.
Toll_Description: A ducal toll in Braunschweig on foreign commodities sold in town is first mentioned in 1204. If the commodities were transported through town without halt, the merchant did not have to pay; if he stopped and rested only half of the toll. The tariffs were specified in the toll regulations around 1300. Since the mid-14th century the toll was pawned to the town authorities, and completely acquired by them in 1412 and 1428. Extensive toll tariffs and other regulations date from 1503, 1548 and 1597. The toll booth was located directly west of the town hall of the new town; payment of the toll was controlled at the nine town gates.

Name: Breda
Settlement_Description: Breda is first mentioned in a sixteenth-century copy of a document dated 1152. Core of the settlement used to be around the current Vismarkt and Havermarkt next to the harbour, as the location and orientation of the Grote Kerk still attests.  A chapter is founded in 1309.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted ca. 1198-before 25 February 1212 by Godfried II, lord of Breda and Schoten.
Fair_Description:
In 1290 'cauchidegeld' is known: levied to maintain the roads from incoming wagons, horses and cattle. In 1355 the magistrate obtained from the lord of the town the right of the weighhouse and the hall for the butchers near the corn-market . A tariff (called 'oude caerte') of the exises is dated 1397 and edited. Here a.o. a wine-crane is mentioned and 'caudsidegeld' levied from horses. An edited tariff dated circa 1436 from the lord of Breda for his toll levied on land and on water names 'weggeld' (tax on road) levied from incoming or outgoing traffic at the Gasthuisgate, toll from cattle and gooses and from ships. Then two fairs are found: with Bamis (Oct. 1) and Sinxen (Pentecost). Another tariff of cauchide is also edited and dated 1467 and concerns also the toll and 'weggeld' (tax on roads). Steenbergen, Oudenbosch, (Oud-)Gastel, Van der Hoeven, Loenhout and Hoogstraten had a special tariff in the marktets. Loenhout and Hoogstraten had to pay all three taxes if they just passed through Breda on their way to Holland with goods. In the Meierij van Den Bosch were freed from tolls except during the markets: Den Bosch, Eindhoven, Oorschot, Beke, Helmond, Tilburg, St. Oedenrode, Oosterwijk, Oss en Waalwijk. A third edited tariff dated circa 1475 also concerns the weighhouse, measures ('maten' from a.o. coal, salt and grain) and the crane.
From 1313 at the latest Breda had two fairs. One of which was the Sinxenmarkt, for two weeks starting the day after Pentecost. The Sinxenmarkt continued to be held at least up to 1756. The other is the Bamismarkt, which was held for two weeks after the holy day of saint Bavo on the 1st of October. The Bamismarkt stopped being held in 1653.
Toll_Description:
An edited tariff from the toll belonging to the lord of Breda levied on land and on water dated circa 1436 notes that there is only a single toll in the Land van Breda, one preferably paid in Breda itself but which also had two outposts in Gilze and in Baarle. Those from the Land van Hoogstraten had to pay watertoll for what they got from outside the Land van Breda en transported through it. Those from the Meierij van Den Bosch and from Bergen op Zoom were freed from this toll but had to pay 'weggeld' (tax on the roads). Those from Antwerpen had to pay this toll but who lived inside the 'borcht' (the old town?) not. Those from Turnhout, Weelde and Poppel had to pay toll for the 'houtscat' (wood) and other goods they exported from the Land van Breda.

The toll must have predated Breda becoming a city. Furthermore, the location of the toll was probably the Tolbrug over the Mark, which would likely have extracted a toll from both foot traffic and ships that passed it.

In 1581 Breda obtained a privilege of Philip II that it became a free city (like Tienen, Diest, (Zout)Leeuw en Nijvel) and never again had to contribute to the toll of Brabant,
Staple_Description: In 1355 magistrate and inhabitants of Breda obtained from the lord of the town the right called 'opslag' (storage of goods) in the freedom of the town. In 1397: in the parish. In 1404: in the Land van Breda.

Toll_Description:
An edited tariff from the toll belonging to the lord of Breda levied on land and on water dated circa 1436 notes that there is only a single toll in the Land van Breda, one preferably paid in Breda itself but which also had two outposts in Gilze and in Baarle. The toll must have predated Breda becoming a city. Furthermore, the location of the toll was probably the Tolbrug over the Mark, which would likely have extracted a toll from both foot traffic and ships that passed it.

In 1581 Breda obtained a privilege of Philip II that it became a free city (like Tienen, Diest, (Zout)Leeuw en Nijvel) and never again had to contribute to the toll of Brabant,
Staple_Description: In 1355 magistrate and inhabitants of Breda obtained from the lord of the town the right called 'opslag' (storage of goods) in the freedom of the town. In 1397: in the parish. In 1404: in the Land van Breda.

Name: Bremen

Settlement_Description: Around 780, there existed a settlement at the riverfront at the current street Tiefer at the shore of the Weser river, as well as a religious (episcopal) centre on a river dune.
Town_Description: The settlement acquired market, justice and mint privileges in 965. The first city wall was built after 1030 and a council is first mentioned in 1225. Older town privileges were confirmed by archbishop Gerhard I in 1217. It became an important trading city and member of the Hanse. The town expanded on the southern shore of the river after 1623, but more for defensive purposes than because of lack of space, as the Neustadt ('new town') remained sparsely populated for a long time.
Fair_Description: The fairs in Bremen went back at least to the market privileges of 965, probably even into the 9th century. The oldest fair took place in Autumn, to which a second Spring fair was added in a privilege of 1035. These two fairs both lasted a week and remained in place - with various alterations in the dates throughout the years - until 1638. In that year, the Spring fair was replaced by two three-day fairs, on Quasimodogeniti and Ascension Day; the Autumn market was prolonged to nine days. In the same 1638 privilege, four new horse fairs were installed.
Toll_Description:
Various tolls were levied in the city of Bremen, of which the oldest have their roots in the toll rights of the archbishop from 888. The town levied tolls at each town gate, which were leased to Johan Cruse in 1373, who in return had to maintain the stone road from St Ansgar's bridge to St John's chapel. (Bremer UB III:431). Excluded was the toll on the Weser bridge, which was owned by the count of Hoya.<br/>
The Akzise, import and export duties, accounted for about 86% for the entire income of the city in 1600. Moreover, from 1426 onwards a buoy toll ('tonnengeld') for maintenance of the traffic signs on the lower Weser river, a tidal area, was levied for each incoming and outgoing ship. Responsible for the levying of the latter toll were the eldermen of the common merchant. Akzise and Tonnengeld registers are extant from the year 1532 onwards (StAB, 2-R.2.A.o.2.b.).
Staple_Description:
First signs of a staple can be found in the town rights of 1303/8, but only in 1360, a request from Lübeck shows that Bremen had installed a corn staple. In 1376, citizens of Hannover were allowed to ship all commodities freely, except corn, of which a third part had to be sold in Bremen. The town laws of the "Kundige Rolle" (1450, 1498) contain a three-day staple obligation for commodities coming from the sea and wood coming down the Weser, as well as a prohibition of the trade between non-citizens.<br/>
Complaints from Minden on the Hanseatic Diets in 1506, 1507 and 1511 show that the staple could not be fully enforced. In 1541, the emperor confirmed the staple obligations, but revoked the charter in the same year. Minden citizens were exempted from the Bremen staple in 1552, but from 1611 there were renewed attempts to enforce the staple towards Minden merchants. The "Weddeordnung" of 1612 prohibited merchants from neighbouring towns to transport herring, butter, fish, tar, fish oil, tallow, corn, wine, beer and other commodities through Bremen. The staple was abolished with the "Weserschifffahrtsakte" of 1823.

Name: Wrocław
Settlement_Description: NULL
Town_Description: NULL
Staple_Description: In 1274, Henry IV of Silesia limited the staple for entire Silesia to Breslau; confirmed 1409. However, most of the times the staple was difficult to enforce due to conflicts with Poland. An agreement between Frankfurt (Oder) was made in 1490, that merchants were only allowed to cross the Oder at Frankfurt or Breslau. The Enforcement of this agreement was complicated by counter-measures of the Polish king. Merchants from Poland, Russia, Prussia, Lithuania and Masovia were prohibited to trade further than Frankfurt and Breslau in 1507. The staple of Breslau was confirmed by the Emperor 1510, but the following Polish trade boycott forced the city to refrain from its staple rights between 1515 and 1530. The staple disappeared at the end of the 18th century.

Name: Brugge
Alternative_Name: Brvggas; Brvccia; Bruggis; Bricge; Brycge; in Brugghen; bi Brigghe; Bruges; Brügge
Settlement_Description: A castle was built as a defence against the Normans by count Baldwin of Flanders or his predecessor around 840-875. A settlement developed with a harbour on the sea inlet Sinkfal (later Zwin). It is called "portus" and "oppidum" in the 10th and "colonia" in the 11th and early 12th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges ('keure') were granted by count William of Flanders on 6 April 1127. The city developed into one of the primary economic centres of northwestern Europe in the 13th to 15th century.
Fair_Description: On 14 August 1200, Bruges became one of the five grand fairs in Flanders. The fair started on Sunday after Easter and lasted a month. In the 14th century it gained prominence among the fairs in Flanders and became an important international exchange venue. In 1508/'9 (Jan.) emperor Maximilian and archduke Charles granted a free fair starting January for six weeks.
Toll_Description: The most important toll in Bruges was the comital toll on shipping on the Zwin sea inlet. Citizens of the city were temporarily exempted in 1127. After the closing of the Zwin in Damme in 1180 and the silting of the waterway, the toll was primarily levied at the outports Damme, Monnikerede, Hoeke, Mude and Sluis (see there). Pawn tariffs from the late 15th and early 16th century show the decline of trade on the Zwin. Moreover, there also existed a large and a small toll in the city, of which the former was levied on long-distance trade and the latter was a local toll on produce from the surrounding region to supply the city. Citizens from Bruges were exempted from all tolls in Flanders in 1302. The oldes toll-account is dated 1553/4, the next one  only 1606 and later.
Staple_Description: First privileges of the low German merchants in Bruges date from 1252. The ordinance of the aldermen from 1285 forces citizens to bring all cloth from within a range of 3 miles around the city to Bruges. 1309: Staple for wax, furs, copper and other commodities. The general staple was confirmed by Count Louis II in 1323, with the exception of dried fish, corn, salt, pitch, tar and shipbuilding materials, which are also allowed to be unloaded in Damme, Houcke and Monikerede. Exclusive staple for English wool in 1340-1353. A Hanseatic residence ("Kontor") was established in 1347. During conflicts, the Hanseatic staple was moved to Dordrecht in 1358-1359 and 1388-1392, and to Bergen op Zoom (for wool) in 1388-1392. In the 14th century, Bruges had growing problems in enforcing the staple, in favour of the cities Sluis, Antwerp, Middelburg, Utrecht and Amsterdam. In 1530, the Hanseatic Kontor was finally moved to Antwerp, leaving only a staple for Spanish wool (established in 1490, confirmed in 1531 and 1540) in Bruges.

Name: Burg (bei Magdeburg)
Settlement_Description: The origin of the place lies in an early medieval settlement, probably from the time of Henry I. In the 10th century there was a castle guard and a settlement in close proximity. First written mention in the foundation of the bishopric of Brandenburg, when its tithe mentioned as belonging to St. Moritz' monastery in Magdeburg.
Town_Description:
Town hall and marketplace point towards a trading enclosure, which probably held town rights from the beginning. Dating based on the emergence of the "jus Burgense" in the middle of the 13th century. Revisions of the town rights e.g. 1474, 1558, 1576 and 1598.

Since 1262 Burg had purchased a freedom of tax and trade in Magdeburg.
Fair_Description: The first market privilege was granted in 1562, with fairs on the Assumption of Mary and St Dionysius. Another fair was added between 1635 to 1657 on Simon and Juda's day.
Toll_Description: In 1489 the town of Magdeburg complained to the escort  ('Geleitsmann') of Burg that safe conduct fees had been collected from two citizens, even though they were supposed to be exempted from such payments. The toll station of Burg is also mentioned in 1493.

Name: Celle
Settlement_Description: Mentioned at the old location Altencelle as early as 983. The town was moved to the present location in 1292.
Town_Description: Celle was moved from its previous location at Altencelle ('old Celle') in 1292, and received the Lüneburg town privileges; in 1301 those of Braunschweig. Celle was the principal residence of the Dukes of Lüneburg between 1433 and 1705.
Fair_Description: In 1353, three three-day fairs are mentioned in Celle: on Sunday before St Walpurga, St Maurice and Sunday before St Martin. The fair of St Maurice is moved to the Sunday after the Ascension of Mary in 1412.
Toll_Description: Land and water toll and safe conduct of the dukes of Brunswick--Lüneburg. The toll in Celle is already mentioned in the town privileges of the Braunschweig borough ('weichbild') Hagen in the early 13th century as the only toll at the waterway between Braunschweig and Bremen. Toll registers are available from 1379, see Peters 1913. Name: Chemnitz
Settlement_Description: The name is derived from a river, at which shore a Benedictine monastery was founded in 1136. A river crossing on the old road to Bohemia existed there. First mentioned in a charter when market privileges were granted in 1143.
Town_Description: Urban character after 1170. From 1254 and in 1308 Chemitz had margravial Meißen town law. The town prospered from 1470 by the growth of mining activity in the Ore Mountains.
Toll_Description: A pavement toll and transit toll was levied on salt wagons in 1431. A regulation of safe conduct from 1551 is known (SHStA Dresden, Loc. 37864, Augustusburg Nr. 5, Erbbuch des Amtes Schellenberg 1551, p. 588–596b.)

Name: Coburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1056. The settlement was founded as planned town around the beginning of the 11th century next to the older settlement Trufalistat. It is located at an old road from Bamberg to Frankfurt. A new castle was constructed around 1200.
Town_Description: In 1331 Coburg was granted Schweinfurt rights and an own jurisdiction. Since 1540 residence of the dukes of Saxony-Coburg-Gotha.
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct from 1492 describe the extent of the safe conduct in Coburg as well as the fees that were due. A cart had to pay 9 pennies, a Jew on foot 24 pennies and a horse 1 pound and 6 pennies. The income from these fees belonged to the toll collector, whereas the fees for wagons and their cargoes and wagoners belonged to the territorial lords.

Name: Gdańsk
Alternative_Name: Danzig; Dantzig; Gothiscandza; Gyddanycz; Kdanzc; deutsch Danzk; Dancek; Danczik; Gedanum; Dantiscum; Danseke
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 997 as fishing village and castle of the princes of Danzig. The castrum Gdansk was mentioned in 1148 as a settlement belonging to the castle; a market settlement of German merchants is attested in 1178.
Town_Description: Prince Swantopolk (1220-1266) granted the German town law to the market settlement in 1224. Lübeck town law was granted in 1263, Magdeburg town law in 1295, Kulm town law in 1343. The settlement was first mentioned as a "civitas" in 1236.
Staple_Description: The origins of the Danzig staple are unclear, but in 1411, the staple was moved temporarily to Elbing by Grand master Heinrich von Plauen (HR I, 6 n 12). Apparently, the staple system of Elbing collapsed in favour of Danzig around 1400. In 1425, Danzig declared that it wanted to construct a building where guests could offer clothing. From 1441, there are clear attempts to force merchants to offer their commodities on the market, and in 1451 and 1482, Polish and Lithuanian merchants complained about the prohibition of trading between non-citizens. After Danzig was confiscated by Poland (1454), King Casimir confirmed the prohibition to travel between the sea and the hinterland without a stop in Danzig. In 1584, the staple for English cloth was moved to Elbing; in 1628, Danzig regained the exclusive import rights on foreign cloth.

From 1441, there are clear attempts to force merchants to offer their commodities on the market, and in 1451 and 1482, Polish and Lithuanian merchants complained about the prohibition of trading between non-citizens. After Danzig was confiscated by Poland (1454), King Casimir confirmed the prohibition to travel between the sea and the hinterland without a stop in Danzig. Name: Delft
Settlement_Description: Delft is first mentioned in a 1420 copy of a document from the period 1130-1157. It originated near the court of a count. A hospital is first mentioned in 1252. A breadhouse and a meathouse were granted by the count in 1295. A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1316 (an old and a new one in 1334), a weighhouse in 1342. The 'scroede ambocht' also mentioned in 1342 indicates that there was a crane.
Town_Description:
Delft was granted town privileges on 15 April 1246 by William II of Holland. Cox argues that Delft already was a town-like community before that time, as the grant is the result of an initiative by towndwellers.
One of the smaller ‘Kamers’ (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Delft.
Fair_Description:
The town-privilege of 1254 mentions two fairs: with St. Odulphus (June 12) and the other without a date (in 1316 with St. Gillismis: Sept. 1). The marketfield is found in 1315 and then property of the count. In 1436 it is granted to the town. In 1405 merchants of Delft are first found on the fairs of Frankfurt.
A manual from the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 with a calendar of many horsefairs mentions the horse-fair in Delft on June 9. In 1580 king Philip II granted a seed-fair starting August 25  for 6 days. The mayors said that Rotterdam recently obtained a seed-fair starting August 12. The seed was desended from Overmaas and the isle of Overflakkee and because of this the trade in Delft was halved.
Dated circa 1594 a tariff for the horse- and dairyfair is preserved. Merchants from Flanders, Henegouwen, Brabant, Zeeland, Gelre, Gulik and 'Zuidholland' (the region around Dordrecht) are found in it. The towns and villages in 'Noordholland' (present Zuid-Holland above the Meuse) are free but had to give 1 groot for wax and toll-letter. Waalwijk was freed by trial but also had to pay 1 groot for wax. Permission from the comital audit-office had to be obtained to start the horse-fair two days earlier (3 days before Odulphusday: June 11). The date was now five days before St. Oel (Olevaer? July 29). This had to be published in almanacs, as the horse-fair in Haastrecht hampered the one in Delft too much. For the St. Gillisfair (Sept. 1) or dairy-fair a tariff  is registered. The toll-keeper was situated outside the Ketelgate to collect the 'keizersmarktgeld' (market-toll of the emperor) of butter and cheese.

Name: Dessau
Alternative_Name: Dessau-Roßlau; Dissowe; Dessouwe; Dessowe; Dessow; Dessaw
Settlement_Description: In the Early Middle Ages Dessau probably was a Wendish fishing village. First mention in a record in 1213. Dessau was a market place in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Since 1382 Dessau was referred to as town and was granted Magdeburg rights. An exact date of the awarding of the town rights is not known.
Fair_Description: A third fair is prevented in the town of Dessau in 1573 due to protests of Leipzig.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct was calculated by the horses that pulled a wagon. If someone had loaded herrings and crossed the Mulde river, this person had to pay an additional fee per ton of herring. In 1549 four road tolls and safe conducts are mentioned and the former method of raising fees confirmed.
Staple_Description: Each raft loaded with lumber or planks had to anchor on the Elbe river at Dessau for "three sunshines". In 1549 this staple right is mentioned again in the regulations of safe conduct.

Name: Deventer
Alternative_Name: Dauentre; Deuentre; Dauentria; Davantria; Devendre; Daventre
Settlement_Description: Deventer was founded as a Carolingian missionary centre at a river crossing by St Lebuinus before 774. As such it is first mentioned in the <em>Vita Ludgeri</em> from 840-849 (in a copy from around 1000). In 877, it is called "portus" (a settlement with a harbour).
Town_Description: In 956, Deventer is called a town ('urbs'); in 960 Deventer is called a 'civitas'. In 1123, Holy Roman Emperor Henry V granted a privilege to the town ('stad') of Deventer. Successive bishops of Utrecht will probably have granted additional town privileges which resulted in the town privileges granted to Zwolle in 1230.
Fair_Description: At least from 1340 onward, four fairs were organized in Deventer. One around St John in the summer (24 June), one around St Jacob (25 July), one around St Giles (1 September), and one around St Martin and St Lebuinus (11 and 12 November). Name: Diest
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 837.
Town_Description: NULL
Toll_Description: A toll and tax called 'doorgang' (passage through) is found since 1423. This was probably levied from oxen and cattle. In 1467 the bailiff (schout) of Diest was ordained by the duke of Brabant to prevent evading this toll in Brabant.
Staple_Description: Lier was already reconfirmed in its privilege for a cattle-staple in Brabant in 1469 by duke Charles the Bold. But was opposed by Diest in 1475, who said to have the oldest oxen-fair. In 1477 the duke of Gulik informed Kampen that the oxen-fair in Diest was restored and that safe-conduct was given. In 1485 the staple was moved to Diest by Maximiliaan but in 1498 Lier won a lawsuit. In 1503 Diest granted safe-conduct for merchants with cattle from Deventer, Kampen, Zwolle and other inhabitants of the Oversticht, although Lier tried to prevent that. Den Bosch also opposed the market at Lier at least since 1555.

Name: Döbeln
Settlement_Description: Castle and adjoining settlement of the 10th century, first mentioned in 981.
Town_Description: The town was founded shortly after 1200.
Fair_Description: In the 16th century, there was a cattle market in Döbeln, which held some meaning for the Middle German region as well as the Erzgebirge. Toll_Description: A toll in Döbeln is first mentioned in 1445. The town council bought the toll in 1460.

Name: Dordrecht
Alternative_Name: Thuredrith; Thuredrit; Thuredrech; Durthric; Thurdrecht; Durdreth; Dordreth; Dordreecht; Dojrdre
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Dordrecht dates from 1064, in a falsified copy from the first quarter of the twelfth century. The next mention dates from about 1151-1155.  A chapter in the church is known for the years 1367-ca. 1572.
Town_Description: Dordrecht was granted town rights in July 1220 by William I, count of Holland. However, it is probable that Dordrecht already held town(-like) privileges before 1200. In 1200, Dordrecht is mentioned as 'oppidum' and as 'stede'.
Fair_Description:
A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1310. In 1331 a fair of lord Daniel (van der Merwede) in his manor in Dordrecht is found with St. Bonifatius-eve (June 4). The duration of this fair is found in 1560: 8 days between St. Bonifatius (June 5) and St. Odulphus (June 12). Since 1424 this was combined with a toll, excises and market-stalls.  This was a fief held from the lord of Voorne and since 1371 from the count of Holland.
In 1342 (Nov. 26) count Willem IV granted the town two fairs, each for 14 days with report of the taxes to be paid by the merchants. The dates: 1) 26st day after Easter when people sing: 'Resurrexstio Domini' and 2) 10th day after St. Bavo (Oct. 1) with preservation of the rights of the lord Van der Merwede. In 1379 (Oct. 18) duke Albrecht ordained that the Bamisfair was moved to the first Friday after St. Victorsday (Oct. 10) as there were problems with the visit of merchants on the 'toog'-(display)days before the Bamisfair (possibly regarding the Bamisfair of Antwerp). In 1414 (Sept. 3) duke Willem stated that Dordrecht would be exempt of tolls on all fairs. In 1404 merchants of Dordrecht are first seen on the fairs of Frankfurt.
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships is first mentioned in 1220, but is probably older.  In the oldest list of fiefs of count Floris V dated 1282-'84 the 'Hulctol' is found (a hulk is a seaworthy type of ship), fief of the lord of Wassenaer. In 1289 (March 1) he gave this toll to the town of Dordrecht. Afterwards this toll is unknown. Exemption from tolls for Easterlings in 1313 who brought their wares directly to Dordrecht; preferable tariffs for Hanse merchants in 1358 and between 1388-1392 while the Kontor in Bruges was displaced. A tariff for merchants from Prussia and Westfalen is dated 1340. A general tariff is preserved and edited for the years 1356-1358, accounts of the toll for the years 1380-1385. A list with exempt places, abbeys and convents at the tolls of Dordrecht and Geervliet is s.d. (first half of 16th century). A special account for all imported wines is dated 1565/6.
Staple_Description:
Count John of Holland established a staple market for oats in 1298, which was extended to all commodities on Merwede and Lek in 1299, confirmed in 1304. From 1388 compulsory market for all ships coming from the east to the Maas. Staple for Rhine whine of eight days in 1324, which became a general wine staple in 1401. The staple obligations became hard to enforce after the St Elizabeth's flood (1421), after which Dordrecht became located on an island, making it easier to bypass the city. In 1441, commodities coming downstream with destinations elsewhere had to be transferred to other ships, but did not have to be offered for sale any more. Hanseatic staple for Rhenish wines in 1452, together with Antwerp. Staple for wine and salt for Holland and Friesland in 1453. In the 16th century, there were growing conflicts with other cities about the staple, which led to Middelburg being freed from staple obligations in Dordrecht in 1533. The staple was still confirmed by the emperor in 1540, but restricted in the following year: only corn, legumes, salt, wine, lime, coal, millstones and iron transported on Lek, Merwede and Maas had to be brought to Dordrecht. Despite ever growing conflicts and violations of the staple, it remained in place until 1670.
In 1377 it was ordained that all peat dug in the Grote Waard had to be traded at the market in Dordrecht. In 1442 the same was stated for all dairy-products from Zuidholland. In 1520 the socalled 'Octrooi Serviel' was granted by king Charles V which caused that of the remaining 40 villages around the town in Zuidholland after the St. Elisabethsflood, 25 were forced to market their agricultural products in Dordrecht, the other 15 only had to pay excise of beer and were obliged to help deepen the harbour in Dordrecht. In 1553-'57 a trial layed by the other towns in Zuidholland (Schoonhoven, Gorcum en Rotterdam) and some local lords against this market-right was pending but in 1562 it was lenghtened for another 25 years. In 1589 however it was abolished.

Name: Tartu
Settlement_Description: The Russians conquered the Estonian settlement in 1030. The castle was then expanded. In 1224-34 the German conquerors built a new castle that served as the centre of the diocese.
Town_Description: In 1248 the town received Riga town rights and also became a member of the Hanseatic League.
Staple_Description: A privilege of King Sigismund III from 1562 obliged every Russian travelling on his way to Livonian ports to offer his wares for sale in Tartu for four days. Foreign merchants wishing to trade in Russia were not allowed to travel further than Tartu.

Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 880 and 890. The origins of the settlement are unknown. 939 it is called 'urbs' and in 979 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: The exact date when the town was established is unknown, because a town fire in 1231/32 destroyed the relevant charters. In 1236 Emperor Frederick II confirmed the old privileges, which are believed to have been issued between 1138 and 1152. The town is first mentioned as a Free Imperial City in 1232 and was an important member of the Hanse.
Fair_Description: In 1232 King Henry VII granted Dortmund a second fair next to the already existing one from Ascension Day until Pentecost. The new fair took place on 14 days after St Michael's Day (29 September).
Toll_Description:
Both the county of Dortmund and the city of Dortmund levied a land toll in 1074. In 1241, half of the fees and the county itself, then in 1431 completely, fell to the town of Dortmund. According to the tariffs of 1330/40, fees were only levied in February and from the end of March to the end of April. 1330/40 resulted in a tariff of 4 pfennigs per wine carriage (detailed tariff: RÜBEL, Urkundenbuch II, no.
456). In 1390 an annual yield of 9 marks 10 shillings, in 1391 one of 10 marks and 7½ shillings and in 1392 one of 11 marks and 12 pfennigs could be achieved. For further yields see source.

Name: Dresden
Settlement_Description: The town developed from a Sorbian port settlement; by c. 1150 there was fortress with a settlement.
Town_Description: Niemeyer dates the town’s foundation to 1200/1210; town fortifications existed in 1216. Today’s Dresden-Neustadt to the north was buit in the 17th century.
Toll_Description: A toll in Dresden is first mentioned in 1343. Probably this was only a toll on the land road, not on river traffic. The regulations of safe conduct recorded in 1716 are a copy of the regulations from 1547. They also include land and water safe conduct regulations from 1630.
Staple_Description: In 1455, Elector Frederick II of Saxony moved the staple right of Brüx (Most), which had been conquered by Bohemia, to Dresden. Salt, fish, honey and other commodities which were transported through Saxony to Bohemia, had to be offered for sale in Dresden. However, enforcing merchants to travel through Dresden proved to be difficult, and the road via Freiberg was still often used. The staple was confirmed in 1603, with special mention of corn and wood for the supply of the town.

Name: Duisburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement dates back to Roman times. Later it was a Frankish royal residence, which was first mentioned when it was plundered by Vikings in 883. It was enlarged to a royal palace in the 10th century.
Town_Description: Due to its location on the Rhine, Duisburg developed rapidly into a merchant centre that developed into a town in the 12th century. A privilege from 1129 to quarry stones for construction works in town still refers to the settlement as 'villa'. In 1145 a community of citizens is mentioned, and a document from 1165 implies that the settlement had become an Imperial Town. After the Rhine changed its course after 1200 and the Rhine arm on which Duisburg was located silted up, the town gradually lost its position as primary trade centre. Moreover, the town lost its status of Imperial town and became subjugated to the count of Cleves in 1290.
Fair_Description: Emperor Frederick granted two 14-day fairs on St Bartholomew (August 24) and Mid Lent (Sunday Leatare) in 1173. The fair of St Bartholomew was moved to Orsoy in 1428. Before 1276 there were three fairs, on Palm Sunday, August 29 and December 21. In 1577 three horse fairs were granted. A weekly market on Friday-Sunday is mentioned in 1408.
Toll_Description:
1) A river toll on the Rhine was levied here from 1184 to 1348/52. The toll changed hands frequently. Until 1248 it was held by the Empire, from 1248 to 1280 by Duke Walram of Limburg, from 1280 to 1288 by Count Renald of Geldern and from 1290 by the Count of Kleve. In addition, a (fair) market toll, which also applied to ships, has been documented since 1065. The Rhine toll was transferred to Kaiserwerth in 1348 by Count Gerhard von Berg. At the same time, the Count of Kleve continued to levy toll until he moved it to Büderich in 1352. The tariff in 1348 was 6 Turnosgroschen. 

2) A land toll was also levied from 1280 onwards.
Staple_Description: Uncertain: a "jus stapulae" in Duisburg is first mentioned only in 1708, when it is moved to Wesel because of changes in the course of the Rhine. A charter of Duke Walram IV of Limburg from 1273 allows citizens of Cologne to transport their commodities unhindered through Duisburg, indicating that the town already claimed some kind of staple privileges in that period.

Name: Düsseldorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1135
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by the counts of Berg in 1288.
Fair_Description: Duke William of Jülich and Berg granted Düsseldorf a fair on St Albin's day (22 June) and a weekly corn market on Wednesday in 1482.
Toll_Description:
1) The Duke of Berg levied a river toll on the Rhine in 1374/77. In 1380, 6 turnosgroschen were collected per foder of wine. In 1386, it was 12 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine. For more detailed tariffs and yields, see source. In 1427 the annual yield was about 6782 gulden, in 1428 about 4810 gulden and in 1429 5507 gulden.

2) In 1398/99 the Duke of Berg levied a fee for free conduct on the river. Rates and revenues have not been preserved.

3) The duke also levied a land toll in 1476. 

4) In 1395 he levied a road toll. One shilling had to be paid per carriage with heavy goods such as wine, fish or cloth.

1) The Duke of Berg levied a river toll on the Rhine in 1374/77. In 1380, 6 turnosgroschen were collected per foder of wine. In 1386, it was 12 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine. For more detailed tariffs and yields, see source. In 1427 the annual yield was about 6782 gulden, in 1428 about 4810 gulden and in 1429 5507 gulden.

2) In 1398/99 the Duke of Berg levied a fee for free conduct on the river. Rates and revenues have not been preserved.

3) The duke also levied a land toll in 1476. 

4) In 1395 he levied a road toll. One shilling had to be paid per carriage with heavy goods such as wine, fish or cloth.

Name: Eilenburg
Alternative_Name: Hilburg; Ihleburg; Ileburgh; Ilburch; Ilberc; Illeburck
Settlement_Description: In the 10th century a castle was built that was mostly destroyed during a Slavic uprising. The settlement at the castle, however, remained. It is already referred to as town ('urbs') in 981.
Town_Description: The acquisition of town rights probably occurred at the beginning of the 13th century.
Fair_Description: Over decades the town of Eilenburg requests a second fair, but always fails due to the resistance of Leipzig. The date of the first fair is unknown.
Toll_Description: An uncommonly detailed regulation of safe conduct lists the toll on the transportation of several commodities in 1524 (ThHStA Weimar, Reg. Cc 676, Geleitsrechnung Eilenburg 1524/25, p. 2–6.).

Name: Eindhoven
Alternative_Name: Endehouen; tEndouen; Eyndoven; Endoven; Eyndhoven; Endehoven
Settlement_Description: Assumably, Eindhoven was founded between 1212 and 1232. The first mention of Eindhoven can be found in a sixteenth-century copy of a document dated 1232.
Town_Description: Eindhoven was granted town rights in 1232 by Henry I, duke of Brabant. Eindhoven was surrounded by a stone wall and had a moat.
Fair_Description: In 1232 or 1233 Eindhoven obtained the right for a weekly market from te duke of Brabant. Before 1340 Eindhoven had a fair and a cloth-hall, in 1340 a weigh- and meat-house. In 1419 three fairs and a weekly market are mentioned. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Eijndoven' then has five fairs: 1) first day after 'Jaers'-day (Jan. 1), 2) first Tuesday before 'Pallemen'-day (Sunday before Eastern), 3) Tuesday before Sacraments-day (Friday after Eastern), 4) first Tuesday after St. Jacobs-day (July 25), 5) first Tuesday after the Sunday before festum nativitatis Mariae (Sept. 8). In 1572 the town had a weigh-house for butter.

Name: Eisenach
Settlement_Description: Eisenach develops from a market village which lay at the roads called the "Long Hessians".
Town_Description: In 1189 the settlement was referred to as civitas; town development was probably connected to the construction of the Wartburg. The ladgraves of Thuringia boosted town development since the 12th century; long distance trade destination since the 13th century; from 1384 to 1387 the town rights are written down and collected in the "Eisenach lawbook" ('Eisenacher Rechtsbuch').
Fair_Description: Around 1300, there were three fairs in Eisenach, although it can be assumed that the fairs were established earlier. In the regulations of safe conduct of 1517/18 four fairs are mentioned.
Toll_Description: In Eisenach, a toll and a fee for overland safe conduct ('Feldgeleit') was due, which was determined by the mode of transport and the amount of the load. (ThHStA Weimar, Reg. Bb 1237, Rechnung des Amtes Eisenach 1517/18, p. 1–7.)
