Name: Lutherstadt Eisleben
Alternative_Name: Eisleben; Isileiben; Islebe; Islevo; Ysleiben; Eißleben
Settlement_Description: First mention between 780 and 802. In 994 the market borough ('Marktflecken') earned market-, coin- and tollrights.
Town_Description: Around 1180 mentioned as civitas. In 1286 the town wall is mentioned in a record. Around 1500 a new town is established.
Fair_Description: In 1522 Leipzig complained about the fairs ein Eisleben, who claimed that the fairs there would benefit Leipzig, since wares in Eisleben had to pass through Leipzig first. They had also owned their fairs since 100 years already. In 1690 the fairs on the Sundays Reminiscere, after St. Viti, St. Gallus and St. Mauritius were moved to the following tuesdays.
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct of the counts of Mansfeld

Town_Description: A town was founded by the Teutonic order in 1237, Lübeck merchants settled there, the town was granted Lübeck town law by Wilhelm von Modena in 1240, but the documents do not survive, the eldest copies are from between 1263 and 1267, a handfast from 1246 granted restricted Lübeck town law, but it was extended in 1288, 1339 and 1343, the municipal ordinance made it an official town in 1808 and again later in 1853
Staple_Description: The staple existed already in 1388, when it was confirmed that the town was the only import harbour for english cloth; English merchants were only allowed to buy corn and wood from Prussia and Poland in Elbing. The staple was expanded in 1393 to include the export of corn, malt, tar, pitch, ash, tin, lead, timber and wood from the entire region between the Vistula and the Curonian Lagoon. Soon after, the entire system must have collapsed in favour of Danzig: in 1411 the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order moved the staple of Danzig temporarily to Elbing. A request of Elbing to instate a staple on the Diet of Prussian estates in 1440 shows that by that time, nothing was left of the Elbing staple.

Name: Emden
Alternative_Name: Emathae; Amatha; Amuthon; Amethis; Emethen; Emutha
Settlement_Description: Emden arose from a Frisian trading settlement, where a Carolingian missionary church was erected around 800.
Town_Description: While Emden was occupied by Hamburg in 1433-1439 and 1448-1453, the settlement acquired urban character and institutions. However, town privileges were never granted.
Fair_Description: In 1440, it is first mentioned that fairs were organised in Emden. In 1497 they were specified as two eight-day fairs, taking place eight days before Laetare Sunday and eight days after St Michael.
Staple_Description: The staple right was officially granted in 1494, but already practised in times that the town was controlled by Hamburg (1433-1439, 1448-1453). Merchants from Groningen were initially freed from staple obligations in Emden, but the 1483 prohibition to export corn, butter and cheese from East Frisia was also strictly implemented towards Groningen. Under Count Edzard of East Frisia in 1506-1514, Groningen merchants were privileged again. Emperor Charles V removed the Emden staple in favour of Groningen in 1548, but it was still practised, and his successor Ferdinand I declared Charles's decree invalid in 1558. In the following years, Emden's staple was acknowledged by Hamburg, Osnabrück and Münster. Emden was staple port of the English Merchant Adventurers in 1560-1564, 1580-1587 and 1599-1602. The staple was practised without many conflicts until the 1680s, afterwards often restricted and finally abolished in 1765.

Name: Emmerich
Alternative_Name: Emmerich am Rhein; Embrici; Emberic; Eymerich; Emmerik; Emmerick; Emericke
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 828. A cloth-hall is first found in 1353.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in 1233. A town council is mentioned in 1316, a burgomaster in 1334.
Fair_Description: In 1294 two fairs are mentioned: 1) Sept. 14 and 2) Nov. 1. Before 1450 three fairs are mentioned, next to Sept. 14 (duration 7 days) on Sunday after June 24 (3 days) and on Oct. 28 (2 weeks). In 1450 the September and June fairs were relocated to Apr. 26 (duration 3 days) and June 6 (7 days). Weekly markets from Tuesday to Thursday and Friday to Sunday are mentioned before 1233.
Toll_Description: The monastery of St. Maria in Utrecht levied a river toll on the Rhine here in 1318. A toll was mentioned for the first time as early as 1142. This was probably a market fee. Fees on river and land traffic, documented in 1233, were also market-related. In 1324, a preferential tariff of 4 pfennigs per foder of wine applied to citizens from Duisburg. A right and tariff dated 1393 with the freedom of Nijmegen was confirmed, which was also valid for the other towns of Gelre. Free were goods owned by citizens on their own or foreign ships, foreign goods on these ships were taxed. It states further that Cologne, Neuss and Kaiserswerth are free 'upverdich' (upstream) but not 'uytverdich' (downstream). Dusseldorf, Uerdingen, 'Berck' (Rheinberg), Dorsten, Recklinghausen, Dortmund, Soest and  the 'Mercksen' towns are not free. Towns of old belonging to Gelre and Kleef situated between Roer and Linge are free. Tiel and Grave as not of old belonging to Gelre and Duisburg and Culemborg are not free. Wesel, Kleve and Xanten are half free, but should not be as they were not of old belonging to Kleef. In 1436/37 the annual yield was about 650 gulden, in 1489/90 579 gulden. Accounts are preserved and partly digitised for the years: 1436/7, 1489/90, 1493/4, 1495-1507, 1509, 1511, 1515, 1522, 1533, 1626-29, 1636. The river toll was moved to Schenkenschanz around 1635.

Alternative_Name: Emmerich am Rhein; Embrici; Emberic; Eymerich; Emmerik; Emmerick; Emericke
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 828. A cloth-hall is first found in 1353.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in 1233. A town council is mentioned in 1316, a burgomaster in 1334.
Fair_Description: In 1294 two fairs are mentioned: 1) Sept. 14 and 2) Nov. 1. Before 1450 three fairs are mentioned, next to Sept. 14 (duration 7 days) on Sunday after June 24 (3 days) and on Oct. 28 (2 weeks). In 1450 the September and June fairs were relocated to Apr. 26 (duration 3 days) and June 6 (7 days). Weekly markets from Tuesday to Thursday and Friday to Sunday are mentioned before 1233.
Toll_Description: The monastery of St. Maria in Utrecht levied a river toll on the Rhine here in 1318. A toll was mentioned for the first time as early as 1142. This was probably a market fee. Fees on river and land traffic, documented in 1233, were also market-related. In 1324, a preferential tariff of 4 pfennigs per foder of wine applied to citizens from Duisburg. A right and tariff dated 1393 with the freedom of Nijmegen was confirmed, which was also valid for the other towns of Gelre. Free were goods owned by citizens on their own or foreign ships, foreign goods on these ships were taxed. It states further that Cologne, Neuss and Kaiserswerth are free 'upverdich' (upstream) but not 'uytverdich' (downstream). Dusseldorf, Uerdingen, 'Berck' (Rheinberg), Dorsten, Recklinghausen, Dortmund, Soest and  the 'Mercksen' towns are not free. Towns of old belonging to Gelre and Kleef situated between Roer and Linge are free. Tiel and Grave as not of old belonging to Gelre and Duisburg and Culemborg are not free. Wesel, Kleve and Xanten are half free, but should not be as they were not of old belonging to Kleef. In 1436/37 the annual yield was about 650 gulden, in 1489/90 579 gulden. Name: Erfurt
Settlement_Description: Erfurt developed at the site of a ford ('furt') in the Gera river. The area was already settled in the Palaeolithic. In the 8th century centre of a Catholic bishopric, as well as Carolingian royal court ('Pfalzort'), it is first mentioned in 742.
Town_Description: Erfurt appears as trade centre in 805 and had urban characteristics since the 10th century. Expanded into a town since the early 12th century; in 1167 it is referred to as civitas. A university was founded in 1392.
Fair_Description: Erfurt hosted two large international fairs, the first of which was a four-week spring fair after Misericordia Domini granted in 1331. A second fair of three weeks on Trinity Sunday was added in 1473. Both fairs were reduced to two weeks in 1497. Additionally, Erfurt held several free markets which were less prestigious than the large fairs.
Toll_Description: Merchants from outside Thuringia hat to pay a fee of 4 pennies for wagons and 2 pennies for carts for entrepot ('Niederlagegeld') in Erfurt in 1289. They had to pay the same fee when they loaded their wares again. The transit toll was probably higher. Around 1495 the fee of entrepot had been changed to a fee of 6 pennies for every entrepot and wagonload of every foreign trader. The toll was paid in the toll station on the cathedral plaza. Regulations of safe conduct from 1315 and 1441 (in a copy from 1533) remain.
Staple_Description: The town legitimised its staple policy by the capitulary of Charlemagne of 805. It exercised a toll policy with staple characteristics in the law ('weistum') of 1289, to which later prescribed roads for the East-West-traffic between the Thuringian Forest and the Harz were added. The staple was abolished with the instalment of a staple in Leipzig in 1507, which led to resistance in Erfurt. The town tried to regain its staple in vain until the 17th century. Weight ordinances from 1631 and 1738 show that the town exercised a limited staple policy, in the sense of a pre-emptive right by its citizens.

Toll_Description: Merchants from outside Thuringia hat to pay a fee of 4 pennies for wagons and 2 pennies for carts for entrepot ('Niederlagegeld') in Erfurt in 1289. They had to pay the same fee when they loaded their wares again. The transit toll was probably higher. Around 1495 the fee of entrepot had been changed to a fee of 6 pennies for every entrepot and wagonload of every foreign trader. The toll was paid in the toll station on the cathedral plaza. Regulations of safe conduct from 1315 and 1441 (in a copy from 1533) remain.
Staple_Description: The town legitimised its staple policy by the capitulary of Charlemagne of 805. It exercised a toll policy with staple characteristics in the law ('weistum') of 1289, to which later prescribed roads for the East-West-traffic between the Thuringian Forest and the Harz were added. The staple was abolished with the instalment of a staple in Leipzig in 1507, which led to resistance in Erfurt. The town tried to regain its staple in vain until the 17th century. Weight ordinances from 1631 and 1738 show that the town exercised a limited staple policy, in the sense of a pre-emptive right by its citizens.

Name: Essen
Settlement_Description: A first mention around 870 is debatable. Around the middle of the 9th century, bishop Altfrid of Hildesheim founded a women's monastery, around which the settlement developed.
Town_Description: A civic community appears in a charter from 1244, in which permission is granted to fortify the town. However, the town never became completely independent from the monastery.
Fair_Description: Abbess Theophanu of the Essen monastery received the right to hold a one-week fair on the feast of St Cosmas and Damian in 1041. By the 13th century, the fair had been reduced to two days and was overshadowed by the fair on St Kilian, the dedication day of the Münster church, and in the 14th century by the August market around the Assumption of Mary. Name: Flensburg
Alternative_Name: Flensborg; Flensborgh; Flensaburgh; Flensaaburgh; Vlensborch; Flenßburg
Settlement_Description: A permanent settlement with an urban character developed around the Church of St. John in the 12th century, probably around 1150. Flensburg benefited from its location in the bottom of Flensburg fjord near Hærvejen/ Ochsenweg.
Town_Description: Around 1190 a Saint Canute Guild (Danish: Sankt Knuds Gilde) in Flensburg was taken under royal protection, and at this time Flensburg must be considered as a town. Flensburg is mentioned in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in 1231, and the town was granted a town law in 1284 by Duke Valdemar IV. It was confirmed by Duke Eric II in 1314. At this time a town council had also been established. A Franciscan monastery was founded in 1263. In the early 15th century a royal castle, Duborg, was built northwest of the town as part of the ongoing conflict between Denmark and different counts of Holstein. The town wall is probably from the middle of the 14th century, when Flensburg was in the hands of count Nicolaus of Holstein. Throughout the late medieval period and in the early modern era Flensburg played an important role in the export of oxen from Denmark.
Toll_Description: Probably first mentioned in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in 1231. Tolls on different goods are mentioned in 1300. Citizens from Flensburg were exempted from the toll in 1337 and 1354. The toll was probably mainly levied on ships that visited the harbour of the town. Lists of toll tariffs exist from 1314, the 14th century, 1480 and 1594. Throughout the middle ages and the early pre-modern period Flensburg was an important toll station.
Harbour_Description: A natural harbour located in the bottom of Flensburg Fjord. From the 13th century onwards one of the most important ports in Denmark. Wharf in the bottom of the fjord in the medieval period. The port of Flensburg was central to trade between continental Europe and the Baltic Sea.

Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 794 in a document of Charlemagne. In 815 it became a the seat of a Carolingian royal palace. A Celtic settlement is said to have existed way before, which was conquered by Germans and was inhabited by the Romans in Augustan times.
Town_Description: A market town developed around the second half of the 12th century. It was mentioned as "oppidum" in 1142, and as "civitas" in 1226. In 1372 it became a free imperial city.
Fair_Description: The fairs in Frankfurt are first mentioned in 1227. They became large international fairs, attracting visitors from as far as France, Flanders, northern Italy and northern Germany. In 1240, Emperor Frederick II granted safe conduct for visitors of the fairs. The exact dates of the fairs were first mentioned in 1349. The oldest one was the Our Lady's or autumn fair ('Frauenmesse'); in 1330 a Lent fair was added.

The oldest one was the Our Lady's or autumn fair ('Frauenmesse'); in 1330 a Lent fair was added.

Name: Frankfurt (Oder)
Alternative_Name: Frankfurt a.d. Oder; Vrankenuorde; Frankinfurd; Frankenuorde uff der Odir; Frankenfordt; Frankenforde; Franckfurth
Settlement_Description: A marketplace existed (perhaps from 1226) in the vicinity of the Church of St Nicholas before the settlement’s foundation as a town in 1253.
Town_Description: Town foundation and provision of town rights by Margrave John I of Brandenburg in 1253.
Toll_Description: In the town privileges of 1253, Margrave John I also installed a toll in Frankfurt, which was levied on land and water traffic. Exact toll tariffs are registered in a town register of 1516.
Staple_Description: The mention of the staple in the foundation charter of the town from 1253 is probably a later addition. A privilege by the Margrave of Brandenburg from 1351 limited the land and river traffic to routes through Frankfurt; other river crossings were prohibited. A treaty with Breslau from 1490 limited the crossing of the Oder by merchants to Breslau and Frankfurt, but proved difficult to enforce because of Polish counter-measures. In 1507, merchants from Poland, Russia, Lithuania, Masovia and Prussia were prohibited to trade further than Frankfurt and Breslau. The staple privileges were confirmed in 1510 and 1512, but could not be reinforced in the wake of the collapse of the staple of Breslau in 1515. However, both staples were reinstated in 1530 and confirmed in 1555, 1624 and 1643. The street via Landsberg was not allowed to be used by transit traffic. The prohibition of shipping on the Oder South of Frankfurt from 1459 was cancelled in 1555 for salt transports; all other commodities had to be transported on the land route. The staple was abolished in 1752, having been reduced to a monopoly on the linseed trade.

Name: Freiberg
Settlement_Description: The place grew out of the village of Christiansdorf; after the laying down of old town in 1170, the town developed into an important trading and mining town in the high medieval period.
Town_Description: The old town probably received its market, town and mining rights when it was founded in 1170; rights renewed at the end of the 13th century and 1433. From 1223 the term ‘civitas’ is used.
Fair_Description: Margrave Henry III of Meißen granted a 14-day fair to Freiberg in 1263.
Toll_Description: The toll and safe conduct of Freiberg came into possession of the town council in 1323.
Staple_Description: The staple of Freiberg is first mentioned in 1381. The foundation of the Dresden staple led to conflicts with Freiberg about bypassing Freiberg (1466). The staple was confirmed by the Elector of Saxony in 1470.

Name: Gent
Alternative_Name: Gandensis; Ganda; Gandauum; Ganth; Gend; Ghent; Gand;
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in first quarter of the eighth century in a tenth-century copy.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description:
Around the year 1000 a fair with St. Bavo (Oct. 1) is known. Probably this fair was much older. It lasted al least till 1199. Possibly it was first organised outside the city-walls near the St. Baafs abbey. In 1199 market-tolls are levied at the Brabant-gate, at the Drongen-gate, at the bridge near St. Jacob, the socalled 'Wasselintol' and inside the center of the town.
In 1453 (Oct. 13) duke Philip the Good granted two fairs of each 14 days during 7 year with Lent and in the beginning of August, while paying him 1/4 of the excises.
Staple_Description: In 1251, a staple between Aardenburg and Ghent was prohibited. It was prohibited to manufacture cloth within five miles of Ghent in 1314; in 1338 to trade woad within the same area, and yarn within three miles. A corn staple was introduced in 1343, whereby half of the corn from the region around the city had to be stored within the town. Conflicts with Ypres because of the corn staple were solved in favour of Ghent in 1424, and it was further enforced in 1484. Further fixation of the grain stapel in 1484: a quarter of the corn shipped through the city and all corn grown in Flanders had to be offered to the local population for 8-14 days. In 1486 and 1514, the staple was reiterated. The forced offering of commodities for sale was abolished in 1540, but in in its place came a forced transshipment between Scheldt and Leie, and in 1547 for the Sassevaart. The staple was reinstated in 1587, with the exception of all commodities intended for personal use of the merchants.

Further fixation of the grain stapel in 1484: a quarter of the corn shipped through the city and all corn grown in Flanders had to be offered to the local population for 8-14 days. In 1486 and 1514, the staple was reiterated. The forced offering of commodities for sale was abolished in 1540, but in in its place came a forced transshipment between Scheldt and Leie, and in 1547 for the Sassevaart. The staple was reinstated in 1587, with the exception of all commodities intended for personal use of the merchants.

Name: Gorinchem
Alternative_Name: Gornichem; Gurinchem; Gorichem; Ghorchem; Gorckum; Gorchvm; Gorcom; Gorkum; Ghorinchem; Goerinchem
Settlement_Description: Gorinchem is first mention about 1200 (document is fourteenth-century copy). In the thirteenth century, it was a trade settlement near a castle. A chapter in the church is found in the years 1378-1572.
Town_Description: Gorinchem was granted town privileges on 11 November 1382 by Otto, lord of Arkel. A hospital is first mentioned in 1321. During the reign of William VI, count of Holland (r. 1404-1417), the castle near Gorinchem was demolished and a smaller castle was built in the town itself.
Fair_Description: Before 1382 already six fairs exists, including a cloth-fair, a cattle-fair and a horse-fair. A tariff dated 1387 for the watertoll of the fair with 'Sinxen' (Pentecost-fair) is edited. A tollregister dated early 16th century with the market-tolls on the Maas mention: 8 days before Pentecost during 14 days with a tariff. In 1553 five market-tolls are found (together 30 pound worth) and a watertoll on the river Merwede (46 pound) (to compare: the combined toll on sailing ships of Gorinchem and Schoonhoven with its outposts is then farmed for 12500 pound). In 1565 the second horsefair starts the first Tuesday in Lent, duration 4 days with freedom equal to the first fair. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mention a horse-fair in Gorinchem on July 5 in a calendar of many horse-fairs. In 1580 (August 24) king Phliip II granted a free horse-fair on 28/29 September with two days before and after freedom as a compensation for the heavy burdens of the war and the cut dikes. In 1596 there are nine fairs: 1) a horsefair starting the first Tuesday in Lent, duration: 4 days, 2) Midlent starting Friday before Sunday when people enter the Holy church, till the end of May, duration 2 weeks, 3) Pentecost starting the third Friday before that, duration 2 weeks, 4) horsefair starting the third day of July on St. Maartensday-eve translation (July 3), duration 4 days, 5) horsefair on Sept. 28 and 29 with St. Michelseve (Sept. 29) starting, except on Sunday, duration 2 marketdays and 2 days before and after, 6) Bamis (Oct. 1) 2 weeks starting the Friday before Bamis, 7) Thursday after St. Victor (Oct. 10?) a cattle-fair starting the Tuesday before the Thursday, duration 4 days, 8) cattle-fair with All-Saints starting the Friday before, duration 2 weeks, 9) cloth-fair on Monday after St. Maartensmis (Nov. 11), duration 6 days starting the Saturday before the Monday.

Name: Görlitz
Alternative_Name: Goreliz; Yzhorelik; Gorliz; Zgorliz; Gorlizc; Zhorjelc
Settlement_Description: By the 11/12th century there were boroughs with a Bohemian castle. Previously settled by Slavs, it was an important junction for long distance trade.
Town_Description: The old town was laid out around 1200, and expanded with the addition of a new town around 1250.
Staple_Description: A staple for woad was granted in 1339 and confirmed in the Golden Bull of 1356, but was probably enjoyed earlier. Woad traders in the Margraviate of Bautzen needed to travel through Görlitz and were not allowed to bypass the city. In a settlement of 1340 the length of the staple right was set at four weeks.

Alternative_Name: Gosleri; Gosilare; Goslaria; Gozlare; Gosler; Gosseler; Goselare; Goslarie; Goßlar
Settlement_Description: Founded by king Henry I around 922; first mentioned in 1005.
Town_Description: The development of the market town Goslar was driven by the exploitation of the Rammelsberg mines. Goslar already had town-like characteristics in the 11th century. Official representatives of the market settlement are mentioned in 1108, and it was characterised as "civitas" in 1131. The first town right exists from 1320, which codified the privileges granted by Emperor Frederick II in 1219. Goslar became Free Imperial City in the first half of the 14th century.
Fair_Description: It is known that fairs were organised in Goslar, for example in 1429, 1444 and 1466, but dates are not known before the 16th century. Only in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) from 1598 two fairs are mentioned in Goslar, on Sunday Jubilate and Holy Innocent's Day.

Name: Gotha
Settlement_Description: The existing settlement became a royal court in the 8th/9th century, which owned a castle in the 11th centruy; because of its advantageous position in the traffic network the settlement developed into a market village, which mostly traded grain in the 16th century.
Town_Description: Around 1168 Gotha was owned by the landgraves of Thuringia, who promoted road construction. Awarding of town rights probably around the end of the 12th century (1180/1189). Gotha had Gotha Eisenach town rights.
Fair_Description: The toll- and regulations of safe conduct from the 16th century mention fairs in Gotha, during which the toll is doubled.
Toll_Description: Toll- and regulations of safe conduct remain for the town of Gotha from the 16th century (ThStA Gotha, Kammer Stadt Gotha 66 Nr. 222).

Name: Gouda
Settlement_Description: Gouda was first mention in a (+/-) 1420 copy from a text dated 1143. It originated from a castle. In the eleventh and twelfth century, cultivations ('ontginningen') took place on the banks of the River Gouwe close to this castle. A port was constructed after 1250, after which Gouda grew into an important trade settlement.  A hospital is first mentioned in 1315.  A weighhouse and cloth hall are mentioned in 1356.
Town_Description: Gouda was granted town rights on 19 July 1272 by Floris V, count of Holland. In the 1350s, fortifications were added to the town.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Gouda are first mentioned in 1336 and 1356, taking place on St James's and St Lambert's Day. In 1381 they were characterised as horse and cloth markets. In 1501, the two fairs on St James and St Matthew were extended from three to six days. In 1505 a third fair was added on Saturday after Letare. A market toll was levied during market times, since 1410 only from horses. A tariff levied of old dated 1436 (June 6) is edited. In it several ship types are found, wagons and horses and barges from the Sticht (of Utrecht) and Gelre. The account of the comital steward of Gouda dated 1446 states that exempt of the market-tolls are citizens of Gouda, Schoonhoven, Middelburg, Goes, Schiedam, Woudrichem, Montfoort, Eethen en Meeuwen in Brabant and all people living in the socalled Blois territory. In 1465 Vlissingen, Tholen and Zierikzee are added. Citizens of Gouda were since 1407 (as a reward for the support to the count in his battle with the lord of Arkel, like many other towns in Holland and Zeeland) exempt of market-tolls levied in Woudrichem, Heusden and Middelburg. Heusden is not found in the list of exempt places on the fairs in Gouda. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions horse-fairs in Gouda on Febr. 11 and March 11 in a calendar of many horse-fairs.

Name: Greifswald
Alternative_Name: Grifeswold; Gripeswold; Gripheswald; Gripeswald; Grifeswolde; Gripeswalt; Gripeswald
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed around saltworks that were first mentioned in 1193, since 1209 owned by the Cistercian monastery Eldena.
Town_Description: A market settlement is attested in 1241, mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1248. Wartislaw III of Pomerania granted Lübeck town privileges in 1250.
Toll_Description: The toll existed in connection to the staple.
Staple_Description: A staple in Greifswald is granted by Barnim I of Pomerania in 1274. At its confirmation in 1361, it was defined that all inhabitants of Pomerania who shipped corn or other commodities on the Peene through Wolgast or to Anklam, Gützkow or Ueckermünde, were obliged to offer their commodities on the Greifswald market and pay the toll there.

Name: Groningen
Alternative_Name: Groningi; Groniggea; Groninga; Groningon; Grvoningen; Villa Cruoninga; Groninghe; Groninge
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1040.
Town_Description: Groningen was never officially granted town rights by a land lord. However, Groningen had several town-like features and developed into a town between the eleventh and thirteenth century. By the thirteenth century the town was already walled ('ommuurd'). The earliest document from a city government dates from 14 November 1245.
Fair_Description:
Possibly from the twelfth century onward, a 'vrijmarkt' took place in the town of Groningen around the Feast of Saint Otger (10 September). In 1250 a flowering horse-fair is mentioned in a chronicle of the convent Bloemhof at Wittewierum. In 1434, five additional fairs were instituted: on Laetare Sunday, Quasimodo Sunday, Saint Vitus (15 June), Saint James (25 July) and Assumption of Mary (15 August). In 1436, another fair was instituted on Saint Michael (29 September). 
From 1446 onward, cloth merchants were allowed to sell their goods for a longer period in the cloth hall, namely one day before and two days after the market day, except during the 'vrijmarkt' around Saint Otger. It is not clear whether this held true for all other markets. The 'vrijmarkt' was extended during the sixteenth century, until it lasted until the 2nd of October. In 1609, the duration of this fair was limited to 7-13 September.
Toll_Description: A toll on oxen en horses was collected at the Poelepoort. First known yields in the oldest preserved city-account dated 1526/'7. Unknown when it was installed.
Staple_Description: From 1430 onwards, the town attempted to dominate the economy of the Frisian coastal area between Ems and Lauwers. It acquired full staple privileged for all commodities from the Ommelanden and a beer monopoly in 1500. This led to conflicts with Emden and Appingedam, which organised fairs. The States General recognized the forced offering of commodities for sale on the market in 1559, but the duration was limited to one or two hours. In 1599, all foreign commodities except horses and cattle were exempted from staple obligations. For domestic commodities, the staple obligations existed mainly for corn, butter and cheese. The staple is still mentioned in 1649, but seems to have collapsed shortly afterwards.

Name: Großenhain
Alternative_Name: Ozzec; Hagen; Indago; Hayn; Hayn ober Elbe; Großen Hayn
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortress and settlement in place before its foundation in the 12th century as a fortress of the margraves of Meißen.
Town_Description: Town foundations laid down around 1200; development into an important weaving town by the 15th and 16th centuries. Town privileges confirmed in 1464.
Fair_Description: In 1545 Leipzig protests against a new fair in Großenhain. The town's council answers that it wasn't aware of a new fair and the other fairs had been held since the olden times.
Toll_Description: A toll of the Margrave of Meißen in Großenhain is first mentioned in 1323, as well as in in 1399 and 1404. Safe conduct of the Duke of Saxony is mentioned in 1490. Extensive regulations of safe conduct remain from 1547 (SHStA Dresden, Loc. 40 085, Hain Nr. 116 b, Erbbuch des Amtes Großenhain 1547, p. 731–780v).
Staple_Description: Staple for woad in the duchy of Saxony, granted in 1477. The rival Görlitz succeeded in repressing the staple rights for ten years, but staple was reinstated in 1490. Only woad that was unsold after four weeks could be taken onwards to Görlitz. In 1523 the council of Großenhain decided that only one quarter of the woad should be offered for sale in their town; the staple was intensified in 1592 and 1607.

Name: Den Haag
Alternative_Name: Haag; 's-Gravenhage; The Hague; Haghe; Die Haga; Hagen; Die Haghe; Haga; 's Graven-Hage; 's Gravenhage
Settlement_Description:
The earliest mention of 's-Gravenhage dates from a 1390-copy of a 1242 document. The settlement orginated in the vicinity of the court of a count. Although the government of the settlement has town-like features and 's-Gravenhage is sometimes even considered a town by contemporaries, it is only elevated to town rank on 25 November 1806 by Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland.
A chapter in the church is found in the years 1367-1572.
Fair_Description:
In the comital account of 1334 market-tolls are found. In the account dated 1343/'4 the toll of 'St. Katrijnenmisse' (Catharina) is mentioned (Nov. 25). In 1407 count Willem VI replaced a fair from July 25 juli to May and granted a free horse- and cattlefair in May during 14 days. Right (tariffs) and freedom should be as in Delft.
In 1537 a new 'wagenveer' (location for carts with regular destinations) was made at  the St. Anthonisbridge (Wagenstraat), previously this was at the Voorhout. Here wagons from Delft, Rijswijk and Voorhout were found. In 1562 a toll with a tariff was installed to finance the costs for the pavement of the Noordeinde. Toll was levied from wagons and carts belonging to fishermen and merchants from Amsterdam, Hoorn and Enkhuizen and those from the 'Zijde' (the fishing villages at the Noordzee). Fish, game and poultry was transported to Brabant, Luik, Maastricht and Cologne. 
In 1581 (Jan. 8) (or 1580 Dec. 28?) admission for a fair of horses, cattle and other goods was obtained. Date: 8 days before Mayday, duration 14 days. The fair of 1406 (sic: 1407) and other privileges were decayed because of the Guelders and had long not been organised. As a result of the war there was poverty. The fair was granted on the same date. In 1597 (March 15) the Estates of Holland gave permission to organise the horse- and cattle-fair after the horse-fair of Valkenburg.

Name: Haarlem
Alternative_Name: Haralem; Harleim; Harlem; Herlehe[m]; Harlehem; Harlhem
Settlement_Description: Haarlem is first mentioned in an eleventh-century copy of a document dated 918-948. Haarlem became situated at the crossroad of several trade routes and gained importance as an military-strategic location. A hospital is first mentioned in 1282.
Town_Description: Haarlem was granted town rights on 23 November 1245 by William II, count of Holland.
Fair_Description:
A toll levied at the fair with St. John (June 24) is found since 1267. A detailed right granted for 10 years (in order to strengthen the town) by count Floris V regarding traded and self produced goods is dated 1274 (Dec. 13). In it cloth from abroad, imported wine and beer from Bremen are found. In 1355 (Sep. 11 sep.) duke Willem V granted a fair wit St. Luke-eve (Oct. 17). The duration of this fair in the 15th century is 14 days. In 1387/8 three fairs are mentioned, only one is dated then: on St. Peter and Paulsday (June 29). In 1558 it is called a oxen-fair on October 10. In the period 1374-'93 the count of Blois owned the market-tolls and a tariff dated circa 1372 is preserved. In it 'gordelgeld' and 'roertol' (ruddertoll) are levied from anybody living south of the river Meuse or in Zeeland or outside Holland. Dordrecht only had to pay halff of both. The fair would be as free as the fair of Daniël van der Merwede in Dordrecht, except for all corn which was for the bailiff and court of justice. Afterwards the fairs are registrated in the comital accounts of the steward of Beverwijk (formerly in the Blois period the steward of the 'Wijk'), e.g. in 1456/'7 with St. John midsummer and St. Luke.
In 1508 (Oct.) Maximiliaan of Oostenrijk granted a free horse-fair to compensate the heavy duties of the war. The town asked for three fairs each of 3 or 4 days. Granted were two fairs: 1) 29-31 Jan., 2) 29-31 May, with 6 days before and after for a secured travel to the town. The right would be as in Delft, Gouda, Alkmaar a.o., who had obtained this right earlier. This market however, according to the comital accounts, decayed already in the twenties.
Staple_Description: Haarlem tried, after complaints of towns in the Baltic about the quality of the herring, since 1514 to establish a staple for all exported herring catched by Rotterdam, Schiedam, Vlaardingen, Delfshaven, Den Briel, Goeree, Bommenee and other places. All herring should first be packed and marked in Haarlem, like was the case in Dordrecht and Antwerp. In 1516 (April 26) king Charles granted this staple. Furious protests followed by Delft, Leiden, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Schiedam and places in Waterland and Westfrisia. This matter continued till after the death of Margaretha of Oostenrijk (1530) and even then was still undecided.

Name: Halberstadt
Alternative_Name: Alfurtested; Halverstad; Halverstede; Halberstadensis; Alberstetensis; Halverstidensis; Halverstidi
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 781 and became seat of a bishop in 827. Mint, market and toll rights were granted in 989.
Town_Description: In 1105, the bishop confirmed the "iura et statua civilia". Court, police and administration emerged during the following years. In 1184 Halberstadt already adapted the town rights of Goslar. In the first third of the 13th century the first council forms after several conflicts with the episcopal town lord. 1241 a town hall is mentioned for the first time.
Fair_Description: In 989 emperor Otto III. grants market privileges to the settlement.

Name: Halle (Saale)
Alternative_Name: Halle a.d. Saale; Halle an der Saale; Halle/Saale; Hall in Sachsen; Halla; Hal
Settlement_Description: Numerous prehistorical finds are witness to an early settlement of the region. Mention of castle "Halla" on the eastern bank of the Saale in 806, its location is not known. The second mention of Halle in 1064 indicates a growing independence from Giebichenstein, the former political centre. A market settlement developed in the 11th century around the booming saltworks.
Town_Description: Town privileges after the fashion of the Magdeburg town law must have been granted before 1170. First explicit referral to the settlement as a town in 1177. It only received a full autonomous town status in 1310, but lost part of its autonomy after the archbishop conquered the town in 1478 and made it his residence.
Fair_Description: A fair in Halle is first mentioned in 1128. Probably this was the fair on the Nativity of Mary, which is mentioned a century later. A second fair on New Year's Day appears in 1464 during a conflict with Leipzig about conflicting fairs.
Toll_Description: The archiepiscopal coin and toll were moved from Giebichenstein to Halle around 1064. The monastery Paulinzella was exempted from the salt toll in Halle in 1154, in 1176 the Merseburg monastery of St Peter and one year later the entire diocese of Merseburg. In 1281 the town acquired the income from the tolls. The toll was levied at the town gates, as mentioned in 1182. Escorts ('Geleitsmänner') are attested at the Steintor and Galgtor gates in 1499.

Name: Hamburg
Alternative_Name: Hammaburg; Hammenburg; Hamborch; Hamburgum; Hammonis castrum; Hammonia; Hamborg
Settlement_Description: Precarolingian refuge fort of the Saxons north of the Elbe, bishopric since 831, archbishopric since 834. A market settlement outside of the fortress is first attested in 845.
Town_Description: The archiepiscopal old town (Altstadt) became a town no later than the mid-12th century. The new town (Neustadt) was founded by Duke Adolf III of Schauenburg and received Lübeck town privileges in 1188. Both parts were united around 1215.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Hamburg was the market of St Felicianus in the old town, which probably went back into the 11th century. The town privileges of the new town from 1188 mention two fairs on St Vitus and the Assumption of Mary. In 1365, emperor Charles IV founded a large three-week Pentecost fair, which was not well received and cancelled in 1383, five years after his death. An eight-day horse fair was founded on the Sunday after Lent in 1435, four additional four-day horse fairs were added in 1471: on three weeks before Sunday Estomihi, Sunday Oculi, Palm Sunday and All Apostles' Day.
Toll_Description: Four tolls existed in Hamburg:<br/>1) the Count, Priest or Schaumburg toll of the territorial lords was first mentioned in 1188 and in 1460 half went to the Danish royal house and from 1640 in its entirety. The levying of the toll was, however, in the hands of the town, to whom it was regularly pawned. Payment of the toll was handled at the town gates and at the harbour entrance; merchants from Bremen, Brandenburg, Meißen, Magdeburg, Braunschweig and Saxony were exempted.<br/>2) The Werkzoll, first mentioned in 1309, was raised by the council of Hamburg to finance navigation beacons for the isle of Neuwerk and the Lower Elbe; it was privileged by the Emperor in 1628. It has been mentioned that the toll was originally levied at the island of Neuwerk in the mouth of the Elbe itself, but this was probably an attempt by the city of Hamburg to legitimise its staple claims for the entire Lower Elbe river. <br/>3) A toll for securing the sea lanes from pirates and robbers was raised as a pound toll first in 1362, then from 1424 with some breaks until 1528. From 1541 the toll was raised in cooperation with Lübeck; in 1552 the toll was imposed unilaterally by Hamburg and converted into a grain toll after complaints from Lübeck in 1557. After the foundation of the Admiralty in 1623 a new toll for the defence of the sea lanes was introduced, which was almost exclusively levied on the shipping with Portugal and Spain.<br/>4) The Land and Elbe toll for trade heading inland by both water and land; toll records are edited by Pitz. Registers from the Land and Elbe toll and the Admiralty toll have survived from the 17th century; they were partly assessed by Reißmann. Pound toll records from 1485-6 have been edited as well.
Staple_Description: First attempts to establish a staple can be seen in the toll tariffs of 1236, where it is recorded that merchants were exempted from toll payment when they offered their commodities for sale on the market in Hamburg. In the following centuries, ever more trade limitations were taken; the town law of 1458 first contained an obligation for merchants to offer butter, cheese, fish and corn for sale on the local market for three days. The staple was confirmed by king Christian I of Denmark in 1480 and by the emperor in 1482. Merchants from Brandenburg were exempted from the staple between 1518 and 1555, but had to sell 2/3 of their grain in Hamburg afterwards. A threat for the staple was posed by the possible circumvention of town via the southern Elbe arm, which Hamburg tried to prevent from the 14th century. This led to conflicts with Brunswick-Lüneburg, Stade and Buxtehude in the 16th and 17th centuries. Despite a verdict of the imperial chamber court from 1619 that traffic on the southern Elbe should be free, the emperor confimed the staple privileges in 1621, and in 1628 Hamburg's control over the southern Elbe as well. After the mid-17th century, the staple was ever more difficult to enforce and finally abolished in 1748.
Harbour_Description: Until the construction of a new crane on the inner harbour in the 16th century, the only crane was that on the square adjacent to the town hall. This crane is first mentioned in 1291, but was probably older. Lighter boats transported commodities to here from the larger sea-going ships in the lower and inner harbours.

Name: Hameln
Alternative_Name: Hamelo; Hamelon; Hamala; Hamalam; Hamelensibus; Hamelensis; Hamele; Hamela; Hamelen; Hamelenses; Hameluncus; Hammelen; Hamelin; Hamlen; Hamelowe
Settlement_Description: Hameln, which consisted of more than one settlement, is first mentioned in the 9th century, but was considerably older.
Town_Description: A planned town with Minden town privileges was founded around 1200.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Hameln are first mentioned around 1240, among others on St Peter and Paul's Day. In the oldest town register from ca. 1350, three fairs are mentioned: on St Boniface, St Michael and "tho der hoighen kerkemisse", probably on All Saints' Day. The dates were changed in 1556: the St Michael and All Saints fair took place on Monday after the feast days, and the fair on St Boniface was replaced by two new ones, on Monday after Letare Sunday and on the second Monday after Trinity Sunday.
Staple_Description: In practice, there existed a forced transshipment in Hameln for a long time because of the barrier of the Hamelner Loch (see harbour). A formal staple right, however, is first attested in 1627, and it is uncertain whether it was ever really enforced.

Name: Hamm (Lippe)
Settlement_Description: After the nearby castle and town of Nienbrügge were destroyed, Count Adolf von der Mark founded a settlement in "Hamm" in 1226.
Town_Description: Since its foundation, the settlement has been mentioned as an 'oppidum' and 'civitas' and got Lippstadt rights approved in 1279.

Name: Hannover
Alternative_Name: Hanabruinborgar; Hanofra; Hanovere; Honovere; Honnovere; Honouir; Honover; Hanover; Hoenover; Hannouer
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1150; there are traces of permanent settlement from ca. 1000. The settlement was fortified in the second half of the 12th century.
Town_Description: Hannover developed into a town in the 1230s; the Minden town privileges were confirmed in 1241.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Hannover are first mentioned in 1399, taking place on the feast of St James and Maundy Thursday. According to a 1444 letter from Hildesheim, there also existed a fair of St Simon and Jude at the time, which was to be replaced by a fair on St Walpurga and the day before and after, with the addition that no other free fair was to take place in Hannover. St Walpurga's fair is mentioned again in 1453, when Hildesheim complained about hindrance of their citizens during the said fair. However, in 1445 there is also mention of a fair of St Giles in Hannover.
Toll_Description: Next to a market toll, which was levied by the duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, there existed a transit toll for the town area. This belonged to the duke as well, but in practice it was levied by the town authorities since 1293, who in return acquired part of the revenues. In the middle of the 15th century, the toll was acquired by the town; customs for many commodities were raised around the same time.

In the middle of the 15th century, the toll was acquired by the town; customs for many commodities were raised around the same time.

Name: Harderwijk
Alternative_Name: Harderewich; Herderewich; Harderwyc; Herderwick; Harderwike; Herderwich; Herderwig; Harderwyck
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1231, when Harderwijk received town privileges. A dispersed agrarian settlement is known from the 12th century.
Town_Description: At the end of the 12th century, large floods had created the Zuiderzee and Harderwijk became located on the sea shore, leading to its rapid development as a harbour town. Town privileges were granted on 11 June 1231, by Otto II, count of Guelders and Zutphen.
Fair_Description: In 1294/95, Harderwijk had one fair on Pentecost. In 1424, the town received a second fair held from Sunday Reminiscere to Laetare Sunday. An urban degree from 1431 ordained that merchandise coming to this fair was free of paying toll. At least around 1524, there was an additional oxen fair on October 6th.
Toll_Description:
Toll had to be paid on land and water. 
An urban degree from 1431 states that people from Frisia, Hattem, Staveren, Sloten en Kuinre did not have to pay land toll (‘weggeld’). The same was applicable to ‘those of whom the aldermen of Harderwijk knew that they were free of charge’. The latter phrase was also mentioned for shipping tolls. A degree of 1437 stated that beasts from people from Frisia were free of charge, just like ‘sleden’ (sledges). The tariffs on land and water ordained in 1431 can be found in Berns’ edition of the urban degrees.
Staple_Description: A renewed privilege in 1443 for a fish staple in Harderwijk for all fish brought ashore between Muiden and Kampen was given by the duke of Guelders as a reaction on the fish staple of Naarden in Holland from 1442. However, there is no evidence that a formal fish staple existed before that year, although there was a fee levied on fish brought ashore ('numeratio piscium'), which was given to the town council by the count in 1302. A tariff exists from 1431. The staple had only limited success, as the revenues from the fish trade declined after 1442.

Name: Helmstedt
Settlement_Description: A missionary church was founded around 800 near the village Helmonstedi (first mentioned in 802), which developed into the Benedictine St Ludger monastery. The later town developed around the current market place in the 12th century. West of it, the monastery of Augustinian Canonesses Marienberg was founded in 1176. Between the monastery and the walled town, the planned suburb Neumark was located, which is first mentioned in 1249.
Town_Description: Helmstedt is first mentioned as "civitas" in 1228. Town privileges were confirmed in 1247.

Name: 's-Hertogenbosch
Alternative_Name: Herzogenbusch; Den Bosch; nouo opido super siluam juxta Orten; noua civitate apud Siluam; silua iuxta Orten; Orten que nunc Silua dicitur; Busco ducis; Boscho ducis; sHertoghen bosche; super Silvam juxta Orthen; de Orthen cum Buscho; van Ordunen, dat men nu seegt Bossche; Bussche; Sylvaducis
Settlement_Description: 's-Hertogenbosch is first mentioned in 1185.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in May 1195 by Henry I, duke of Brabant. In 1363 the king of Denmark granted Den Bosch a 'vitte' (trading-post) situated at Schonen (most southern point of Sweden) in the Baltic, with rights as Kampen.
Fair_Description: On the market-place opposite of the town hall was a hall where a cloth-hall (first mentioned 1287), meat-hall (1310) and a bread-house (till 1339) are found. The weigh-house (1299) was situated next to the town hall. The cattle-market must date before 1200 but is ony found in 1464. The fishmarket is mentioned in 1299. In 1374 inhabitants of Den Bosch are first present on the fairs at Frankfurt. In 1403 (Sept. 25) duchess Johanna granted two new fairs. Dates: 1) Monday after Midlent for 3 days, safe-conduct: Saturday before to the Sunday after the fair, 2) day after St. Bartholomeus (August 23) and two days after that, with safe-conduct till St. Gillis-eve (August 31). The duchess would collect the tolls. In an excise-ordinance dated 1444 two new fairs are mentioned. In the same ordinance the socalled 'vestgeld' levied for the safe-conduct from the waggons or chariots is found, with a tariff. Leuven, Diest, (Maas)Tricht and Gorcum had to pay this. Nijmegen had to pay for the cattle they sold in Den Bosch, but the cattle they only passed through the town was free. The inhabitants of the Meierij of Den Bosch, Turnhout, Hoogstraten, St. Geertruidenberg, Baarle, Breda, Land of Breda, Tiel, (Zalt)Bommel, Heusden and the Land of Heusden were free. Duke Philip stated in 1465 that the fair which started till then the day after St. Luke till Severijnsday (Oct. 19-22) should furthermore start the day after Severijnsday (Oct. 23) during a week. This as the fair coincided with the one granted by the duke in Arnhem. In 1540 (July) emperor Charles granted a free fair for meager cattle on Tuesday and Wednesday in the Holy week (before Eastern). According to an old town-history there would have been even seven fairs in Den Bosch. In the years 1535-'39 some 57000 waggons passed the Vughter-gate yearly. That is 230 per day, assuming 260 working-days per year.
Toll_Description: The landtoll in Brabant was partly collected in Den Bosch. Income was rising up to 1468/9, after that it stagnated. In 1480 with 1815lb. at a maximum for the 15th century, this level was only after 1506 reached again. Around 1500 there were many problems regarding competency, in 1530 the collection was suspended and in 1533 it was leased for 12 years to Den Bosch, afterwards this was enlengthed many times. Delegates of the comital council tried to recover 2/3 of the yields on the countryside. The Meierij was finally obliged to pay after a lawsuit for the Council of Brabant. Yields of this comital landtoll are published for the years 1531-'85.
Staple_Description: In 1585 the governor prince of Parma granted a staple for oxen and horned cattle like Lier had and a free weekly market for meager and fat cattle. In 1587 king Philip II confirmed this right but also for Lier in Brabant. Lier was already reconfirmed in its privilege for this staple in Brabant in 1469 by duke Charles the Bold. But was opposed by Diest in 1475, who said to have the oldest oxen-fair. In 1503 Diest granted safe-conduct for merchants with cattle from Deventer, Kampen, Zwolle and other inhabitants of the Oversticht, although Lier tried to prevent that. Den Bosch also opposed the market at Lier at least since 1555.
Ferry_Description: 's-Hertogenbosch and the surrounding area often flooded during autumn and winter, due to flooding of the river Meuse, and the smaller rivers Aa and Dommel. Small ferries came into function when the elevated access roads flooded. This started out as private enterprises, but at least from the end of the seventeenth onward, the town council of 's-Hertogenbosch controlled these ferries. The ferries were located at the Orthenpoort, Sint-Janspoort, Vughterpoort, Grote Hekel, Kleine Hekel, and Hinthamerpoort. The hydraulic situation did not change much until 1875, when the 'vestingwet' (a law for fortified towns) was repealed.

Name: Hildesheim
Alternative_Name: Hildenisheim; Hiltineshimensi; Hildinemensem; Hildinensem; Hildensem; Hildenshem; Hilmsen
Settlement_Description: Emperor Louis the Pious founded the diocese of Hildesheim near a merchant settlement in 815. The settlement received market privileges around 1000.
Town_Description: Around 1146, Hildesheim is already characterised as 'civitas'. A town hall is first mentioned in 1217, and in 1300 the old town granted itself town rights. The new town, which was founded around 1220, formed a union with the old town since 1583, but both parts were only formally united in 1803.
Fair_Description: The town rights of 1300 mention three fairs, on the Annunciation, the Ascension of the Virgin Mary, and on St Michael's day. According to the stand fees in the town accounts from 1379 onwards, the Annunciation fair was the most visited of the Hildesheim fairs. A fourth fair on St Gotthard is mentioned in 1310. In 1460, the old fairs were replace by two six-day fairs, for a trial period of four years: the fair of St Michael remained, and a new fair took place on Misericordia Sunday. Apparently the trial was a success, because in 1476, the two fairs were reiterated for the period of 12 years with slight modifications. After that period and before 1523, the situation must have changed again, since it is mentioned in the latter year that there were four three-day fairs in the town, which had been held since times of old: next to the fairs of St Michael and Misericordia Sunday, the Annunciation fair had been revived and a new fair on Wednesday after Pentecost was added.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Hildesheim is first mentioned in 1382, when it was pawned to Aschwin von Meienberg. In 1389 it was pawned to Gunzel von Lutter.

Name: Hoorn
Alternative_Name: Hoern; Horne; Hoirne; Hoirn; Hoerne; Horn
Settlement_Description: According to Cox, Hoorn is first mentioned in 1298. Van Berkel & Samplonius, however, state that the 1298 mention is a forgery dating from 1424. The following mention they note, dates from 1312. A hospital is first mentioned in 1347. Revenues from a weighhouse belonging to the count are first found in 1344.
Town_Description:
Hoorn was granted town rights on 26 March 1357 by William V, count of Holland. 
One of the smaller ‘Kamers’ (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Hoorn.
Fair_Description:
In 1343 cattle is sold by 'Oosterlingen' (merchants from the Baltic) on the market of Hoorn to comital servants. In 1389 duke Albrecht granted Danish traders to visit the market with oxen and horses while paying a toll. In 1446 (March) a dairy-fair was granted by duke Philip of Burgundy with St. Laurensdag (August 10) for three days. The two existing fairs with Palm-eve and Pentecost-eve had little revenues and huge costs as a result of competition from neighbouring fairs, which caused poverty. In 1449 duke Philip of Burgundy ordained after complaints from Alkmaar (there would be no tax collecting in Hoorn and the fair was 8 days before the fair in Alkmaar) at the Court of Holland that the dairy-fair was forbidden. In 1450 however Hoorn still announced this fair even in Flanders, so the landlord had to act again.
In 1564 Hoorn requested the Secret Council in Brussel admission for a free leather-fair. The town said to have high costs of dikes and little negotiation. In the town lived many shoemakers and some traders in fells. According to Hoorn in Holland there was only in Beverwijk a leather-fair. The town asked and obtained from Philip II, after advice from the steward of Kennemerland and the audit office, in December admission for no less than three free leather- and fell fairs. These would not hamper Beverwijk because of the distance and dates. The dates are: 1) Monday after Lent-eve, 2) Thursday after Pentecost, 3) the day after St. James (July 26 juli), each with a duration of 3 days. In 1575 (Nov. 1) Philip II granted another privilege for a leather-fair, the day after All Saints (Nov. 2), duration 3 days before and after. In 1582 (August 25) the mayors of Hoorn obtained from prince William of Orange a free fat and lean cattlefair on 15-18 November. In autumn mechants from Denmark, Eiderstedt, Friesland and Overijssel arrived, and income for Hoorn was derived mostly from shipping.

Name: Husum
Settlement_Description: The bridge Husembro is first mentioned in 1252. After the "Mandränke" flood of 1362, a navigable connection with the sea was created, upon which the harbour settlement Husum developed in 1372; in 1398 divided into Oster- and Westerhusum.
Town_Description: In the 1430ies Husum had around 250 taxpayers. Market privileges were granted to the borough ('blek'/’flække’) Husum in 1465, and it acquired its own jurisdiction in 1472. Town privileges were granted in 1608. Throughout the late medieval period and early modern era Husum benefited from a lucrative trade, especially export of oxen from Denmark, with the Low Countries and Germany.
Fair_Description: Husum was an important market for oxen driven from Jutland. Markets are first attested in 1493 and took place each Thursday in May and April, with the main fairs taking place on the last Thursday in April and the first Thursday in May. In autumn, there was an oxen fair on St Simon and Jude. In 1607, two three-day cattle markets were granted in spring and autumn. Additionally, Heinrich Rantzau mentions two fairs on Trinity Sunday and St Matthew in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein. These are also mentioned in an almanac from 1598, printed in Neudamm (Dębno).
Toll_Description: The exact age and character of the important royal transit toll at Husum is unknown. Toll registers are available for the years 1496-1497 and 1504-1506 (The National Archive/Rigsarkivet) and from 1553 (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein).

Name: Jena
Alternative_Name: Jani; Gene; Jene; Jenis; Jhene; Yhne; Yen; Jehene; Jehna
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from c. 830-850. The settlement benefitted from an advantageous position at a Saale river crossing.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted around 1230 by the lords of Lobdeburg. Citizens are attested in 1236. Gotha town rights were granted around 1332. Elector Johann Friedrich founded a university in the former Dominican monastery in 1548.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Jena are already mentioned in the 13th century. In 1354 there were three fairs, but their dates can only be inferred indirectly. One probably took place on Sunday Cantate, the second between 22 October and 3 November (possibly on St Simon and Jude), the third remains unknown. A cattle fair was granted on 20 June 1486, once again with unknown date, and a fair on St Giles on 10 December 1492. Weekly markets are first mentioned in 1406.
Toll_Description: A toll of the lords of Lobdeburg is first mentioned in 1316. The mint, toll and safe conduct rights were acquired by the town in 1352. The toll had to be paid by wagons and carts, for the maintenance of the roads around Jena. Furthermore, there was a water toll, from which we only know the fees.

Name: Kampen
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention dates from 9 July 1227. Archaeological finds indicate habitation from the twelfth century onward. It has been suggested that the town was founded by merchants from the Rhineland as a transshipment port at the mouth of the IJssel river.
Town_Description: It is not known for sure whether Kampen has been granted town privileges. Possibly, those privileges may have developed from customary law, and afterwards been acknowledged and confirmed by the landlord. It is, however, likely that town privileges have been granted by Wilbrand of Oldenburg, bishop of Utrecht, between 1230 and 1233.
Fair_Description: In 1382, Floris van Wevelinkhoven, bishop of Utrecht, granted the rights for three fairs: one around the fourteenth day after Eastern, one around St Martin of Tours Translation Day (4 July), and one around St Victor (10 October). A fair around Pentecost was already in place before 1382.

Name: Kassel
Alternative_Name: Cassel; Chassella; Chassalla; Cassella; Cassele; Cassela; Cassle; Casla; Kasle
Settlement_Description: Developed from a Frankish fortification of the 10th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted around 1180, Kassel is first characterised as "civitas" in 1189. Town privileges were confirmed in 1239. The new town on the opposite shore of the Fulda appears in 1283, the "Freiheit" around 1330; the three parts were united in 1378.
Fair_Description: Since 1336, three fairs are known to have taken place on the Altmarkt in Kassel: on Sunday Invocavit, St James and St Martin.
Toll_Description: Toll on commodities, introduced by Landgrave Moritz after the Fulda river had been made navigable between Kassel and Hersfeld. In an ordinance from 1613, the toll duties were set at the rate established in 1604. At each lock in the Fulda, it was checked whether the toll had been paid.
Staple_Description: A staple in Kassel with a forced stay of three days was introduced in 1336, in a conflict about the older staple of Münden.

Name: Kiel
Alternative_Name: Civitas Holsatorum; Civitati Holsatiae; Holstenstadt tom Kyle; Kyl; tom Kyle; Kilo; Kil; Kylo; Kiehl
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1232. Before the foundation of the town, there already existed a merchant settlement at this place.
Town_Description: Count Adolf IV of Holstein founded "Holstenstadt tom Kyle" as a planned town between 1238 and 1242. Johann I of Holstein granted Lübeck town privileges in 1242. Kiel was pawned to Lübeck between 1469 and 1496.
Fair_Description: The most important fair in Kiel was the one-week so-called 'Kieler Umschlag', which must date to 1431 at the latest, but was first mentioned in 1469. It became the most important international capital market for the nobility of northern Germany and Denmark in the 16th and 17th century. There are many different dates known for the fair, among others on St Martin, St Michael, the Presentation of Jesus, Easter, Ascension Day, Pentecost or Christmas. From the 16th century onwards, it usually took place in the week after Epiphany. In some years, it was also held in other towns such as Rendsburg and Oldesloe. The Umschlag was discontinued in 1911, but revived as a funfair in 1975. Next to the Umschlag, there existed three other one-week fairs in the early modern period, after Sunday Invocavit, Monday after St Peter and Paul, and on Monday after St Francis.

Name: Koblenz
Alternative_Name: Confluentes; Conbulantia; covelenze; Kovelenze; Cobelenze; Covlentze
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned between the second and fourth centurie. The Franks conquered the place around 500 and a Frankish royal court was established here around 550. In 882, the settlement was destroyed by the Normans.
Town_Description: In 1276, a town council was mentioned.
Toll_Description:
1) Until 1018, the empire levied a river toll on the Rhine here. This was levied from 1000/1018 to 1302, 1309 to 1343 and from 1350 to 1362. A tarif roll from 1140 exists. The Archbishop of Trier held the toll from 1018 to 1042. From 1042 to about 1300, the monastery of St. Simeon in Trier held it. From about 1250 to 1267 and from 1300 onwards, the property went back to the Archbishop of Trier. In 1309 and 1314, 6 Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine. From 1317 to 1321, 12 Turnosgroschen had to be paid per foder of wine, in 1345 15 Turnosgroschen and in 1358 already 17 Turnosgroschen. In 1267, 500 to 800 marks could be collected. From 1345 to 1348 the toll was leased for 655 pounds turnosgroschen (equivalent to 13100 guilders) a year.

2) The Archbishop of Trier collected a fee for safe conduct on the Rhine from 1250 to 1267. The annual revenue in 1267 was about 40 mark.

3) Parallel to the Rhine toll, there was a river toll on the Moselle, which was paid together with the river toll on the Rhine until about 1336. The owner and early tariffs are therefore identical. In 1354, 12 Turnosgroschen had to be paid per foder of wine, in 1430 1 Gulden per foder of wine.
In 1336/37 and 1338/39 the annual rent was 40 pounds turnosgroschen. In 1344/46 59 pounds Turnosgroschen and in 1358/61 120 pounds Turnosgroschen could be collected.

4) In addition to the two river tolls, a land toll was also levied. Before 1000, 4 denarii per pack animal had to be paid. Annual revenues are not known.
Staple_Description: Archbishop John II of Trier gave Koblenz staple rights between Boppard and Engers; specified in more detail in 1480. Cattle and grain from the Bonn-Wetzlar-Bingen-Wittich region and fish caught in the Rhein between Platzenborn and Oberlahnstein needed to brought to market in Koblenz.

Name: Koblenz
Alternative_Name: Confluentes; Conbulantia; covelenze; Kovelenze; Cobelenze; Covlentze
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned between the second and fourth centurie. The Franks conquered the place around 500 and a Frankish royal court was established here around 550. In 882, the settlement was destroyed by the Normans.
Town_Description: In 1276, a town council was mentioned.
Toll_Description:
1) Until 1018, the empire levied a river toll on the Rhine here. This was levied from 1000/1018 to 1302, 1309 to 1343 and from 1350 to 1362. A tarif roll from 1140 exists. The Archbishop of Trier held the toll from 1018 to 1042. From 1042 to about 1300, the monastery of St. Simeon in Trier held it. From about 1250 to 1267 and from 1300 onwards, the property went back to the Archbishop of Trier. In 1309 and 1314, 6 Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine. From 1317 to 1321, 12 Turnosgroschen had to be paid per foder of wine, in 1345 15 Turnosgroschen and in 1358 already 17 Turnosgroschen. In 1267, 500 to 800 marks could be collected. From 1345 to 1348 the toll was leased for 655 pounds turnosgroschen (equivalent to 13100 guilders) a year.

2) The Archbishop of Trier collected a fee for safe conduct on the Rhine from 1250 to 1267. The annual revenue in 1267 was about 40 mark.

3) Parallel to the Rhine toll, there was a river toll on the Moselle, which was paid together with the river toll on the Rhine until about 1336. The owner and early tariffs are therefore identical. In 1354, 12 Turnosgroschen had to be paid per foder of wine, in 1430 1 Gulden per foder of wine.
In 1336/37 and 1338/39 the annual rent was 40 pounds turnosgroschen. In 1344/46 59 pounds Turnosgroschen and in 1358/61 120 pounds Turnosgroschen could be collected.

4) In addition to the two river tolls, a land toll was also levied. Before 1000, 4 denarii per pack animal had to be paid. Annual revenues are not known.
Staple_Description: Archbishop John II of Trier gave Koblenz staple rights between Boppard and Engers; specified in more detail in 1480. Cattle and grain from the Bonn-Wetzlar-Bingen-Wittich region and fish caught in the Rhein between Platzenborn and Oberlahnstein needed to brought to market in Koblenz.

Name: Kołobrzeg
Alternative_Name: Kolberg; Cholbergiensis; Colbrech; Colubregam; Colberg; Coluberch; Cholberg; Choleberch; Cholberch; Colberch; Colberge; Choleberg; Kolbrzegu; Kolberka
Settlement_Description: Two settlements developed near saltworks in the 6th or 7th century, with a small castle nearby, which was extended during the middle of the 9th century. The settlement is first mentioned in 975. Boleslaw Chrobri of Poland made it into a bishopric under the archdiocese of Gniezno (Gnesen) around 1000.
Town_Description: The German settlement received Lübeck town privileges in 1255 from Duke Wartislaw of Pomerania and the bishop of Kammin.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Invocavit in Kołobrzeg is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

Name: Köln
Alternative_Name: Cologne; Keulen; Cöln; Colne; Coln; Collen
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as the birthplace of Agrippina 50 A.D. Since the middle of the 5th century under Frankish rule.
Town_Description: Already in the Middle Ages, Cologne was a spiritual centre and town of pilgrimage. In 1388 the university was founded. A town council or regiment probably existed already in the 13th/14th century. Niemeyer does not mention the granting of town rights before 1475. Cologne was referred to as a free imperial town in 1475.
Toll_Description:
1) Cologne levied a river toll on the Rhine from 1317 to 1321. This also existed in 1363 and from 1475 to 1494. In the period between 1317 and 1321, 6 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine had to be paid. From 1475 to 1494 the tariff was 2 guilders and 2 turnosgroschen per barrel of wine. In the years 1317 to 1320, 1400 pounds 14 shillings and 5 turnosgroschen could be collected. This corresponds to about 9338 guilders a year. For other annual revenues, see Pfeiffer. 

2) In 1103 a gate toll was also levied. Around 1360 1/3 of the revenue went to the town and 2/3 to the Archbishop of Cologne. In the 12th century only special tariffs are known. In 1453, 3 heller had to be paid for a loaded carriage across the Rhine. At the end of the 14th century, 4 heller had to be paid per wine carriage. For other tariffs see Pfeiffer. Annual revenues are not known.

3) Road toll was collected in 1262 parallel to the gate toll. Tariffs are therefore similar.
Staple_Description: Developed probably shortly before 1169, but original plans not always enforced. Confirmed in 1259, 1349 and 1355; revoked in 1356. Staple rights were probably not exercised after 1300. In late 1300s renewed attempts for the imposition of a staple; wood must remain in the town for one day; the Fishmonger ordinances of 1397 forced foreigners to seller their fish to the merchants of Cologne; ordinances of 1407 stipulated that wine, wood, fish, salt and iron should be offered for sale in the city; regulations regarding these matters became stricter throughout the 15th century. The Ordinances of the Merchant Store and the Old Market of 1486 contained new regulations for the staples for meat, oils and fats, iron, steel, lead and leather. Attempts at end of the 15th century to enforce staple rights in the trade of cattle, cloth and wool. The unloading of goods while travelling along the lower Rhine banned in 1497, but not mentioned in the imperial staple privileges for 1505. The staple after 1505 appears to decline, but is re-enforced in 1525/6. The bypassing of the staple via Neuss, Bonn and Mülheim encouraged the council in 1603 to forbid the unloading of goods along the Rhine in both directions. From 1616 there were exemptions for stone from Andernach. Staple confirmed once again by the emperor in 1635; after the Thirty Years’ War the staple was gradually transformed into a requirment to transfer wares and was finally dissolved with the Rhine Shipping act of 1831.

Settlement_Description: The first castle of the Teutonic Order was built on the remains of an Old Prussian castle, a marketsettlement of craftsmen and farmers grew next to it, their church is documented since 1256, the first settlements were destroyed between 1262 and 1263
Town_Description: After the settlement was rebuilt, the Landmaster of Prussia, Konrad von Thierberg, granted the Kulm town law in 1286
Staple_Description: Imposition of ordinances and rules for the compulsory inspection of ash, tar, pitch and honey and also a reduced staple for wood in the 1390s. An agreement in 1466 made arrangement for a staple for ash, which must have been lost shortly after 1476. Mandate of Grandmaster Albert of Brandenburg ordered merchants from Lithuania, Maosvia, Moscow, Gdansk and Torun to offer their wares for sail when travelling through Königsberg, but was forbidden in the treaty of Krakow in 1525. Trade outside of the town forbidden in 1529, and livestock from Lithuania and Samogitia should be kept at market for three days. A mandate of 1565 ordered merchants of Bartenstein, Rastenburg, Friedland, Wehlau, Tilsit, Memel and Insterburg to bring their wares solely to market in Königsberg; repeated in 1622.

Name: København
Alternative_Name: Kaupmanna haufn; Hafn; Haffn; Mercatorum portus; Copendehaafn; Kiopmanhafn; Copmannæhauæn; Cøpmanhauen;Køpmanhaffn; Køpendhauen; Kiøbenhavn;  Hafnia; Copenhagen; Kopenhagen
Settlement_Description: Large-scale archaeological excavations in the oldests parts of Copenhagen have revealed trading and craft activities in the late Viking Age, and that Copenhagen was a permanent settlement with an urban character in the 11th century. The settlement was located at one of the best natural harbors on eastern Zealand and at a place with overland routes across the large island of Zealand.
Town_Description: Copenhagen was first mentioned in a papal document from 1186, by which pope Urban III confirmed that king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182) around 1167 had donated the castle of Copenhagen (“castrum de Hafn”) to archbishop Absalon of Lund, who was also bishop of Roskilde. The pope also confirmed that the castle and town of Copenhagen by the death of Absalon should be handed over to the diocese of Roskilde. Thus, when Absalon died in 1201, the town went to the church in Roskilde, and the bishops of Roskilde were town lords until 1417, when king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) took over the town. In the following decades Copenhagen developed into the most important town in Denmark; in time it came to be the Danish capital. Up until recently the papal document from 1186 was seen as the foundation document of Copenhagen, but thanks to archeological excavations it is now clear that Copenhagen had already an urban character, when archbishop Absalon took over the town. In his Gesta Danorum from c. 1208 the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus touched upon the recent history of the town, which he described as  “urbs Absalonica” and “portus mercatorum”. Absalon established a strong castle on the small island of Slotsholmen near the coastline, where the settlement and later town also developed, and in the 13th century the town was also fortified. Both the castle and the town fortification were rebuilt several times. In the early modern era the castle was one of the most important royal castles in Denmark, and Copenhagen was surrounded by a strong town wall built of bricks. The town was granted its first town law by the bishop of Roskilde in 1254, which was replaced by the second town law in 1294. A town council and members of the council (consules) were also well-established by the end of the 13th century, as was a town hall. The latter was relocated in the later middle ages to the town’s main square (Danish: Gammeltorv). A Fransician monastery was founded around 1240. As an illustrative example of the growing importance of the town, the first university in Denmark was founded in Copenhagen in 1479, and at this time the town's main church, the Church of our Lady (Danish: Vor Frue), had also become the preferred place for royal coronations and weddings. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era Copenhagen grew in political and economic importance as well as size. The town benefited from its central location in the Danish realm and at the shore of the narrow strait of Øresund. By the 17th century Copenhagen was undisputedly the largest and in many ways most important town in Denmark.
Staple_Description: As part of his struggle with Lübeck king Christian II (1513-1523) established a staple in Copenhagen, as the king aimed to make his capital the leading entrepôt of the Baltic. The ambitious attempt failed, and Copenhagen only functioned as a staple town in a few years during the reign of Christian II.
Ferry_Description: According to the two oldest versions of the town law, granted by the bishop of Roskilde in 1254 and 1294, the town had to ferry the bishop across the Sound (Danish: Øresund) to Scania without payment. This is a strong indication that ferries between Copenhagen and Scania, most likely the town of Malmö, were well established by the middle of the 13th century. Throughout the middle ages and early-modern era ferries connected Copenhagen and Scania, in general Malmö. Another ferry connected Copenhagen with the island of Amager. This ferry departed from a bridge called “Myndrikkebroen”, the possible precursor to the bridge called “Holmens Bro”, which probably was located at the eastern outlet at the harbour. The ferry between Copenhagen and Amager was first mentioned in the early 16th century, but is most likely much older.
Harbour_Description: Protected by the larger island of Amager and several smaller islands such as Slotsholmen Copenhagen was one of the best natural harbors on eastern Zealand and from the beginning of the settlement this was of great importance. A jetty is mentioned for the first time in the town law from 1294, and the port was also mentioned during the 14th century. This medieval port was located in the narrow strait between the small island of Slotsholmen and the coastline with the town. The port was constantly improved and expanded. In the 15th century this central part of the port was dominated by a long wharf. In the early 16th century a naval shipyard was established on the island of Bremerholmen near the eastern outlet of the harbour, and Copenhagen soon became the most important naval port in Denmark. During the reign of king Christian IV (1596-1648) the naval shipyard was relocated to Holmen, and the port of the town was also expanded. A copper engraving of Copenhagen seen from Amager in Civitates orbis terrarum by Georg Braun and Frans Hogenberg (1588) shows a large and advanced eastern end of the harbour. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era the port of Copenhagen was important to both regional and international trading networks, and was often used by both German as well as other foreing merchants.
