Town_Description: Copenhagen was first mentioned in a papal document from 1186, by which pope Urban III confirmed that king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182) around 1167 had donated the castle of Copenhagen (“castrum de Hafn”) to archbishop Absalon of Lund, who was also bishop of Roskilde. The pope also confirmed that the castle and town of Copenhagen by the death of Absalon should be handed over to the diocese of Roskilde. Thus, when Absalon died in 1201, the town went to the church in Roskilde, and the bishops of Roskilde were town lords until 1417, when king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) took over the town. In the following decades Copenhagen developed into the most important town in Denmark; in time it came to be the Danish capital. Up until recently the papal document from 1186 was seen as the foundation document of Copenhagen, but thanks to archeological excavations it is now clear that Copenhagen had already an urban character, when archbishop Absalon took over the town. In his Gesta Danorum from c. 1208 the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus touched upon the recent history of the town, which he described as  “urbs Absalonica” and “portus mercatorum”. Absalon established a strong castle on the small island of Slotsholmen near the coastline, where the settlement and later town also developed, and in the 13th century the town was also fortified. Both the castle and the town fortification were rebuilt several times. In the early modern era the castle was one of the most important royal castles in Denmark, and Copenhagen was surrounded by a strong town wall built of bricks. The town was granted its first town law by the bishop of Roskilde in 1254, which was replaced by the second town law in 1294. A town council and members of the council (consules) were also well-established by the end of the 13th century, as was a town hall. The latter was relocated in the later middle ages to the town’s main square (Danish: Gammeltorv). A Fransician monastery was founded around 1240. As an illustrative example of the growing importance of the town, the first university in Denmark was founded in Copenhagen in 1479, and at this time the town's main church, the Church of our Lady (Danish: Vor Frue), had also become the preferred place for royal coronations and weddings. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era Copenhagen grew in political and economic importance as well as size. The town benefited from its central location in the Danish realm and at the shore of the narrow strait of Øresund. By the 17th century Copenhagen was undisputedly the largest and in many ways most important town in Denmark.
Staple_Description: As part of his struggle with Lübeck king Christian II (1513-1523) established a staple in Copenhagen, as the king aimed to make his capital the leading entrepôt of the Baltic. The ambitious attempt failed, and Copenhagen only functioned as a staple town in a few years during the reign of Christian II.
Ferry_Description: According to the two oldest versions of the town law, granted by the bishop of Roskilde in 1254 and 1294, the town had to ferry the bishop across the Sound (Danish: Øresund) to Scania without payment. This is a strong indication that ferries between Copenhagen and Scania, most likely the town of Malmö, were well established by the middle of the 13th century. Throughout the middle ages and early-modern era ferries connected Copenhagen and Scania, in general Malmö. Another ferry connected Copenhagen with the island of Amager. This ferry departed from a bridge called “Myndrikkebroen”, the possible precursor to the bridge called “Holmens Bro”, which probably was located at the eastern outlet at the harbour. The ferry between Copenhagen and Amager was first mentioned in the early 16th century, but is most likely much older.
Harbour_Description: Protected by the larger island of Amager and several smaller islands such as Slotsholmen Copenhagen was one of the best natural harbors on eastern Zealand and from the beginning of the settlement this was of great importance. A jetty is mentioned for the first time in the town law from 1294, and the port was also mentioned during the 14th century. This medieval port was located in the narrow strait between the small island of Slotsholmen and the coastline with the town. The port was constantly improved and expanded. In the 15th century this central part of the port was dominated by a long wharf. In the early 16th century a naval shipyard was established on the island of Bremerholmen near the eastern outlet of the harbour, and Copenhagen soon became the most important naval port in Denmark. During the reign of king Christian IV (1596-1648) the naval shipyard was relocated to Holmen, and the port of the town was also expanded. A copper engraving of Copenhagen seen from Amager in Civitates orbis terrarum by Georg Braun and Frans Hogenberg (1588) shows a large and advanced eastern end of the harbour. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era the port of Copenhagen was important to both regional and international trading networks, and was often used by both German as well as other foreing merchants.

Name: Köthen
Settlement_Description:
1115 mention of an "oppidum" Köthen, near which a battle against the Slavs took place.

From 1180 - 1212 duke Bernhard of Saxony had coins minted with "kotene civitas", which indicates the existence of a fortified market. One can assume an earlier, slavic settlement.

From 1396 a castle can be proven in Köthen.
Town_Description: Since the beginning of the 14th century, Köthen is referred to as "civitas" in the records and a sheriff, councilmen and jurymen are mentioned. Jurisdiction stays with the town lord, however.
Fair_Description: In 1643 Leipzig prevents the establishment of two additional fairs in Köthen.
Toll_Description: A regulation of safe conduct remains from 1563 (LHASA, DE, Z 10, Nr. 48, Amtsregister und Anschlag des Amtes Köthen.).

Staple_Description: In 1306 the town was made the staple for wares from Hungary, especially metal. After conflicts with the Hungarians, salt transported from Torun to Sandek is excepted. Citizens of Wroclaw exempt from the Krakow staple; in 1354 trade with guests forbidden. Decres of the Polish King of 1372 and 1389 making Krakow the staple market for all merchants coming to Poland (except those from Sandomir and Lublin) lead to several conflicts with Torun. In 1391 both towns removed themselves from the staple, but in 1398 merchants of Krakow forced once again to the offer their wares in the town. The important stapel for the copper trade from Hungary and for Baltic wares was confirmed in the Polish Staple law of 1565.

Name: Kostrzyn nad Odrą
Alternative_Name: Küstrin; Cozsterine; Custerin; Costerin; Custryn; Kostryn; Custrina; Cüstrin; Costrzin; Custeryn; Kistrzyn; Kistryn; Kostrzyn
Settlement_Description: Belonged to Greater Poland in the Middle Ages. A German market settlement came after 1232, mentioned as oppidum in 1261, when it was acquired by Brandenburg.
Town_Description: Magdeburg town law was likely granted by margrave Albrecht III shortly before 1300. Mentioned as civitas in 1317 and 1372, as opidum in 1323.
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1338, when it was pawned for three years. A river toll on the Oder is mentioned in 1345. Citizens from Bärwalde (Mieszkowice) and Schönfließ (Trzcińsko-Zdrój) were exempted from the toll in 1356, and an older similar privilege was confirmed for Königsberg (Chojna) in 1371 as well. A bridge toll is mentioned in 1436, and a privilege from 1482 allows a bridge and dam toll of 4 pennies for each wagon. In 1457, parts of the revenues of the river toll were owned by the Benedictine women's monastery of Guben.
Staple_Description: In 1424, Poles were exempted from the staple in Kostrzyn.

Name: Gorzów Wielkopolski
Alternative_Name: Landsberg a.d. Warthe; Landsberg an der Warthe; Landesbergk; Landisberch Nova; Nuenlandesberch; Nuwen landisberg; Landesberghe; Landsbergk; Lantzbergk; Neu-Landsberg
Settlement_Description: Developed from a late Slavic settlement. First mentioned in 1257 when it became a town.
Town_Description: The knight Albert of Luge was certified to found the town "Landisberch Nova" by Margrave John I in 1257. The town acquired Magdeburg town law after ten years.
Staple_Description: The first mention of a staple in a charter from 1257 is probably a later addition; furthermore mentioned in 1391 and 1400. In 1424, Poles are exempted from the staple. In 1539, the use of the road via Landsberg for transit traffic was prohibited in favour of Frankfurt, and the staple limited to commodities transported downstream from Poland. In the other direction, there existed no staple obligations.

Name: Bad Langensalza
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Breviarum sancti Lulli from the 9th century. The settlement was located near the Dryburg of the lords of Salza, which controlled the crossing at the ford of the roads from Gotha to Mühlhausen and from Eisenach to Tennstedt.
Town_Description: After a siege of the settlement by Kaiser Otto IV in 1212, the lords of Salza received the privilege, to develop the settlement into a town. First referral to the town as "oppidum" in 1222. Extensive destruction of the town in 1346. In 1356 the old town was merged with its two suburbs, the Jakobsstadt and the Neustadt ('new town'), under one communal administration, which was corroborated by the construction of a town wall.
Fair_Description: Since 1438 two, since 1484 three fairs are attested.
Toll_Description: According to the regulations of safe conduct from 1516, there was no safe conduct in the department of Salza, only the toll in town. In 1558 the safe conduct was given to the town council with an option of repurchase, in 1663 it was ultimately given to the prince electorate.

Name: Leer
Alternative_Name: Hleri; Lare; Lage; Lier; Lyer; Leher; Leehere
Settlement_Description: A missionary church was erected by Liudger around 790, next to which a market borough developed. Borough ('flecken') statutes are first known from 1585 and the settlement acquired urban characteristics, although formal town privileges were granted as late as in 1823.
Town_Description: NULL
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of East Frisia is mentioned in 1577 complaints from Emden. In 1640, Emden merchants complain about a new toll on flax and wine in Leer.
Harbour_Description: Leer was an important harbour on the rivers Ems and Leda in the 16th century, although it suffered from the staple privileges of Emden. The importance of the harbour for the borough is indicated by the fact that the market, which originally took place at the Kaakskpütte, moved to the waterfront, where a weigh house was erected in the middle of the 16th century. Name: Ljouwert
Alternative_Name: Leeuwarden; Liwwadden; Liunvero; Liunvert; Linvvar; Lienward; Linuuard; Linewert; Liuwerth; Lewart; Liuwerd
Settlement_Description: First mentioned on a coin from 1038-1057.
Town_Description: Leeuwarden never officially received town rights. However, Leeuwarden was recognized as a town by other cities. The earliest mention of this dates from 31 October 1285.
Fair_Description: In 1453 there are three fairs: 1) Thursday to Saterday after Eastern 2) St. Margaret (July 13/Schuur: July 20!?), 3) St. Matthew (Sept. 21). The last two fairs were there of old, the first seems new. A weighhouse is found in 1486 but dates probably back before 1435.
Toll_Description: In 1533 (1531? on instigation of the stadtholder) with permission of the Court of Frisia the magistrate installed a toll for 3 years on the new Zwartenweg(road) which connected Leeuwarden eastern (in the direction of Ryptsjerk) with the Wolden and Groningen. This road replaced the old one via Lekkum and Miedum. In 1535 the Landen (countryside) protested against this. Leeuwarden removed without consultation the bridge at Miedum and so made this route unusable. The Court gave order to repair the bridge but extended the levying of the toll on the new route. The countryside opposed this. In 1554 this was not yet solved.
Harbour_Description: In the 17th century, Leeuwarden became the centre of regular barge ('trekvaart') services with Franeker and Harlingen (1646, with five departures daily in both directions), Dokkum (1647), Bolsward and Workum (1648), Groningen (1656) and Sneek (1661).

Name: Leiden
Alternative_Name: Leithen; Leyden; Ledene; Leythen; Leda; Ledam; Leithon
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius Leiden is first mentioned in a document from 1143. Cox, however, states that Leiden was first mentioned in copy of ninth century text (tenth or late eleventh century). A hospital is first mentioned in 1276. A chapter in the Pancras-church is known for the years 1366-1574.
Town_Description: Leiden was granted town rights on 19 December 1266 by Floris V, count of Holland. Cox argues that four grants outdate the 1266 grant, the earliest of which could have been given during the reign of Dirk VII, count of Holland (r. 1190-1203) or even Floris III, count of Holland (r. 1157-1190).
Fair_Description: In a charter dated 1266 and in the town rights of 1266 fines on the disturbing of the fairs (or markets?) are found. In 1303 (June 4) count John granted a fair with Margaretha-eve (July 12), with equal freedom as other fairs. Next to this fair a fair with 'Kruisdag' (Crossday: Sept. 14) existed. Around 1400 this was September 11 or the consecration day of St. Peter. Circa 1360 a toll of the burgrave is found in a list of his possessions. This must be the toll of the Cross-fair. In it are also found his weigh-house, ell and buttermeasure, which were ceased by the town. In 1422 inhabitants of Leiden are first found on the fairs of Frankfurt. In 1497 (Dec.) the archduke Philip granted a free fair of 8 days, starting St. Margaretha-eve. This is the fair granted in 1303 but it was decayed. In 1521 the toll of the Cross-fair is owned by the burgrave. In 1546 he leased this right to the town for a fixed sum. The yields are found in the oldest preserved account of the steward of the lord of Wassenaer (burgrave of Leiden), dated 1554. Free of this toll are Haarlem, Gouda, Amsterdam, Delft and the subordinate villages. Others payed the '100e penning' (1%). In 1565 (May) king Philip II granted the town two free leather- and fill-fairs both for 8 days, to compensate the decaying drapery. The dates: 1) Friday before Oculi (Lent Sunday) and 2) Monday after St. Lambert (Sept. 17). The town is a good place for tanning as there was plenty of water and meadows with cattle in the surrounding Rijnland. In 1599 the dates were altered with permission of the Estates of Holland. In 1573 William of Oranhe granted a free horse-fair in September as of old. On 12 January 1577 the town requested stadtholder William of Orange to have a free fair between 1 and 15 October, in memory of the relief of Leiden. Later this year king Philip II granted this free fair for alle commodities and relocated the leather-fair. In 1624 (March 23) the mayors asked the Estates of Holland for two free meager cattle fairs. The granted dates were April 27 and November 21 with 4 days before and after safe-conduct.

Town_Description: Leiden was granted town rights on 19 December 1266 by Floris V, count of Holland. Cox argues that four grants outdate the 1266 grant, the earliest of which could have been given during the reign of Dirk VII, count of Holland (r. 1190-1203) or even Floris III, count of Holland (r. 1157-1190).
Fair_Description: In a charter dated 1266 and in the town rights of 1266 fines on the disturbing of the fairs (or markets?) are found. In 1303 (June 4) count John granted a fair with Margaretha-eve (July 12), with equal freedom as other fairs. Next to this fair a fair with 'Kruisdag' (Crossday: Sept. 14) existed. Around 1400 this was September 11 or the consecration day of St. Peter. Circa 1360 a toll of the burgrave is found in a list of his possessions. This must be the toll of the Cross-fair. In it are also found his weigh-house, ell and buttermeasure, which were ceased by the town. In 1422 inhabitants of Leiden are first found on the fairs of Frankfurt. In 1497 (Dec.) the archduke Philip granted a free fair of 8 days, starting St. Margaretha-eve. This is the fair granted in 1303 but it was decayed. In 1521 the toll of the Cross-fair is owned by the burgrave. In 1546 he leased this right to the town for a fixed sum. The yields are found in the oldest preserved account of the steward of the lord of Wassenaer (burgrave of Leiden), dated 1554. Free of this toll are Haarlem, Gouda, Amsterdam, Delft and the subordinate villages. Others payed the '100e penning' (1%). In 1565 (May) king Philip II granted the town two free leather- and fill-fairs both for 8 days, to compensate the decaying drapery. The dates: 1) Friday before Oculi (Lent Sunday) and 2) Monday after St. Lambert (Sept. 17). The town is a good place for tanning as there was plenty of water and meadows with cattle in the surrounding Rijnland. In 1599 the dates were altered with permission of the Estates of Holland. In 1573 William of Oranhe granted a free horse-fair in September as of old. On 12 January 1577 the town requested stadtholder William of Orange to have a free fair between 1 and 15 October, in memory of the relief of Leiden. Later this year king Philip II granted this free fair for alle commodities and relocated the leather-fair. In 1624 (March 23) the mayors asked the Estates of Holland for two free meager cattle fairs. The granted dates were April 27 and November 21 with 4 days before and after safe-conduct.

Name: Leipzig
Alternative_Name: Libzi; Libiz; Libz; Libizke; Lipzin; Lipz; Liptz; Lipczk; Lipzk; Lipzik; Leipczke; Leipczigk
Settlement_Description: Developed from an originally Slavic settlement since c. 800, first mentioned in c. 1015. The settlement developed on the early trade routes of the 'Hohe Straße' and 'via imperii/Salzstraße'. Centre of a castellany since the 10th century.
Town_Description: A planned town was founded around 1170 by Margrave Otto of Meißen with Halle-Magdeburg town rights. Because of its fairs and the favourable traffic situation, Leipzig became an important trading centre between Nuremberg and the towns of the Hanse, copper trade in Hungary and mining in the region of Mansfeld. In 1409 a university was founded. Severe damage was inflicted during the 30 Years' War and Leipzig was occupied by the Swedes in 1632-1633 and again in 1642-1650.
Fair_Description: In a document from between 1156 and 1170 a protected zone for the annual fair was imposed around the town of Leipzig, which is the first evidence for fairs in Leipzig. In 1268 a document refers to the fair at Leipzig being visited by foreign merchants, who were under the protection of local territorial lords during fair times. In the 15th century the three eight-day fairs of Leipzig on New Year's Day, Sunday Jubilate and St Michael's Day became large international trading venues. They were confirmed in 1497 by Maximilian I, including a safe conduct of three weeks, and in 1507 extended by a ban zone ('Bannmeile') of 15 miles around the city and a staple. Since the 16th century the fair of St Peter and Paul in Naumburg was aligned with the Leipzig fair calendar (see Naumburg (Saale)).
Toll_Description: A special safe conduct in Leipzig was in place eight days before and after the fairs. During this time, the citizens of Leipzig had to pay the fees as well, where they would normally be exempted. In 1558 the safe conduct, including the secondary station in Taucha, is pawned off by the Elector to the council of the town of Leipzig. The council was supposed to maintain roads, paths, dams, ditches, bridges and footbridges from the revenues.
Staple_Description: The staple requirements appears first in the market privileges of Emperor Maximilian in 1507. However, other records indicate that the staple existed before, e.g. citizens were forbidden to trade outside of town within a designated zone. Such prohibitions are already known from the last decades of the 15th century. The staple was valid within a protected zone ('Bannmeile') of 15 miles around the town. Confirmed by Pope Leo X in 1514 and renewed in 1521 by Emperor Charles V. A complete enforcement of the staple was, however, not possible: conflicts with Erfurt, Halle, Magdeburg, Dresden and Prina ensued, all of whom wished to keep their staple rights. In the Seven Years’ War the Leipzig staple finally deteriorated.

Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, among others for carts and herring.
Staple_Description: Beginnings are unclear. In 1379 a staple for various wares was confirmed, which were guaranteed in a treaty between Lemberg, Waldimir and Luzk. A provision of King Louis of Poland in 1380 stipulated that merchants from Hungary and Poland should offer their wares for sale for 14 days; renewed in 1387 with the addition of salt to the list of goods that should be offered for sale. A privilege of 1444 forbade foreign merchants from travelling east or west via Lemberg; confirmed in the Polish Staple Law of 1565.

Name: Lier
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1146.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: In 1309 (Sept. 8) duke Jan II granted Lier the cattle-staple for Brabant and its cattle-fair. Before this the staple was situated in the village Wespelaar next to Leuven. At first it was foremost a fair for sheeps in connection with the local important drapery. But when the drapery perished in the second half of the 15th century it was tiring changed to a horned cattle-fair, in particular oxen. However there was more and more competition from Diest and Hoogstraten. In 1468 the cattle-fair privilege was confirmed by Charles the Bold but with a yearly payment. In the last quarter of the 15th century some 7000-10000 oxen were traded. In 1567 Guicciardini told that Lier had a famous oxenfair lasting from 'St. Jansmis' (June 24) till 'Martensmis' (Nov. 1) one day per week. In the slaughter-time some 11000-14000 oxen were traded per day.
Staple_Description: In 1309 (Sept. 8) duke Jan II granted Lier the cattle-staple for Brabant and its cattlefair. Before this the staple was situated in the village Wespelaar next to Leuven. In 1485 the staple was moved to Diest by Maximiliaan but in 1498 Lier won a lawsuit. In 1564 (May 20) king Philip II confirmed the staple for oxen. In 1566 Guicciardini told that Lier had a famous oxenfair lasting from 'St. Jansmis' (June 24) till 'St. Martensmis' (Nov. 1) one day per week.

Fair_Description: In 1309 (Sept. 8) duke Jan II granted Lier the cattle-staple for Brabant and its cattle-fair. Before this the staple was situated in the village Wespelaar next to Leuven. At first it was foremost a fair for sheeps in connection with the local important drapery. However there was more and more competition from Diest and Hoogstraten. In 1468 the cattle-fair privilege was confirmed by Charles the Bold but with a yearly payment. Name: Lippstadt
Alternative_Name: Lyppia; Lippia; Lippa; Lippensis; Lippense; Stat zu der Lippe; Stadt Lippe; Lipstatt
Settlement_Description: Lippstadt was founded by the counts of Lippe around 1184 as a planned town on the shore of the Lippe river.
Town_Description: Lippstadt must have been granted town privileges after Soest model around 1220.
Fair_Description: A confirmation of town privileges from 1244 included the right to hold a fair, including market freedom of two days before and after the fair. The oldest fair probably took place on St Martin's Day. In 1553, a fair that formerly took place on 9 September was moved to the second day of Christmas and in 1574 to Innocent's Day. In 1580, four fairs are attested: next to the two already mentioned, there were fairs on St Michael and Thursday after Sexagesima. Given the fact that the fairs took place in autumn and winter, it is likely that mainly agricultural products and cattle were traded there.
Toll_Description: Although an export tax on corn existed since 1366, the town acquired a privilege to levy a toll on merchant's commodities only in 1449. Moreover, in 1481 a toll was introduced on cattle sold in town and on carriages passing the bridges, to cover the maintenance of the town walls and the bridges.

Name: Leuven
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 884, in an eleventh-century copy. Next mention in 1015 is a forgery from the first quarter of the twelfth century. Next mention in circa 1050, is in a late eleventh century copy.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: A wel attended fair in Leuven is mentioned in a chronicle written by a canon of the abbey in Ninove in 1152.
Toll_Description: Headquarter of the Brabantse (land)toll. A tariff of the 'old' toll of the duke of Brabant and the old 'geleide' (conduct) of goods passing through the town to be paid by people from outside of Brabant, is partly older then 1287 when Gorcum was freed of it. The part of the tariff called 'new' toll must be dated before 1303. This tariff is edited, together with later 15th-17th century versions. In 1479 a toll collector is mentioned. In 1523 (June 1) this tariff was renewed from a board hanged on the wall of the 'tolkamer' (toll-office) of Leuven which was 80-100 years old and is called old 'geleide' or 'nuwen ' (new) toll of Brabant.

Name: Lübeck
Alternative_Name: Liubice; Lobeke; Lubche; Lubecae; Lubece; Lubeckh; Lubeg; Lubegk; Lubek; Lubeke; Lubic; Lubicensis; Lubick; Lubik; Lubyk; Lubyke; Lupeke; Lupke; Lybch; Lübcke; Lybiku; Lybyk; Liubeke; Lybbeke; Lubice; Lubike; Lubeke; Lubek; Lubeca
Settlement_Description: Downstream from today’s old town there was a Slavic settlement called Liubice (nowadays Alt Lübeck), where German merchants stayed. After the destruction of Liubice in 1138 the Bucu peninsula was settled, where a town was founded in 1143.
Town_Description: The town was founded by the Counts of Holstein in 1143, with the name of the Slavic settlement destroyed in 1138. After a failed relocation of the town after a fire in 1157, Duke Henry the Lion refounded the town with considerable privileges and made it the seat of a bishopric. The town soon grew into one of the most important Hanseatic centres for long distance trade.
Toll_Description: According to the oldest toll regulations of the town from 1225, foreign merchants who wanted to trade in Lübeck had to pay a fare of 4 denarii each. Moreover, tolls were levied on the cargo of ships leaving the town, as well as for wagons, carts, cattle, pigs and sheep entering town at the town gates. Special regulations were made for Slavic people. In lists of town revenues from the 15th century, a "graventol" at the Holstentor and Mühlentor gates is mentioned as well, which was levied on the shipping on the Stecknitz canal ("graven"). Moreover, between 1492 and 1496, a "pound toll" for the suppression of piracy was levied on sea-going ships, of which extensive registers still exist.
Staple_Description: Lübeck's staple was defined by its role as transshipment point in the trade between the North and Baltic Sea, which allowed avoiding the long detour of circumventing the Danish peninsula. The Hanserecesse of 1417 and 1418 forbade the transport of grain through the Danish straits and outside of the Hanseatic towns. A prohibition for foreigners trading with each other is first attested in 1472. Hollanders were obliged to offer bacon, butter and oil from Scandinavia and wine for 4-7 days; the Treaty of Utrecht (1474) reduced the duration to three days on account of the perishable nature of the wares, with stockfish, herring, cod and seal blubber excepted. In the 16th century the east-west trade through the Sound increased, bypassing Lübeck. Negotiations with the Hollanders regarding this ended in 1532 to Lübeck’s disadvantage. The ordinance of 1607 codified the staple: trade among guests was forbidden, as well as the transit passage of commodities of Danish merchants (except for wine), and the same for copper, iron, pelts, oil, tar and other wares from Sweden and Finland; commdities from Russia (such as leather, tallow, wax and flax, among others) were exempted. After a legal decision arising from a dispute with Hamburg in 1625, Lübeck largely relaxed the compulsory sale of staple goods in the city. Renewed attempts at imposing the staple in the 18th century led once again to conflict, until the council implicitly let it fall into abeyance after 1728.

Name: Lüneburg
Alternative_Name: Hliuni; Luniburc; Lhiuniburg; Luneburg; Liuniburch; Luneborch; Lunenburg
Settlement_Description: A place called Hliuni was first mentioned in 795. In 951 a castle was founded next to the settlement. A monastery of St Michael is attested in Ottonian times before 956, in combination with the local saltworks, which would be the backbone of the local economy for centuries.
Town_Description: Henry the Lion destroyed the neighbouring settlement Bardowick in 1189, after which Lüneburg gained prominence as an important centre of trade and acquired town privileges. Duke Otto the Child confirmed the rights in 1247; from 1273 Lüneburg held the privilege of being the sole salt producer in the duchy.
Fair_Description: Regulations for the cloth trade from the early 14th century show that two fairs were taking place in Lüneburg, on St Michael and on Sunday Jubilate. According to a document from 1360, the St Michael's market attracted visitors from Stade, Hamburg, Braunschweig, Hannover, the Rhineland, Hesse and Holland.
Staple_Description: According to ducal privileges from 1365, 1367 and 1369 one could only ship grain and wood out of town with permission of the council; the regulation included Winsen, Harburg, Bleckede and other places in the duchy from where grain and wood was shipped. The prescription to use the roads leading through Lüneburg followed in 1392 and was extended to include the drift of cattle in 1467 and 1497. It was compulsory to offer corn, hops, wood, cattle and fish for sale on the local market for 3 days. This compulsion was extended to all commodities in the 16th century. In addition, trading between foreign merchants was prohibited. The town also sought to extend the staple claims to the trade on the Aller and Elbe river systems, with limited success. In the 16th ships on the Elbe were increasingly forced to unload their goods in Bleckede and carry them to market in Lüneburg, which led to a conflict with Hamburg and Magdeburg, and in 1574 the stopping of the traffic on the Elbe was limited to ships carrying boy salt (from the Bay of Biscay) upstream. The staple was limited to the payment of a fee in the 18th century, and finally abolished in 1843.

Name: Maassluis
Alternative_Name: Mafelandersluse; Maselandersluys; Maeslandersluys; Maeslantse Sluys; Maaslandsluis; Sluis; Maassluisae
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1367. Maassluis originated at a lock ('sluis') in the sea dike around the Maasland region. Maassluis was elevated to town rank on 26 August 1814 by William I, king of the Netherlands.
Town_Description: NULL
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Brielle is first attested in 1365.
Harbour_Description: Maaslandsluis was part of Maasland. In the 16th century already some fishermen lived near the lock, at the end of this century this was a fast growing community. In 1555 harbour-heads and beacons were made for the fishermen. The Estates of Holland saw this harbour as an important chain in the traffic from Holland to Voorne and Zeeland via the ferry to Brielle. As a result the lock was fortified in 1571 (a 'schans' was made) against attacks by the Beggars. In 1614 the Estates gave permission to levy a tax during 24 year on fish in order to enlarge the harbour and erect a crane. With socalled 'hoekers' (boats) cod was caught. Usually some 50 boats for haddock  were harboured here but in 1636 only 10 as a result of hijackers from Dunkirk.

Name: Maastricht

Settlement_Description: Maastricht originated as a Roman settlement in 50 C.E. It was located on the road between Cologne and  Tongeren. In the third century, Maastricht was a religious centre (as the episcopal see was moved to Maastricht, untill the eighth century). In written records, Maastricht is first mentioned in 535 (ninth-century copy). In 643 a leper-house is found in Maastricht. The chapter of St. Servaas is first attested in 889, that of O.L.V. (St. Mary) in 1096. Both were ended in 1797. It became a trade centre in the ninth century, and in the twelfth century it developed into an important trade town. The socalled 'Alde Caert' from 1243 with the rights of the bishop of Liège in Maastricht mentions an ell ('mensura pannorum'). Statutes for the weavers and fullers are found in 1276. The oldest city-account from the year 1399/1400 mentions three weigh-houses: for fat, yarn and cloth ('vetwaag, garenwaag en gewantwaag').
Town_Description:
In the twelfth century, Maastricht developed into an important trade town. Most likely, town rights were granted before 12 November 1204.
Untill 1794, Maastricht is the condominium of the dukes of Brabant and the Prince-Bishops of Liège.
Fair_Description: In 919 a weekly-market is first found in Maastricht. Merchants from Maastricht are found in a toll-tariff for the fairs in Enns at the Donau-river in 1191. In 1243 three fairs and multiple day-markets in Maastricht are mentioned. In 1259 a safeconduct right is certified by the archbishop of Cologne for the merchants from Maastricht on their travels via Cologne to Hungary and vicinity. In 1332 the emperor certified toll-exemption of Nűrnberg in Maastricht. In 1335 merchants from Maastricht are first found on the fairs in Frankfurt. Mid 14th century Maastricht had its own cloth-hall there. In the first half of the 13th century the 'forum lignorum' (holtfair) is mentioned. In the 14th/15th century comital accounts of the steward a fair-toll levied in Maastricht from the charriots from Aix la Chapelle and Nűrnberg ('Noerenberch') is found. The fairs are then with St. Servatius (May 13), St. Remaclus (Sept. 3) and St. Remigius (Oct. 1), duration eight days before and after the fairdays. 'Wegehegelt' (tax on the roads) found in the only surviving medieval city-account dated 1399/1400 was levied during the fairs in 'Trijcht and Wijc' at the following gates ('poorten'): Hogebrugpoort and Symon Mertijnspoort (a small watergate) both in Wijc, St. Maartenspoort, Aldenhofspoort (possibly the old St. Pieterspoort), Lenculenpoort, Tweynbergerpoort, Hochterpoort (=Bospoort) and the Lendercrucepoort.
Staple_Description: Around 1500 Maastricht obtained the staple for raw woollen imported from Hessingen and Thüringen. It stayed there for most of the 16th century. The only surviving medieval city-account dated 1399/1400 already suggests a staple for wool from Cologne at Maastricht.

Name: Magdeburg
Alternative_Name: Meideborg; Magadoburg; Megdeburch; Magdeborch; Maidburg; Megdeborch; Meyborch
Settlement_Description: Originally a trading point with Slavs east of the Elbe. A castle built by Charlemagne is mentioned in 805, later an Ottonian palace. Seat of an archbishopric since 968.
Town_Description: In 1188 the Magdeburg town law is first securely attested, which would become the foundation for numerous other town rights in Central and Eastern Europe. In 1295 Magdeburg joined the Hanse.
Fair_Description: The most important and oldest fair in Magdeburg is the so-called "Herrenmesse" (lord's fair), which is first mentioned in a charter from 1179, but might be connected with an earlier mention from 1010. In 1448, two new three-day fairs were granted, but afterwards we don't hear about them anymore. Again in 1497, two three-day fairs were established, but these were forbidden only two years later by the Duke of Saxony, due to competition with the Leipzig fairs.
Toll_Description:
A toll in Magdeburg is first mentioned in 937, although it is unclear what character it had. In 1208 Otto IV relinquishes his right of toll and mint in favour of the archbishop. New tolls were not to be collected without the confirmation of the archbishop. In 1309 and 1324 the archbishop relinquishes some tolls, like the wine and bridge toll. Several tolls in the course of the Elbe river are also mentioned within the oldest fief records of the town of Magdeburg.
In 1463 an agreement between archbishop Frederick and Magdeburg settles that the council may collect part of the toll for the maintenance of the roads and bridges. The oldest toll tariffs date from 1478. A regulation of safe conduct remains from 1519, as well as a report on the practice of the regulations of safe conduct from 1571.
Staple_Description: Exclusive shipping rights on grain ('Kornverschiffungsrecht') for the archbishopric of Magdeburg are granted in 1309, which leads to decade-long conflicts with the archbishop. A contract from 1463 confirms Magdeburg town rights as well as free shipping rights on grain for the prelate, the clergy and knights, which was confirmed again in 1497. In the 16th century, the staple right were threatened by Leipzig, since Magdeburg was located in its zone of influence. This led to a contract with Hamburg concerning the protection of the staple rights of both towns in 1538. During the imperial ban 1547-1567 the staple in Magdeburg was revoked, but later re-established as a three-day depot right and mandatory turnover. In 1571 this is changed into a depot fee. Starting from 1596 it was handled as a depot and turnover right again. The destruction of the town during the Thirty Years' War (1631) meant an end of the staple, but soon thereafter there were several attempts to re-establish it. Shipping rights on grain were confirmed in 1638. The staple was finally abolished with the 'Elbschiffahrtsakte' in 1821.

Name: Mainz
Alternative_Name: Mogontiacum; Mogontia; Magancia; Maginza; Megenze; Meynce; Meintz; Meintze
Settlement_Description: By the end of the 1st century BC, Mainz was already serving as a Roman camp. First written evidence from 44 AD as 'Mogontiacum'.
Town_Description: Mainz was first referred to as a 'civitas' in 297 AD. In late Roman times, Mainz was the capital of a Roman province and served as a royal court under the Frankish rule. From 1244 to 1462 Mainz was a free imperial town.
Staple_Description: Beginnings are unclear; first documentary mention of a staple comes from the 1470s, including obligation to exchange and offer wares for sale; recognised by the emperor in 1486 and official confirmed in 1495. A tightening of the staple in 1534 led to conflict with the Count Palatine from 1542. During the Thirty Years’ War the staple was suspended, but was back in force by 1641 at the latest. The staple was dissolved in 1831 with the Rhine Shipping Act.

Name: Meiningen
Settlement_Description: Old Thuringian settlement and a royal Frankish court in the 8th/9th century. First mentioned in 982, in a copy from 1293. In the 11th century there existed a moated castle of the bishop of Würzburg, next to which the town developed.
Town_Description: Development of a town around 1200. Referred to as "civitas" in 1230. Acquisition of Schweinfurt town privileges in 1344.
Fair_Description: The oldest fairs in Meiningen date back to the foundation of the settlement. By 1565, their number had grown to eight, which were confirmed in that year by the counts of Henneberg and in 1612 by elector Johann Georg of Saxony. The latter also established two additional cattle markets on St Francis and St Martin and one horse market on Monday after Reminiscere. Name: Meißen

Settlement_Description: In the 10th century a German royal castle was constructed, below which a moated castle and a settlement developed. Bishopric since 968.
Town_Description: Foundation of a town probably around the middle of the 12th century. The town right was closely related to the Magdeburg town law.
Fair_Description: The fair on Saturday after Letare was moved from Lommatzsch to Meißen in 1475.

Name: Klaipėda

Settlement_Description: A Kurish wooden fortress from the early 13th century was conquered by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1252, who built Memelburg castle here.
Town_Description: A town was founded next to the castle in 1253. It acquired Lübeck town privileges in 1258 and Kulm town law in 1475.
Staple_Description: Memel began to oblige merchants from Königsberg to staple their wares in the city from 1522. Princely mandate in 1580 forbade any exports by see; repeated in 1619 and 1622.

Name: Merseburg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement in the Hersfelder Zehntverzeichnis (HZV A 212, HZV B 243). In the 10th cenutry, Merseburg becomes royal court and in 968 episcopal seat.
Town_Description: The royal privilige of market, coin and toll had to be granted before 981 and was confirmed in 1004. First mention of a council and burghers in 1289. Several privileges and registers are destroyed in a town fire in 1444, the "jurisdiction and freedom" of the town are restored in the same year. A more independent town constitution is achieved only after 1435, since the town was very dependent on the bishops.
Fair_Description: A fair took place until 1323, when a fire destroyed several booths on the market and foreign traders stayed away. It was not re-established, due to the growing influence of the fairs in Leipzig.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct in Merseburg also had special regulations during the time of the fairs in Leipzig; during this time, every passerby had to pay a fee until the fair ended, after that, the regular fees only had to be paid once if one returned in the course of four days.

Name: Minden
Alternative_Name: Mimda; Minda; Mimidona; Mindyn; Mimthum; Munthiun; Mimida; Mindonensis; Mimidomensis; Mindun; Mindunensis; Minde; Mundioborg; Mindon; Mynden
Settlement_Description: Fishing and shipping settlement near a ford on the Weser river, where a bishopric was founded by Charlemagne around 800. The settlement acquired toll, market and minting privileges in 977.
Town_Description: Minden developed into a town around 1230, with Dortmund town privileges. It is unknown on which date these privileges were exactly granted.
Fair_Description: In the 15th century, three fairs are mentioned in Minden: on the Nativity of the Virgin and St Gorgonius, on St Martin and on Candlemas. Of these fairs, at least the fair of St Martin can probably be traced back to the market and toll privilege of 977. In 1528, the number of fairs was reduced to two. Next to the fair of St Martin, a new fair was held on St Walburga. These fairs still exist today as the Autumn and May fairs.
Toll_Description: Toll privileges were granted in 977; in 1155-1206 the toll is still mentioned, among others in a conflict about tolls with Hameln. Possibly, the toll was levied since the 13th century at the harbour (Schlagde), until it was moved to Petershagen in 1377.
Staple_Description: Staple for corn and timber. Already around 1200, citizens from Hameln were exempted from toll, if they ended their journey in Minden. Skippers on the Werre were obliged in 1457 to offer their commodities on the market in Minden. In 1530, the free transport of firewood was prohibited. In Bremen, complaints that shipments of corn were being withheld in Minden are known from 1532, which led to a centuries-long conflict between both towns. The staple privileges were confirmed by the emperor in 1627, although it was enforced relatively mildly in the 17th century. The staple was finally abolished with the "Weserschifffahrtsakte" of 1823.

Settlement_Description: Fishing and shipping settlement near a ford on the Weser river, where a bishopric was founded by Charlemagne around 800. The settlement acquired toll, market and minting privileges in 977.
Town_Description: Minden developed into a town around 1230, with Dortmund town privileges. It is unknown on which date these privileges were exactly granted.
Fair_Description: In the 15th century, three fairs are mentioned in Minden: on the Nativity of the Virgin and St Gorgonius, on St Martin and on Candlemas. Of these fairs, at least the fair of St Martin can probably be traced back to the market and toll privilege of 977. In 1528, the number of fairs was reduced to two. Next to the fair of St Martin, a new fair was held on St Walburga. These fairs still exist today as the Autumn and May fairs.
Toll_Description: Toll privileges were granted in 977; in 1155-1206 the toll is still mentioned, among others in a conflict about tolls with Hameln. Possibly, the toll was levied since the 13th century at the harbour (Schlagde), until it was moved to Petershagen in 1377.
Staple_Description: Staple for corn and timber. Already around 1200, citizens from Hameln were exempted from toll, if they ended their journey in Minden. Skippers on the Werre were obliged in 1457 to offer their commodities on the market in Minden. In 1530, the free transport of firewood was prohibited. In Bremen, complaints that shipments of corn were being withheld in Minden are known from 1532, which led to a centuries-long conflict between both towns. The staple privileges were confirmed by the emperor in 1627, although it was enforced relatively mildly in the 17th century. The staple was finally abolished with the "Weserschifffahrtsakte" of 1823.

Name: Münster (Westfalen)
Alternative_Name: Münster; Monasterium; Mimigernaford; Mimegardevurdensis; Mimmegardeuurdensis; Mimiernevordi; Munstre; Munstere; Monastre; Monasteriensis; Monestere
Settlement_Description: The foundation of Münster was related to missionary activities of St Ludger. A monastery was founded in 793, and a diocese in 799. The settlement is first mentioned by name in 819. A market settlement developed next to the cathedral.
Town_Description: Around 1170 Münster was was first characterised as town. Town privileges were granted gradually. After the anabaptist rebellion of 1534/5, town privileges were temporarily suspended, but re-conferred in 1541 and 1553.
Fair_Description: The two most important fairs in Münster were connected with the annual diocesan synods, hence they were called 'Send'. Although the Send as market is first mentioned only in 1525, it was much older. The synods are first mentioned in 889; around 1282/1290 their dates were recorded as the Mondays after Sunday Letare and the day of St Gereon and St Victor - from 1652 on the Tuesdays after these days. According to Kerssenbroick's history of the Anabaptist rebellion (ca. 1570), the fairs started on Monday midnight and lasted three days. Two other five-day fairs took place on St Peter and Paul's Day and St Jerome's Day (Dedication day of the Cathedral), but were less significant than the Send fairs. Especially the fair of St Jerome is not mentioned anymore after 1538/1550 because of its insignificance. Additionally, Kerssenbroick mentions three cattle markets, which were held in front of the St Liudger and Jüdefeld gates.

Name: Narva
Settlement_Description:
The settlement developed on an old and important trading route at the beginning of the 13th century. In 1277, a Danish castle was mentioned for the first time, which was probably built around 1256.
In 1492, Ivan III built a castle called Ivangorod on the right bank of the river. Since then, it was distinguished between the Russian and Estonian part of the town.
Town_Description: At the end of the 14th century the village developed into a town and was referred to as 'civitas' in 1329. Town privileges by Lübeck and Reval were confirmed in 1345. In 1347, Narva belonged to the Teutonic Order.

Name: Nauen
Settlement_Description: Findings from the Stone Age, as well as Germanic and Slavic times. Priests in Nauen are mentioned in 1186 and 1197.
Town_Description: The Margraves of Brandenburg acquire the land in 1292 and grant the right to build a town hall. First mentioned as town in 1305. Additional privileges are granted in 1315 and 1317. Brandenburg town law is mentioned in 1429.
Fair_Description: Two fairs were held in Nauen in the Middle Ages, after the construction of the town hall in 1302. In 1345 one fair is explicitly mentioned.
Toll_Description: A toll was levied by the town on the causeway constructed north of the town ('Dammpfennig'); it was sold in 1326 to the cathedral chapter in Brandenburg. Engel et al. mention Nauen as a royal main toll station only since 1805.

Name: Naumburg (Saale)
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by margrave Ekkehard around 1000, it is first mentioned in 1012. Naumburg was given to the bishopric of Zeitz in 1028, soon after which the episcopal residence moved to Naumburg and formed the basis for the town’s initial development.
Town_Description: In 1033, merchants who moved from Kleinjena to Naumburg were granted the freedom of trade and the inheritable possession of their homesteads. This record is regarded as the oldest record of a German town foundation. Referred to as civitas in 1142. A privilege for fortification of the town was granted in 1287, a council is attested in 1305. The town developed into an important market for the long-distance trade in the 14th and 15th century. A trading house was built in 1379. Jews were allowed to settle in the city in 1410. Between 1432 and 1433 Naumburg was a member of the Hanse. The council bought judicial sovereignty in 1486.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Naumburg are first mentioned in 1278, but probably date back to the early days of the town in the 11th century. The most important fair was the fair on St Peter and Paul's Day, which attracted an interregional public since the 15th century. In the 16th century, the Naumburg fairs led to heavy resistance from Leipzig, who had acquired an exclusive fair privilege within 15 miles around the city in 1507, inside which the city of Naumburg was located. The Peter and Paul's fair survived these quarrels, but not a second fair on Holy Thursday, which was intended to be moved to Sexagesima in 1514. Heavy resistance from Leipzig led to its ultimate revocation in 1667. Instead another fair on Monday after Palm Sunday was allowed, but without extended privileges for foreign merchants. It is known until today as the Topfmarkt and was moved to Friday after Easter in 1894.
Toll_Description: In 1397 the bishop abstained from the toll in Naumburg in favour of the town. Twenty years later the salt toll was given to the town by the bishop. The extensive toll registry of Naumburg lists all the wares upon which one had to pay a fee on the market (StA Naumburg, Rep. XLVII – 2 – 1567).

Name: Neuss
Alternative_Name: Neuß; Nussiam; Novaesium; Nouesium; Niuisium; Niuisi; Neusz; Nuys; Nuysse; Nuyß
Settlement_Description: The Roman fortress Novaesium was founded around 16 BC on the shore of the Rhine. In the vicinity a trading settlement developed that became the old town of Neuss. In Carolingian times a castle is mentioned here.
Town_Description: Neuss is first characterised as "oppidum" in 1170 and probably became a full town around 1200. The oldest town seal dates from 1245. Various privileges were granted in the next centuries. Among others, Neuss was granted the privileges of a Hanse town in 1475 by emperor Frederick III.
Fair_Description: It is unknown when the fairs in Neuss originated. In the 14th century, there were three fairs, on St Walpurga, St John and St Remigius. A fourth one on St Bartholomew was added before 1419. The four fairs were confirmed by emperor Frederick III in 1475, who also granted a fifth fair on St Martin. All fairs were to last four days before and after the said dates. The St Walpurga fair, which coincided with the feast on the dedication day of the church of St Quirinus, attracted most visitors, together with St John's fair in the 15th and 16th centuries.

Name: Nijmegen
Alternative_Name: Nimwegen; Ulpia Noviomagus; Noviomagus; Municipium Batavorum; Nieumegen; Nieumeghen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 98-117. Around 98, emperor Trajanus granted market privileges and the title Ulpia Noviomagus to the settlement. In the second century, possibly in 161, town privileges were granted. In the second half of the eight century, a royal palace ('palts'/ 'pfalz') was built.
Town_Description: Nijmegen is mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1204. Town privileges similar to the town privileges granted to other free imperial cities are granted to Nijmegen by Henry VII, on behalf of his father, Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, on 31 August 1230. The palace and the city were acquired by the count of Guelders Otto II in 1247, who moved the central market place next to the newly founded parish church of St Stephen. A burgomaster and councillors are first mentioned in 1282. Most taverns and inns were located in the Grotestraat: the street between the town square and the town gate to the river Waal which was located next to the crane and called 'Kraanpoort'.
Fair_Description: In Nijmegen, two fairs already existed before 1294/95. In the sixteenth century, an oxen fair was added on St. Victor's Day. Two horse fairs were instituted during the Gueldern Wars. Those fairs existed for three years only, between 1540 and 1543. In Nijmegen, three days of each fair were dedicated to cloth trade.
Staple_Description: Statutes from 1468 (in the 'keurboek') mention a staple on woad. It was related to the wool-dyeing which flourished in the fourteenth century, and died out in the fifteenth century. The related cloth hall is first mentioned in 1382, and lost its function at least before 1542, when it was remodeled. Gorissen suspects that this staple has been of limited importance.

Name: Norden
Settlement_Description: The village of Norden developed from the merger of the two hamlets Ekel and Lintel, which are first mentioned in 785.
Town_Description: A central market place was established in the first half of the 13th century. Norden is documented in 1255 as the centre of the land of Norden and must have had a town-like character at that time. In 1455 the town had two mayors, in 1498 it had a town seal and in 1535 town regulations are known. However, a year for the acquisition of town rights is unknown.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Norden are first explicitly mentioned in 1440 in a letter of safe conduct. They are also mentioned in the town regulations of 1535. Dates are only known later: the fair of St James in the mid-16th century, the Pentecost market in 1598, and the large three-day autumn cattle fair ('Beestmarkt') on the day before St Martin. All of these fairs must have been older.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of East Frisia was levied in Norden. In 1497, it was specified that commodities for which toll had already been paid in Norden were exempted from toll in Emden. For each horse or piece of cattle 1 Krummstert had to be paid. A more specific list of toll fees for various commodities is known from 1629. A toll register exists for the years 1596-1599.

Town_Description: Nordhausen is declared free imperial city before 1220. Probably around 1180.

Name: Oldenburg (Oldenburg)
Settlement_Description: Residence of the counts of Oldenburg from ca. 1150.
Town_Description: Bremen town privileges were granted in 1345, but the settlement already had an urban character before: fairs and burghers are first mentioned in 1243, a magistrate court around 1300, and a council and town seal in 1307.
Fair_Description: Two fairs in Oldenburg are mentioned in an agreement between Oldenburg and Bremen from 1243, on St Vitus and St Margaret. These two markets are also mentioned in 1307, together with a fair on St Lambert (17-9), and in the town privileges from 1345, no less than seven fairs are mentioned. However, it is the question whether these were organised for a long time: in the 15th century, only St Vitus's and St Margaret's fairs are still mentioned. In the "Verordnung wegen der Oldenburger Krahmer-Marckte" from 1608, it is mentioned that there were four traditional fairs. However, older evidence for the two additional markets, on St Michael and Quasimodogeniti, is not known.
Toll_Description: An agreement from 1243 grants merchants from Bremen exemption from tollsin Oldenburg and free conduct. Oldenburg citizens complained in 1383 that the Count had increased the tolls to be paid by citizens from Bremen, Wildeshausen and Friesoythe. More specific toll amounts are known from the 15th century (1428) for beer, salt, oil, corn and other commodities.
Staple_Description: An agreement with Bremen limited the trade of merchants from Bremen and Westfalia in Oldenburg to the fairs on St Vitus and St Margaret. This restriction was removed in 1278, but there still existed the obligation for external merchants travelling through town to offer their commodities for sale on the market.

Name: Osnabrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in ca. 772. The cathedral, which belonged to the bishopric founded by Charlemagne, was probably dedicated in 787. The merchant settlement acquired market, toll and minting privileges in 1002.
Town_Description: Characterised as "civitas" since 1147. Emperor Frederick I granted town privileges to Osnabrück in 1171.
Fair_Description: The oldest fairs in Osnabrück went back to the market privilege of 1002. Before 1190, two four-day fairs are mentioned, the "Herrenmesse" of the Dedication of the cathedral on St Crispin and Crispinian, and on mid-Lent. From 1190, a third fair, the "new fair" was held on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, which disappeared in the late 15th century. The large fairs were especially important as markets for the locally produced cloth, and attracted visitors from as far as Bremen, Lippstadt, Dortmund, Wesel, Xanten and Deventer. Smaller fairs of a single day were held on the dedication days of the churches of the Franciscan, Dominican, Augustinian and Teutonic knights' monasteries.
Toll_Description: The bishop of Osnabrück levied a market toll since the foundation of the market. A third part of the toll which was levied on the "new" fair on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross was ceded to the cathedral chapter in 1190. The toll of the fair on the cathedral square is mentioned in 1242 as "thelonium cimiterii". From 1359 the toll was mostly leased out, with the exception of the toll on salt. The latter was finally also leased to the burgomaster in 1487. The citizens of Osnabrück were exempted from toll payments between 1388 and 1424.

Name: Paderborn
Alternative_Name: Padrabrunno; Padresbrunnon; Patrisbrunna; Phadrabrunnen; Patresbrunnas; Patherbrunnen; Paderbrunno; Padrabrunnensis; Bodarbrunnensis; Paterebrunne; Boderebronnen; Patherburnensis; Paderburnensis; Parborna; Patherborne
Settlement_Description: Location of a Carolingian palace since 776; in 777 mention of the Salvator church; since 805/06 seat of a diocese. The palace and the cathedral were surrounded by a fortification from the beginning, a wooden-earth construction, which was replaced by a wall in 777. Around 900 the place was called 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: The settlement received market, toll and mint privileges in 1028 at the latest. In the 13th century, the town freed itself of the overlordship of the bishop and acquired legal freedom, which was recorded in a charter in 1327. A town council is mentioned in 1238.
Fair_Description: Paderborn acquired market privileges in 1028. The oldest fair was that of St Gallus, which is mentioned in 1327 as taking place in front of the western town gate according to old custom. It was mainly used for agricultural products. A second fair of St John appears in the early 16th century; it was replaced by bishop Erich in 1521 with two new fairs, on the Chair of St Peter and on Mary Magdalene. Both fairs had three free market days before and after the fair day. In the town accounts from 1575, two other fairs, on Annunciation Day and St Nicholas, are mentioned; they might have been introduced after 1521.
Toll_Description: There were three tolls in Paderborn:<br/> 1) The market toll of the bishop, granted in 1028, was a tax on bought and sold commodities in town. Before 1301, the toll was acquired by the noble Schilder family, in the service of the bishop, and the toll became known as the Schilderzoll. It was probably levied in the Schildern alley, which might have been named after the family and the toll. In the 15th century, the toll was sold to Paderborn citizens and in 1491 to the town. Afterwards it was turned into a road toll.<br/> 2) The "small toll" belonged to the family Endehachte, who sold it to the cathedral treasurer in 1311. Further details are not known.<br/> 3) A fee for safe conduct, called "gheleyde", owned by the lords of Lippe at the beginning of the 14th century. It was sold to bishop Heinrich III in 1367. According to a 16th-century document, this toll was levied on commodities bought by foreigners in Paderborn territory and transported through town. Inhabitants of the territory were exempted from the toll. Some registers of this toll exist from the 16th century.

Name: Pirna
Settlement_Description: There was a Slavic pre-settlement. In the 11./12th century a castle was built. Close to that, there were two fishermen's settlements and a market place since 1200, which was further expanded.
Town_Description: Margrave Heinrich III of Meißen granted Magdeburg town privileges between 1234 and 1245.
Toll_Description: The toll on the Elbe in Pirna is first mentioned in 1269 and was closely connected to the staple. The oldest known tariffs date from 1325, which also mention a land toll for salt wagons. The toll was regulated quite minutely, as well as the duties of the ferrymen. The fee registry mentions that whatever cannot be found listed, should be looked for in the list of Königsstein (Elbe). The registry differentiates between the safe conduct on the water and by land. Returning boats were exempt from the toll. The regulations of safe-conduct do not mention rafts, which leads to believe that traffic with large transport rafts only began from Pirna. It appears to be the starting point of trade down the Elbe river.
Staple_Description: Originally only a staple for salt and grain and a compulsory exchange of goods; later a general staple. The staple is first mentioned in 1291 upon sale of the town; confirmed in 1325. In 1520 and 1565 merchants from Dresden are partially excepted.

Name: Praha
Settlement_Description: NULL
Town_Description: NULL
Toll_Description: Accounts of revenues of tolls in Prague exist for 1311-13 and 1315-23. This was a toll on commodities. In 1331 a wagon toll for the maintenance of the pavement was installed.
Staple_Description: The privilege of King Wenzel II confirmed the staple rights of the old town, with a ban on guest trading and a stay time of five days where guests were obliged to offer their wares for sale. In 1351 trade with foreign merchants in Bohemia and Moravia was restricted to Prague. Staple for wood in Podskal in 1341; expanded to include citizens of the new town in 1356; staple for salt fish established in the new town in 1367. In 1393 further restrictions on guest trading and obligations to use certain roads; repeated in 1415. Staple rights were never complete (they never covered internal Bohemian trade), but they did include an obligation to offer wares for sale. Privileges renewed in 1497 and 1527, but proved difficult to enforce except for the fish staple in the new town which were mentioned again in 1627 and 1649.

Name: Quedlinburg
Settlement_Description: The place traces its roots to an old saxonian estate, which is mentioned in 922 as a ludolfing farmyard. In the 10th and 11th century Quedlinburg becomes an important palace for the saxonian kings, after Henry I. is buried here. The saxonian kings like to have their Easter celebration here.
Town_Description:
In 1327 the former separated communities of the Old City (founded during 10th century) and the New City (founded during the 12th century) are put together under one council.
In 1477 the city succumbs to the regency of the abbess of Quedlinburg monastery, which lets the city lose its autonomy.
Fair_Description: The exact dates of the fairs in Quedlinburg are unknown. One mention occurred in 1585, when a large flood happened during a fair. The exact date of the flood or fair is not mentioned. Because of a plague epidemic a fair on St. Martin's day was cancelled in 1598.

Name: Rīga
Alternative_Name: Riga; civitas tho der Righe; Rige; Ryga; Ryge; Riega
Settlement_Description: The settlement was founded in 1201 by Bishop Albert. The first episcopal palatinate was built before 1234. Shortly after 1202 a castle of the Teutonic Order was built, which was destroyed by the Rigans in 1297. A new castle was therefore built in 1330.
Town_Description: German citizens from Gotland and Germany received Gotland town rights in 1211 and Hamburg town rights in 1294/97. In 1350, however, they got their own Rigian town privileges.
Staple_Description: Staple for the trade along the River Duna. The ban on trade in the Semgaller region [?] formed the basis of the Riga staple. In 1229 all merchants given free passage along the Duna, but privilege withdrawn in the 14th century. Overseas merchants not allowed to trade with Smolensk via the Duna, while Russian and Lithuanian merchants not allowed to trade in the Baltic via the Duna. Riga reported to Lübeck in 1468 a ban on guest trading in their city (HR II, 6 n 143). From 1406 merchants from Polozk free from the Riga staple; in return (until 1498) merchants from Riga freed from the Polozk staple.

Name: Roermond
Alternative_Name: Ruremunde; Roremunt; Ruregemunde, Roremonde; Ruremonde; Rurgemunde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1130. The count of Guelders acquired a domain in Roermond before 1189 and founded the Cistercian monastery Munsterabdij there shortly before 1218. A hospital is found in 1259.
Town_Description: Earliest mention as a town ('oppidum') in 1224. The exact year in which town privileges have been granted is unknown, but this must have been between 16 June 1224 and 22 October 1229 by Gerard IV, count of Guelders. A burgomaster and town council is first mentioned in 1329.
Fair_Description:
Roermond had three fairs: on Tuesday after Pentecost (known since 1294/5), St. Remi and St. Barbara (since 1351). A weighing house for wool (libramentum lane) is mentioned in 1294/5, a cloth hall in 1347. From 1354 onwards inhabitants of Roermond are found on the fairs of Frankfurt. A ducal charter of 1372 extended all fairs in Roermond to 16 days and introduced a fourth fair, of which the date is however unknown.
In 1562 king Philip II granted three fairs with three days safeconduct because of the townfire in 1554: 1) Wednesday before mid-lent, 2) June 12 and 3) Nov. 7. In 1589 he consented another two fairs on Jan. 25 jan. and July 20. In 1596 there are six fairs: another one on the Tuesday and Wednesday after Pentecost.
Toll_Description: Next to the safe conduct on the Meuse, the Count of Guelders also levied a fee for safe conduct on land in 1226/53. Tariffs are not known. In 1284, 8 mark a year were collected.
Staple_Description: Roermond was granted an eight-day staple in 1372 for those outside Gelre and Julich on goods transported through the Maas river, which was moved to Venlo in 1523. It is being questioned whether this staple right has been effective. In 1578 king Philip II granted a privilege that in the 'ambt' (region) Montfort all lime, marl and coal in Roermond had to be transshipped.

Name: Roosendaal
Settlement_Description: Roosendaal is first mentioned in 1268. It was elevated to city rank on 3 May 1809 by Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland. This elevation, however, lasted only untill 1814.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: In 1552 the magistrate of the village Rosendale asked the prince of Orange, as there were passing a lot of horses from Holland, permission for two horse- and other cattlefairs like in Hoogstraten. One to be organised in Spring, one in Autumn. There were already two fairs, one the day after the 'Kermis' (carnival) and one after St. John Baptist (June 24), each to be freed for eight days. As there came much flax and other measurable merchandise they asked for a weigh-house. They also asked permission to install a roadtoll, like in Bergen (op Zoom) and Oudenbosch and elswehere is asked from them. As 'straatgeld' (street-tax) per barrel beer 1/2s. is levied to maintain the big paved roads. In 1572 (Jan. 25) a yearly horsefair is granted on Sept. 20 and the next days, when paying  6 'Arthois' of each 40 groten.

Fair_Description: In 1552 the magistrate of the village Rosendale asked the prince of Orange, as there were passing a lot of horses from Holland, permission for two horse- and other cattlefairs like in Hoogstraten. One to be organised in Spring, one in Autumn. There were already two fairs, one the day after the 'Kermis' (carnival) and one after St. John Baptist (June 24), each to be freed for eight days. As there came much flax and other measurable merchandise they asked for a weigh-house. They also asked permission to install a roadtoll, like in Bergen (op Zoom) and Oudenbosch and elswehere is asked from them. As 'straatgeld' (street-tax) per barrel beer 1/2s. is levied to maintain the big paved roads. In 1572 (Jan. 25) a yearly horsefair is granted on Sept. 20 and the next days, when paying  6 'Arthois' of each 40 groten.

Name: Rotterdam
Alternative_Name: Rotter dam ter haluer rotte; Rotterdamme; Rotterdam ter haluer Rotte; Bokelsambacht
Settlement_Description: Rotterdam is first mentioned in the period 1280-1287. Rotterdam originates from two seperate settlements, each on either side of the River Rotte. Together, these former settlements make up Rotterdam. In the fourteenth century, Rotterdam grows into a town-like settlement. A hospital is first found in 1329.
Town_Description:
Rotterdam was already granted town rights in 1299; however, this grant was soon withdrawn. In the grant of 7 June 1340, by William IV, count of Holland (William II, count of Hainaut), no mention is made of earlier town privileges. 
One of the smaller ‘Kamers’ (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Rotterdam.
Fair_Description: The old town-right of 1340 stated two fairs of each 8 days, whenever they liked it. The comital account of 1343/'4 mentions a market-toll with St. Margaret (July 13): 5 lb. 2sc., and with St. Bartholomeus (August 24): 50 sc. In 1363 the last one is altered to: Mary Magdalenaday (July 22). In 1412 the town obtained two free fairs of each 14 days: 1) St. Margaret, 2) St. Bartholomeus. The town had to pay count Willem 6 pound yearly for this. In 1472 this fee is bought off from Charles the Bold. The early 15th century charterbook mentions two fairs of each 14 days, 1) first Sunday after H. Ascensioens day (Ascension), on Wednesday afterwards the first 'toochdag' (display day) of horses and other goods from of old, 2): O.L.V. dag Assumptio (August 15), 4 days later on August 19 the first toochdag of horses. The location of the fair for horses is in the Lombardtstraat on de Meent next  to the chapel. Yields of the farming out of both the market-tolls are edited for the years 1344-1479. In 1565 (August) king Philip II granted a free fair for leather, to compensate the huge fire of 1563. In 1580 (Jan. 21) surrrounding towns react on the request of Rotterdam dated 1579 29 Oct. for a free seed-fair. On 28 May king Philip II granted a free fair for seeds and leather, in order to compensate the decaying fishery and drapery as a result of the war. Dates: August 12 for 8 days. Regarding this an agreement with Delft was made on May 16.

Name: Schiedam
Alternative_Name: dicho de Scie; Scheidam; Novum Sciedammum; Nuwen Sciedamme; Niewendamme; Sciedam; Nieuwendamme; Scyedamme; Nuwer Scie
Settlement_Description: Schiedam is first mentioned in 1204, according to Van Berkel & Samplonius. Cox mentions a later date, 1264. In the river Schie, a dam was built in 1250. Schiedam was a small port town on the trade routes over the rivers Meuse and Schie. However, the port suffered from sedimentation. The importance of the port diminished in the fourteenth century, when Rotterdam en Delft got a connection to the Meuse. A hospital is found in 1276.
Town_Description: Schiedam was granted town rights on 18 March 1275 by Adelaide of Holland (lady of Schiedam).
Fair_Description: In 1270 (May 29) count Floris V granted together with his aunt ex-regentes Aleid a fair in Schiedam. He gave alle visitors safe-conduct and protection in his countship on the fair and weekly-market. In 1346 (August)  countess Margret donated the market-field to the town. In 1468 (St. Bavo) the fair is moved because St. Bavo (Oct. 1) was a holy day. The fair will now start the first working day after St. Bavo, the freedom however starts with St. Bavo. In 1484 (Febr. 22) Maximiliaan of Oostenrijk granted a free horse-fair on the second Friday in March. The market-rights would be equal to those in Delft and Rotterdam. The yields are destined to improve the harbour. In 1488 (Oct. 3) the town obtained (another?) horse-fair starting 'grote Vastenavond' (Shrove Tuesday) during 8 days, with equael tolls as in Delft and Rotterdam. In 1559/'60 (March 8) king Philip II granted two free fairs. The walled town only had herring-catch as a mean of subsistence, which was in decay since (15)52 as a result of the war with France where many busses were lost. This was cause for one-third of the poverty. Dates: 1) July 5 when the herringbusses had to be provided, 2) Oct. 3 when the citizens provided themselves for the winter, each for 14 days. In 1601 (March 27) The Estates of Holland granted a meager cattle-fair on the day after Allsaints (Nov. 2), or when this was a Sunday the day after that.

Name: Schleswig
Alternative_Name: Slesvig; Sliesthorp; Sliaswich; Slesuuic; Sliaswig; Sleswich; Sleswic; Slésvík; Sleswyk; Slesvic; Slæswich; Sleswig; Sljasvig
Settlement_Description: The predecessor of Schleswig was Haithabu (Danish: Hedeby), the largest town (emporium) in Viking age Scandinavia. Haithabu was located at the southern side of Slien, a narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea, but in the 11th century Haithabu was abandoned, and Schleswig developed on the opposite northern side of Slien. Already in 948 a bishop of Schleswig is mentioned in an Ottonian charter, but if the bishop actually resided in Schleswig at this point is not clear. The emporium of Haithabu as well as Viking age Schleswig was the main transshipment point in long-distance trade between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a 'civitas' in 1196; The Schleswig town law developed in the late 12th century.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions three fairs in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein, but does not provide dates. An almanac printed in 1598 in Neudamm (Dębno) mentions a fair on the Beheading of St John the Baptist.

Name: Schwerin
Alternative_Name: Zuarin; Zverin; Zuerin; Zwerin; Cwerin; Swerin
Settlement_Description: Slavic settlement and castle, first mentioned in 1018. Schwerin became the centre of Christian missionary activity in 1155, seat of a bishop in 1160.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by Duke Henry the Lion in 1160. In 1266, the old town was extended by a new town. Schwerin became the capital of the duchy of Mecklenburg in 1348.
Fair_Description: A fair in Schwerin is first attested in 1171. It took place on the dedication day of the cathedral, 9 september. Another market took place on 15 June since 1248. Until 1222 a fair was also held on Maundy Thursday.

Name: Spandau
Alternative_Name: Berlin-Spandau; Spandow; Spandowe; Zpandow; Zpandowe; Spandaw; Spandawe
Settlement_Description: First traces of settlement have been dated to the 8th century and a Slavic castle existed into the 12th century. In 1197 the German castle is first mentioned and first traces of a German settlement could be dated to the beginning of the 13th century. Around 1200 the settlement around the castle mound in Spandau was abandoned and moved further north, where it became a market settlement around the church of St Nicholas.
Town_Description: The charter that grants the settlement next to the castle Brandenburg town rights in 1232 is a forgery; the actual awarding of the town rights presumably occurred around 1240 after a fire.
Toll_Description: Wagoners had to pay a toll as early as 1320 as well as a street toll ('Deichselpfennig') later on.
Staple_Description: A temporary staple in Spandau is mentioned in a complaint of the Elector in 1450.

Name: Stade
Settlement_Description: The fortress and settlement was first mentioned when it was destroyed by Vikings in 994. Around 1000 the settlement became the seat of the counts of Stade.
Town_Description: King Otto IV granted town privileges in 1209; they were confirmed in 1236.
Fair_Description: Stade acquired the market privilege in 1038; the oldest fair took place on St James's Day. A second fair on Tuesday after Easter is first mentioned in 1593, as well as a horse market on Letare Sunday. A second horse market eight days before Lent was renewed in 1670, but it is unknown when it was first organised. In 1692, St James's fair had a duration of 14 days, the Easter fair 8 days.
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Bremen introduced a market toll in 1038, and in connection to the 1259 staple privilege a toll on the Elbe traffic at the mouth of the Schwinge (see Stadersand). Moreover, a toll existed on cattle driven through town, as well as a wine toll (mentioned in 1487 and 1530).
Staple_Description: In 1259, Archbishop Hildebrand of Bremen founded the Stade staple, which forced all ships coming from the sea to stay in Stade for 3 tides. The staple led to conflicts with Hamburg, which managed to acquire exemption from the staple in Stade in 1340. In the long run, it proved to be impossible to enforce the staple for other seafarers as well. Next to Hamburg and Buxtehude, Stade was a staple market for grain along the Elbe, as confirmed in a treaty from 1487. Staple of the English Merchant Adventurers in 1577-1597 and 1602-1611.
Harbour_Description: The harbour of Stade was located at the Schwinge river. A crane is first mentioned in 1337.

Name: Stendal
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1022. In the 10th century there already existed a small village.
Town_Description: The settlement received market and town rights in 1160 according to the Magdeburg Law. In the 13th century the Stendal seafarer guild was founded. Between 1350 and 1515 Stendal was a member of the Hanse.
Fair_Description: Stendal had three fairs, their dates and durations are unknown. During the siege of Magdeburg between 1547 and 1554, the Magdeburg market and staple was moved to Tangermünde, Stendal and Brandenburg. Since 1563 it was allowed to hold cattle and horse markets on two of the Stendal fair days. A fair on Sunday Exaudi is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) from 1598. A new cattle fair on Monday after St Gall was granted in 1643. Another fair was granted in 1672, which took place in the week after second Advent: a cattle fair on Monday, and a commodity market on Tuesday to Thursday.
Staple_Description: The market and staple rights of Magdeburg were moved to Tangermünde, Stendal and Brandenburg in 1547-1554, due to the siege of Magdeburg.
