Name: Szczecin
Alternative_Name: Stettin; Stettyn; Stetin; Stetyn; Stityn; Stityn; Stitinum; Olden Stettin; Stetina; Stetinam; Stetinenses; Sthetin; Statine; Alten Stettin; Altstettin; Alt-Stettin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1091 as ducal castle. Two German market settlements developed in its vicinity in 1124-1129.
Town_Description: In 1243 the Magdeburg town law was granted by Duke Barnim I of Pomerania after both market settlements were merged.
Toll_Description: A toll erected in 1311 for citizens of the Mark of Brandeburg, who wished to circumvent the Stettin staple.
Staple_Description: First regulations restricting the grain trade in Pomerania to Stettin in 1253 and 1281; staple rights followed in 1283, with obligation to exchange wares and the forbidding of transports on the tributaries of the Oder and the banning of guest trading. Exemptions existed for citizens of Gartz and Greifenhagen and from the Mark of Brandenburg, who after payment of a toll were allowed to pass through Stettin in the same ship. Expansion of staple privileges in 1312. Around the middle of the 15th century a dispute between Stettin and Stargard over the bypassing of the Stettin staple by shipping on the river Ihna was settled in favour of Stettin. Confirmation of the staple followed in 1467, including the stipulation that all wares on ships coming from the sea into the Stettin lagoon and wares entering Stettin overland from the Oder basin should be stapled in Stettin. In 1475 merchants were obliged to store herring in Stettin for three days. Abolition of the staple in 1752, after which Stettin enjoyed only a monopoly over the linseed trade.

Name: Stralsund
Alternative_Name: Stralowe; Stralesund; Sund; Thom Sunde; Sundis; Stralsundt
Settlement_Description: Fishing settlement in Slavic times, German settlers since ca. 1200. First mentioned when it became a town in 1234.
Town_Description: Prince Wistzlaw I of Rügen granted the same town privileges as Rostock (Lübeck town law) in 1234.
Staple_Description: Staple for stockfish from Bergen; in 1446 members of the Hanse only allowed to export flour, malt, and other victuals to Bergen if they brought fish from Bergen back with them to Lübeck, Wismar, Rostock or Stralsund.

Name: Suhl
Settlement_Description: Salt and natural resource deposits facilitated early settlement in the region. In 1445 Suhl became a borough ('Flecken').
Town_Description: Granted town rights by William VI., count of Henneberg.
Fair_Description: In 1544 Wilhelm IV. of Henneberg Schleusingen is given three fair privileges by emperor Karl V. Another is added in 1599. In 1661 the fairs were moved from Sundays to Tuesdays.
Toll_Description: Toll registries show the tolls that had to be paid in Suhl in 1502 and 1524. (ThStA Meiningen, Sekt. III Nr. 510 (1502); ThStA Meiningen, Sekt. III 510 (A 14b) Nr. 3).)

Name: Toruń
Settlement_Description: NULL
Town_Description: NULL
Staple_Description: In the late 14th century, the city attempted to create a staple market, which led to conflicts with Cracow. Both cities gave up their staples in 1391, but as Cracow started to force merchants to offer their wares on the market in 1398, Toruń received new rights from the Grand Master, which included a staple with limitations to the streets to be used for commodities exported from Poland (wax, furs, metals and spices) and imported cloth from England. When the staple lost importance after the peace of Thorn in 1411, it was reinstated in 1428 and now included corn; confirmed in 1448 with the inclusion of river transport, and again by King Casimir in 1457 after Toruń became Polish. The staple was cancelled after 1466, with the exception of the obligation to travel only on roads leading through town. Attempts to reinstate the staple led to many conflicts with other cities, until all obligations were annulled in 1496. There were renewed attempts to establish a staple in the 16th century, which was confirmed by the Pope in 1516. The King decided in 1533 that ships on the Vistula heading upstream had to unload in Toruń, although the full staple was not acknowledged. A renewed obligation to travel via Toruń from Danzig to Poland was instated, but cancelled in 1537 again, with the exemption of fish. In the 17th century, only the fish staple still existed.

Name: Tiel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 850-865 (possibly 855), in a copy of 1170-1175. In 893, Tiel is mentioned as an 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: Tiel was probably granted town privileges by Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI between 1191 and 1197. It is first mentioned as a town in 1195.
Fair_Description: At least from 1447 onward, an unknown number of fairs were held in Tiel. From a source probably dating from the fifteenth century, it is known that four fairs were held in Tiel. One horse fair, a cattle fair, and two cloth fairs.

Name: Tongeren

Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in c. 390, in a sixth and ninth century copy.
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: Tongeren was situated on the Roman road ('heerbaan') between Maastricht and Tienen. In 980 emperor Otto II donated the toll on merchandise traded in the town to the bishop. Name: Utrecht
Alternative_Name: Traiecto; Treiecto; Vttrecht; Ulterius Traiectum; Vultaburch; Vultraiectum; Inferius Traectum; Utreth
Settlement_Description: A 'castellum' (fort) was built at the location of the present-day Domplein in Roman times. It is first mentioned in 300 (in seventh-, eight- and tenth-century copies of the document). Later, the settlement became an episcopal see and a religious centre. Around 925 when the Vikings were gone the bishop returned from Deventer. In 936 the bishop granted mint-rights and in 953 the revenues from the toll at Muiden situated at the mouth of the river Vecht. In the 11th and early 12th century a vicus called Stathe originated west of the castle of the bischop with the first markets.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted between 1114 and 2 June 1122 by Godebald, bishop of Utrecht. The privileges were extended in the 12th and 13th century.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Utrecht probably originate in the 10th or early 11th century. Four fairs are mentioned in 1127, with a duration of two weeks: on Easter, St John the Baptist, Birth of Mary and St Martin. They were visited by merchants from a large region, especially the Rhineland. By the late 14th century, they had lost importance and were reduced to three days. In 1378, they were replaced by three new fairs: three days after Palm Sunday and St Victor and three days before Ascension Day. These seem to have been predominantly cattle and horse markets. A fourth fair, on St Pontian, was added in 1533 and was more important as a festival than for trading. It was merged with the dedication festival of the cathedral on St Magdalene in 1614. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fairs in Utrecht on Febr. 16, March 28, May 24 and August 12, in a calendar of many horse-faires.
Toll_Description: In 975 the bishop obtained permission to relocate the toll at Muiden partly or as a whole to Utrecht. The last option was chosen. Toll privileges were granted in 1122: the charter lists detailed tariffs for visiting merchants from the Rhineland, Frisia and Saxony. Norwegians were exempted from the toll, as well as Kaiserwerth (in 1145), Duisburg (1165) and Tiel (before 1174). Later in the 12th and 13th century merchants from Holland, Zeeland, Flanders, the Meuse-region and England are mentioned.
Staple_Description: In 1542 (Febr. 4) emperor Charles V prohibited horse-fairs in the Sticht of Utrecht, except those in Abcoude and Utrecht.

Name: Venlo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention around 1000.
Town_Description: Earliest mention as 'oppidum' in 1272, and in 1339 Venlo is called 'stede'. Town privileges were granted by Reginald II, duke of Guelders, on 1 September 1343. In the same year Venlo was fortified with a town wall. A town hall is mentioned in 1374, burgomasters and councillors in 1394.
Fair_Description: Venlo probably had one fair from at least 1294/95 onward: a fair of sixteen days on Sunday after Invocavit. When Venlo received town privileges in 1343, it received the right to held three fairs of sixteen days: the one on Sunday after Invocavit, one on St Albinus, and one on Sunday after St Lambert. The ducal account of 1343/'4 states: a cloth-hall on the market: 2 mark 6 sol., the 'big' toll (probably the one on the river Maas) farmed out for 240 mark 'goedgeld': 290 mark 7 sol. 4 den., a market-toll with St. Lambertus: 3 sol. 9 den., a summer-toll: 22 sol. 6 den., half the big toll from St. Margareth till the octave of Easter: 119 mark, from then till July: 11 mark 3 sol. On Jan. 1 1617 three fairs, which were not attended fot a long time as a result of the war, were restored: 1) Monday in the 'Vastelavond', 2) St. Albaensday (June 21), 3) the third Monday after St. Lamberti in Sept. (Sept. 17), each during eight days before and after and with safeconduct for the visitors.
Toll_Description: In 1270 the 'kartol' in Venlo levied on traffic with horses and wagons, was commissioned in fief to the count of Julich. Next to the Meuse toll and safe conduct of the Count of Guelders (see description harbour), the town of Venlo levied a road toll in 1366. Rates and revenues are not known.
Staple_Description: Venlo acquired limited staple privileges in the town privileges of 1343. The council tried to impose a monopoly on the river trade between Venlo and Dordrecht for skippers and vessels from Venlo. Until the early 16th century this was indeed the case, but vessels from other cities increasingly circumvented the town. In 1523, the full eight-day staple of Roermond was moved to Venlo during a conflict with that city.

Name: Verden
Alternative_Name: Ferdun; Ferdi; Feride; Verdi; Ferdiun; Werduun; Verden (Aller); Vehrde
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 782. A royal court of Charlemagne existed here, as well as a bishopric. A cathedral church is attested in ca. 814.
Town_Description: Emperor Otto III granted Verden market, toll and minting privileges in 985. A town council is mentioned in 1235 and town privileges were granted in 1259. Since 1405 at the latest, the town was a Free Imperial City.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Verden, on the Dedication day of the cathedral, can be linked to the market privilege of 985. Later Verden became an important centre for the cattle trade. Bishop Barthold founded four fairs in 1477, predominantly for cattle, and advertised them in a letter to the town of Zutphen (HUB X:527). These took place on 14 days before, 8 days and 3 weeks after St Philipp and James (April/May), and 8 days before St Bartholomew. Apparently, the cattle markets in spring were not a big success. In a privilege from 1491, they are not mentioned anymore: next to the Dedication Day fair (14 days before St Walpurga), there were two cattle markets on 14 and 8 days before St Bartholomew. After the Thirty Years' War in 1651, Queen Christine of Sweden revived the three fairs with different dates.
Toll_Description: The town acquired toll privileges in 985. According to 1460 complaints from the towns Brunswick and Celle, the toll tariff on the Aller river in Verden had at that time been increased to a sixfold of the previous tariff. Three years later, the toll was reduced again to 50 percent.

Name: Vlaardingen
Alternative_Name: Flardingis; Flardingun; Flerethinga; Flardinge; Vlerdinge; Flardinghen; Vlaerdinghen; Vlerdinghen; Vlaerdinge; Flardingen; Vlardinghe
Settlement_Description: Vlaardingen is first mentioned in a mid-fourteenth-century copy of a document dating from about 1018. Van Berkel & Samplonius mention archeological findings from Merovingian and Carolingian times.
Town_Description: Vlaardingen is granted town rights on 14 May 1273 by Floris V, count of Holland.
Fair_Description:
The fair must have existed in the first half of the 13th century and is mentioned in the town rights of 1273 without date or duration. The village was situated on the old landroute along the coast of Holland, used by merchants from Flanders on their way to Friesland. 
In 1276 the lord of Wassenaer donated money off the toll-revenues for the salvation of his father and himself.  In the oldest register with the fiefs of count Floris V dated 1282-'84 the 'teloneum de Vlerdinghen' is found as a fief of the lord of Wassenaer. Circa 1355 it is stated that the fair started Mayday (May 1). 
A cloth-hall is first mentioned in 1351. The accounts of the steward of the lord of Wassenaer preserved from 1554 onwards with gaps, mention a horsefair in Vlaardingen on St. Peter and Pouwelseve (June 28). A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fair in Vlaardingen also on June 28 in a calendar of many horse-faires. An account of this horsefair is dated 1581 and analysed.
Ferry_Description: In 1378 a ferry to Brielle is mentioned.

Name: Warburg

Settlement_Description: A castle is first mentioned in 1017. A charter from 1036 first mentions a settlement near the castle.
Town_Description: Warburg originally consisted of two towns: the old and new town. The granting of town privileges is unknown for both. The old town was mentioned as "civitas" in 1195 and had a burgomaster and council by 1245. For the new town, a burgomaster and council are mentioned in 1239. Both towns were united in 1436.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Warburg was the fair on St Michael's day in the old town, which was predominantly a grain market. In 1372, he permitted both towns each to organise a church consecration fest. Tolls and fares for safe conduct were connected to the fairs, which were pawned to the city by the bishop in 1446.

Name: Weert
Alternative_Name: Werta; Werd; Wertha; Weirta; Weerth; Wirt
Settlement_Description:
Weert originated on the crossroad of several trade routes. It is first mentioned in 1062, but this document is a forgery from the late eleventh century. Its subsequent mention dates from 1155. However, both Cox and Van Berkel & Samplonius mention political development around Weert in the late eleventh century. Between 1452 and 1556 the inhabitants of Weert and Nederweert were free of the roadtax ('weggeld') at Eindhoven, as Eindhoven was at Weert. 
Since al least 1476 Weert had a cloth-hall in Bergen (op Zoom) and since around 1490 one in Antwerp.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted on 5 May 1414 by William VI of Horne (Huis Horne). Further town privileges were added in 1563. During the fifteenth century, Weert flourished socio-economically.
Fair_Description: In 1414 (May 5) the lord of Horn granted three fairs: 1) St. Bonifatius (June 5), 2) St. John's beheading (May 6) and St. Barbara (Dec. 4) and a weekly market on Saturday and the right to levy excises. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Weerdt' then still has three fairs: 1) first Tuesday after Grootvastenavond (Tuesday before start of the Lent), 2) Sunday post visitationis Mariae (July 2) till the Tuesday after that, 3) Sunday before conceptionis Mariae (Sept. 8) till the Tuesday after that. In 1563 (Sept. 27) the magistrate was granted three free horse-fairs by the count of Horn, lord of the town. Dates: 1) Thursday and Friday before 'Papenvastelavond' (Lent-eve), 2) two days before Petri and Pauli Apostolorum in June (June 29, so on June 27), 3) Friday and Saturday after the market at Grevinghen (Greven) in Westphalen (August 24) with safe-conduct and each two days before and after.
Toll_Description:
Before 1240 the toll at Wessem was relocated to Weert by the lord of Horn. It seems to have changed from a toll on sailing ships to a landtoll. When the roads from Cologne to the west which crossed the Maas river above Wessem became of more importance the development of Wessem decayed and Weert en Roermond grew in importance. 
In 1452 Weert obtained freedom of 'weggeld' (taxes levied on the roads) at Eindhoven on the route to the fairs of Bergen (op Zoom). In 1480 (Febr. 16) Maximiliaan en Marie decided in a trial before the Court of Brabant between the count of Horn and the tenants of the toll and the 'oude geleide' (old conduct) of Brabant that citizens of Weert were free of tolls of old for their trade to Antwerp and Bergen (op Zoom). On April 11 that year it was stated that citiziens of Weert only had to pay once the 'oude geleide' in Beke (in the Meierij of den Bosch) to the inn-keeper living in the 'Mane'. The tariff of the old and new toll in Brabant dated 1560 has Weert in a list of toll-exempt places and mentions a sentence dated Febr. 11 1500 of the Council of Brabant which stated they had to pay 'geleiderecht' (conduct-right) each time on the route through Beke to Bergen (op Zoom) or through Oistmale to Antwerp or elsewhere: a coach: 12s., a cart: 6s.

Town_Description: Town rights were granted on 5 May 1414 by William VI of Horne (Huis Horne). Further town privileges were added in 1563. During the fifteenth century, Weert flourished socio-economically.
Fair_Description: In 1414 (May 5) the lord of Horn granted three fairs: 1) St. Bonifatius (June 5), 2) St. John's beheading (May 6) and St. Barbara (Dec. 4) and a weekly market on Saturday and the right to levy excises. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Weerdt' then still has three fairs: 1) first Tuesday after Grootvastenavond (Tuesday before start of the Lent), 2) Sunday post visitationis Mariae (July 2) till the Tuesday after that, 3) Sunday before conceptionis Mariae (Sept. 8) till the Tuesday after that. In 1563 (Sept. 27) the magistrate was granted three free horse-fairs by the count of Horn, lord of the town. Dates: 1) Thursday and Friday before 'Papenvastelavond' (Lent-eve), 2) two days before Petri and Pauli Apostolorum in June (June 29, so on June 27), 3) Friday and Saturday after the market at Grevinghen (Greven) in Westphalen (August 24) with safe-conduct and each two days before and after.
Toll_Description:
Before 1240 the toll at Wessem was relocated to Weert by the lord of Horn. It seems to have changed from a toll on sailing ships to a landtoll. When the roads from Cologne to the west which crossed the Maas river above Wessem became of more importance the development of Wessem decayed and Weert en Roermond grew in importance. 
In 1452 Weert obtained freedom of 'weggeld' (taxes levied on the roads) at Eindhoven on the route to the fairs of Bergen (op Zoom). In 1480 (Febr. 16) Maximiliaan en Marie decided in a trial before the Court of Brabant between the count of Horn and the tenants of the toll and the 'oude geleide' (old conduct) of Brabant that citizens of Weert were free of tolls of old for their trade to Antwerp and Bergen (op Zoom). On April 11 that year it was stated that citiziens of Weert only had to pay once the 'oude geleide' in Beke (in the Meierij of den Bosch) to the inn-keeper living in the 'Mane'. The tariff of the old and new toll in Brabant dated 1560 has Weert in a list of toll-exempt places and mentions a sentence dated Febr. 11 1500 of the Council of Brabant which stated they had to pay 'geleiderecht' (conduct-right) each time on the route through Beke to Bergen (op Zoom) or through Oistmale to Antwerp or elsewhere: a coach: 12s., a cart: 6s.

Name: Wesel
Settlement_Description: First uncertain mention in a note of the monastery Echternach, which can be dated to 719-739. The foundation of a church around 800 and the finds of a grave field from the 8th and 9th century indicate that there existed a large settlement at this time already.
Town_Description: Wesel acquired town privileges in 1241.
Fair_Description: A toll levied with the fair is found in 1241. Before 1430 the Walburgis fair (May 1), 3 days before and after, the fair with St. Matheus (Sept. 21) 3 days before and after, and a fair on Nov. 19, 7 days before and after, the most important fair ('frigidum forum') were founded. A fourth fair was founded in 1431 on June 15. In 1467 (Apr. 29) the St. Vitus horse-fair was granted: 15-18 June with 7 days before and after that.
Toll_Description:
1) The Count of Cleves levied a land toll in 1300. In 1319, 120 mark were collected together with the transhipment toll in Wesel.<br/>
2) In 1319, a road toll was also mentioned, which was levied by the town itself. The Count of Cleves granted the privilege for this fee.

Settlement_Description: First mentioned as early as 50 AD when it was inhabited by the Romans. Around 500 there was a settlement by the Franks. In 1022 the place is mentioned as a 'villa'.
Town_Description: Is mentioned in 1241 as 'civitas' and in 1242 as 'civitas imperatoria'. Still referred to as 'oppidum' in 1344, it was first mentioned as a town in 1348. Name: Wismar
Alternative_Name: Wißmar; Wissemara; Wismaraa; Wissemar; Widmar; Wismer; Wissemariam; Vysmar; Huissemaire; Wissemer; Wyssemaria; Wissemaria; Wismarie
Settlement_Description: The settlement Alt ('old') Wismar, located east of the current town, was a small Slavic fishing village. German farmers and merchants settled around 1200 in the northern part of the old town around the church of St Nicholas. The settlement was first mentioned with a harbour in 1211.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1229, it was most likely founded in 1226 but the charter has not survived. Lübeck town privileges were confirmed in 1266.
Fair_Description: A fair is first mentioned in 1397. According to regulations from 1604, it lasted from Sunday Exaudi until the Friday before Pentecost. A 'Kauffschlagsmontag' on the first Monday of Lent appears in 1547, is characterised as free fair in 1608 and developed into a three-day fair in the second half of the 17th century.
Toll_Description: Toll of the lords of Mecklenburg, that was acquired by the town of Wismar in 1308-1311 and again in 1375. Toll tariffs exist from 1328 and 1628, when it was converted into a toll on the causeways and bridges of the town; it still existed in 1828.
Staple_Description: Staple for stockfish from Bergen; in 1446 members of the Hanse were only allowed to export flour, malt, and other victuals to Bergen if they brought fish from Bergen back with them to Lübeck, Wismar, Rostock or Stralsund. Regulations from 1435 and 1480 refer to a staple for grain.

Settlement_Description: The settlement Alt ('old') Wismar, located east of the current town, was a small Slavic fishing village. German farmers and merchants settled around 1200 in the northern part of the old town around the church of St Nicholas. The settlement was first mentioned with a harbour in 1211.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1229, it was most likely founded in 1226 but the charter has not survived. Lübeck town privileges were confirmed in 1266.

Name: Lutherstadt Wittenberg
Alternative_Name: Wittenberg; Wittenburg; Wittenberch; Viteberga; Wittinberk; Wyttemberch
Settlement_Description: Originally a fishing village from the 11th / 12th century, first mentioned in 1187.
Town_Description: Duke Albrecht II granted town rights in 1293. Additionally, Wittenberg was the residence of the Ascanian dukes in the 14th century. In 1317 councillors, a mayor and a municipality appear in the records.
Toll_Description: First mention of a toll in 1423 in a certificate from duke Friedrich the strident to duchess Barbara, widow of elector Rudolf III. The safe conduct in Wittenberg shows the high amount of trade traffic from north to south and east to west. The regulations of safe conduct also settle the tolls on the Elbe and the bridge toll, while the account books from 1444 to 1545 further mention income from the ferry and cattle tolls. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1513.
Staple_Description: In 1415 King Sigismund gave Duke Rudolf of Saxony staple privileges in his castle and city of Wittenberg; this privilege was confirmed by King Friedrich II for the Dukes Friedrich and Wilhem in 1444. Staple rights were again confirmed in 1478, but proved difficult to enforce.

Name: Wolfenbüttel
Settlement_Description: The castle Wolfenbüttel is first mentioned in 1118. First indications about a settlement near the castle date from the early 14th century. From 1432, the castle was the main residence of the dukes of Brunswick and was reconstructed as a fortress.
Town_Description: Wolfenbüttel acquired market privileges in 1570 and acquired its final form as a renaissance fortress between 1570 and 1626, which consisted of the Heinrichstadt around the castle, the civic settlement Neustadt, and the suburb Gotteslager east of it. Duke Julius attempted to develop the town into the major trading hub Gotteslager from 1582, but the project failed.
Fair_Description: Wolfenbüttel acquired market privileges in 1570 with two fairs, on 9 May and 4 November. When duke Julius tried to raise the town to the major trade hub Gotteslager, he granted four fairs of twelve days, on 14 January, 14 April, 14 July and 14 November. After the failure of the project, the fairs were reduced to two eight-day fairs in spring and autumn again, taking place on 5 May and 5 November.

Alternative_Name: Sutphem; Sutpheni; Sutfene; Sutuene; Sutfenna; Sutphania; Sutfen; Sutphen; Sutfenne; Sutphaniense
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1101, but archeological research shows that the place where Zutphen is located has at least been permanently inhabited from the sixth or seventh century onwards. From circa 900 onwards, Zutphen was walled and functioned as a central place for a duke or lord. Oldest mention as 'oppidum' Zutphen dates from 1059. Between 1120 and 1138, the county of Zutphen was inherited by the count of Guelders.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted between 15 April 1191 and 30 March 1196, by Otto I, count of Guelders and Zutphen. Zutphen was the first settlement in the county of Guelders to receive town privileges and was the example for many other towns in Guelders. The town was enlarged with the new town ('Nieuwstad') around 1230. In 1243 the town had a stone wall. A town council is first mentioned in 1312. Four administrative units (quarters) were distinguished in Guelders from the 14th century; Zutphen functioned as the capital in the Quarter of Zutphen ('Kwartier van Zutphen'). Het Stuvennest or Stuvenest, in the Melatensteeg, was one of the inns in town. It is being named between 1468 and 1531. Already before 1268, a hospital was located just outside the Spitaalpoort along the road towards Emmerich. The course of the river IJssel near Zutphen was influenced by human activity several times. In 1357, the river was changed by cutting the southern meander. Unintentionally, this activated the old IJssel at Empe again. As a result, the town risked to lose its location close to the main stem. In 1406/1407, the meander directly west of the town was being canalized until the Polbeek estuary. As a result, the branch at Empe and the northern meander across the Mars were cut off. The canalized river was located between short banks.
Fair_Description: A weekly market on Thursday is mentioned in the town privileges from 1194/1195. Zutphen had one fair at least from 1294/1295 onwards. Fair trading in Zutphen decreased from the beginning of the fifteenth century onwards, despite an ongoing increase in the number of fairs. This was among others due to constant competition with the fairs in the town of Deventer. Duke Reginald IV of Guelders granted two new fairs in Zutphen in 1420, to enforce the economic strength of the town, and duke Arnold granted four new fairs on the same dates as the Deventer fairs during a trade boycot of Deventer in 1463-1465, but without lasting success. The Saint Walpurgis fair (1st of May) was the only fair in Guelders with a limited supraregional function. An eighth (cattle) fair on St Gregory was founded in 1522 by Duke Charles of Guelders.
Toll_Description: A land road toll ('weggeld') was levied at three town gates. At the Laarpoort (road towards the east: towards Lochem, Twente and Westphalia), the Spittaalpoort or Hospitaalpoort (road towards the south: towards Doetinchem, Emmerich and Cleves), and the Nieuwstadspoort (road towards Deventer). The gates Olypoort and Veerpoort had become redundant after the course of the river IJssel had been altered in the fourteenth century. Sources from the fourteenth century show that the Laarpoort brought in more than the other gates combined.

From circa 900 onwards, Zutphen was walled and functioned as a central place for a duke or lord. Oldest mention as 'oppidum' Zutphen dates from 1059. Between 1120 and 1138, the county of Zutphen was inherited by the count of Guelders.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted between 15 April 1191 and 30 March 1196, by Otto I, count of Guelders and Zutphen. Zutphen was the first settlement in the county of Guelders to receive town privileges and was the example for many other towns in Guelders. The town was enlarged with the new town ('Nieuwstad') around 1230. In 1243 the town had a stone wall. A town council is first mentioned in 1312. Four administrative units (quarters) were distinguished in Guelders from the 14th century; Zutphen functioned as the capital in the Quarter of Zutphen ('Kwartier van Zutphen'). Het Stuvennest or Stuvenest, in the Melatensteeg, was one of the inns in town. It is being named between 1468 and 1531. Already before 1268, a hospital was located just outside the Spitaalpoort along the road towards Emmerich. The course of the river IJssel near Zutphen was influenced by human activity several times. In 1357, the river was changed by cutting the southern meander. Unintentionally, this activated the old IJssel at Empe again. As a result, the town risked to lose its location close to the main stem. In 1406/1407, the meander directly west of the town was being canalized until the Polbeek estuary. As a result, the branch at Empe and the northern meander across the Mars were cut off. The canalized river was located between short banks.
Fair_Description: A weekly market on Thursday is mentioned in the town privileges from 1194/1195. Zutphen had one fair at least from 1294/1295 onwards. Fair trading in Zutphen decreased from the beginning of the fifteenth century onwards, despite an ongoing increase in the number of fairs. This was among others due to constant competition with the fairs in the town of Deventer. Duke Reginald IV of Guelders granted two new fairs in Zutphen in 1420, to enforce the economic strength of the town, and duke Arnold granted four new fairs on the same dates as the Deventer fairs during a trade boycot of Deventer in 1463-1465, but without lasting success. The Saint Walpurgis fair (1st of May) was the only fair in Guelders with a limited supraregional function. An eighth (cattle) fair on St Gregory was founded in 1522 by Duke Charles of Guelders.
Toll_Description: A land road toll ('weggeld') was levied at three town gates. At the Laarpoort (road towards the east: towards Lochem, Twente and Westphalia), the Spittaalpoort or Hospitaalpoort (road towards the south: towards Doetinchem, Emmerich and Cleves), and the Nieuwstadspoort (road towards Deventer). The gates Olypoort and Veerpoort had become redundant after the course of the river IJssel had been altered in the fourteenth century. Sources from the fourteenth century show that the Laarpoort brought in more than the other gates combined.

Name: Zwickau
Settlement_Description: A castle and a market probably existed since the 11th century. The area was previously inhabited by Slavs. The place settled near an old river crossing.
Town_Description: Market and city rights were probably given between 1198 and 1221.
Toll_Description: The Ernestinian safe conduct in Zwickau was predominantly based on the transport of mining products.

Name: Zwolle
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in a donation charter of the bishop of Utrecht from 1040, the veracity of which is debated. The first certain mention dates from a 1129 confirmation of the 1040 charter (in a 14th-century copy). Archaeological evidence points at continuous habitation since the 9th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Wilbrand of Oldenburg, bishop of Utrecht, on 31 August 1230. These town privileges were renewed and extended in 1346.
Fair_Description: On 21 April 1265 Hendrik van Vianden, bishop of Utrecht, granted a nine-day fair on St Boniface (5 June) with safe conduct for the visitors within the bishopric of Utrecht. Probably the fair of St Michael (29 September) already existed at that point as well, which was probably the oldest fair it is named after the patron of the town. In the late 13th century we also hear about fairs on the Assumption of the Virgin Mary (15 August) and Simon and Jude's Day (28 October). On 25 March 1309 the bishop granted a fifth fair of one week around Tuesday after Easter, with safe conduct. The charter also explicitly allows the trade of horses and cattle during all fairs. In the early 17th century, only three eight-day markets remained: on Palm Sunday, St James (25 July) and St Michael, of which the first two are already mentioned in an almanac from 1598 printed in Neudamm (Dębno).
Toll_Description: A toll was levied at the town gates. The oldest toll tariff from 1366 gives an impression of the range of commodities traded in the town via the land and water ways. The tariff of the road toll was heightened by the council in 1596, to fund repairs of the roads and bridges.
Staple_Description: Staple for rye, cattle and other agriculture-products from Overijssel reaching the town via two bridges: Venebrugge (at the Hessenweg connecting Holland via the Veluwe to the German territories) and Nijerbrugge. This right was confirmed by the bishop of Utrecht in 1438. Around 1450 the town built the Berkumerbridge across the river Vecht for the trade to the German territories, thus hampering Kampen.

Name: Middelburg (Walcheren)
Settlement_Description: Middelburg originated as a Caroligian castle, built as a defence against attacks from Norsemen. In the late tenth century, it is already said to have been a port. A hospital is first mentioned in 1289.
Town_Description:
In May 1217, town privileges of Middelburg are confirmed by Joan, countess of Flanders, and William I, count of Holland. Possibly, earlier town rights were granted by Floris III, count of Holland. 
The 'Kamer' (department) of Zeeland, the second largest of the six 'Kamers' of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602), was located in Middelburg.
Fair_Description:
In 1323 (May 1) count Willem III granted two fairs: 1) St. Mary Magdalena-eve (July 21) duration: 5 days, with an extensive tariff, 2) Sunday after Midlent also for 5 days. An extensive excise ordinance is edited and dated 1325 (Febr. 24). In it a fair and marketfield are found. The oldest town-account dated 1365/'6 mentions the fair with St. Jacobsday (July 25) and an excise levied from the marketfield in 1361. A crane, a meathouse and a cloth-hall are found in 1366/'7, a weigh-house ('balans') in 1376. In the account of the comital steward of Bewestenschelde dated 1429/'30 the tolls on the fair with St. Jacobsday are found. This toll appears to be comital. The town-account dated 1443 mentions the erection of the market-cross on St. Mary-Magdalena-eve at all town-gates. In 1439 it was discussed to enlengthen this fair which was done in 1443 with 4 days. In 1522 (Dec.) emperor Charles V granted a free fair on Febr. 3, with 15 'toon'(display)days, and freedom for 15 days before and after the fair. This in stead of the fair which started the week before Palm-Sunday. With equal rights as on the fair with St. Jacobsday. The town of Bruges opposed against this. In 1523 the fair in the week before 
'Palmen' was relocated by Charles V to  Febr. 3.
Toll_Description: In 1304 Middelburg was freed from the staple in Dordrecht. In 1340 Middelburg obtained toll-exemption in Holland. See staple below. In 1473 Charles the Bold stated a decree on the alum-market in Middelburg, St. Anna ter Muiden, Sluis and Antwerp.
Staple_Description: 1347-48 saw the establishment of English and Scottish merchants, with privileges for English merchants following in 1383-88 (yields and amounts of wool are edited). Privileges for merchants from Portugal in 1390. From 1405 efforts made to secure a staple for the entire island of Walcheren that seems to have been merely an obligation to travel through Middelburg for the payment of the pound toll due there. The staple was given up in 1445. In the 16th century new attempts to erect a staple; in 1521 imperial staple privileges for wine, oil, fruit and iron coming from the west over see; in 1522 staple treaty with Scotland for 14 years, after which there were attempts to extend the staple. 1558 saw the establishment of English merchants.

Name: Vlissingen
Alternative_Name: Flushing; Vlissinghe; Vlissinghen; Nyevlissinghen; Vlijssingen; Vlijssinghen; Veteri Vlissnghe; oude Vlissinghen; Vlissigghen; Vlissiniensi
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1235 (in a copy from 1324). This first mention refers to the settlement that would later be called Oud-Vlissingen. It was located just to the west of the old town and disappeared when defence structures were built during the French period. A hospital is first mentioned in 1271.
Town_Description: Near Oud-Vlissingen, count Willem III of Holland constructed a harbour around 1300, around which the town of Vlissingen developed. It was granted town rights on 2 April 1315. The town was fortified after 1485.
Fair_Description: Duke Albrecht granted Vlissingen in 1368 a free fair starting St. Simon and Judeday apostel (Oct. 28), duration four days. With rights and freedom as in the other towns on the isle Walcheren. In 1395 (April 6) he donated a 'korfharingmarkt': a fair for herring sold per basket, with safeconduct, as there was one previously in Den Briel.
Staple_Description: In 1444 a previously by his predecessors donated privilege was confirmed by duke Philip of Burgundy.  It concerned the herringtoll and the staple for the fish and herring caught and brought ashore between Westkapelle and 'Welsingen' harbour (later known as Rammekens, a fortress built mid 16th century, east of Vlissingen). Conflict with Middelburg led to the compromise whereby wine and fruit from the Walcheren region was taken to Middelburg and fish to Vlissingen.

Name: Ribe
Alternative_Name: Riebyii; Ricyebii; Rihbiir; Rinhe; Rypa; Ripensis; Ripis; Ripensem; Ripen; Ripæ
Settlement_Description: Around AD 700 Ribe was a permanent settlement with an urban character. The settlement was located close to the outlet of a river, Ribe Å, and at a relatively easy place to cross the river.
Town_Description: From the 8th century Ribe was among the so-called emporia of northwestern Europe. The site was integrated in long distance trading networks, and stood under the production of the king of the Danes. Around 855 the missionary and bishop of Hamburg, Ansgar, built a church in Ribe, and from the 10th century Ribe was a diocese. This made the town the ecclesial centre of southwestern Jutland during the medieval period and early modern era, and several clerical institutions were founded. A Dominican monastery was established in 1228, and the Franciscans arrived in 1232. Various kings of Denmark also had great interests in Ribe, and the important town was frequently visited by the king. A royal castle was established at the crossing of the river, Ribe Å, in the 12th century, and relocated to the western part of the town in the middle of the 13th century. The citizens were granted their first royal privileges in 1202-1214. A town council is known from c. 1250, and the oldest town law is from 1269. Throughout the viking age and medieval period Ribe was counted among the most important Danish towns, especially concerning long distance trade. Although the town stagnated in the later middle ages, Ribe continued to be one of the most significant towns in Denmark. The town was, for example, an important centre in the export of oxen from Jutland.
Fair_Description: From the Viking age onwards Ribe was a very important market town. During the medieval period the town hosted several annual fairs, and became central to the export of horses and in particular oxen from western Denmark. The fairs of Ribe had either a regional or international character, and were among the most important in Denmark. By the middle of the 17th century the town only had two aanual fairs: one during summer and Our Lady Fair.
Toll_Description: The age of the first toll is unknown. But already during the Viking age the kings of Denmark must have collected some kind of toll in Ribe. In the medieval period Ribe was one of the most important royal tolls. In the late medieval period and early modern era the toll on oxen was an important royal income: around 6000 daler annually in the 1550ties. Toll registers from the early 16th century have been preserved in the court accounts of widow queen Christine, who then was granted the right to the toll (The National Archive/Rigsarkivet). As Ribe played a central role in the Danish export of oxen from the 15th century onwards, the toll on oxen was the most important. At the time of widow queen Christine in the early 16th century the toll was set at 2 shilling  Some of the known medieval and early modern tolls from Ribe are: 1) The first time a toll is documented in the written material is from shortly before 1230, when a royal toll on the export of horses was introduced. 2) In 1283 king Eric Glipping (1259-1286) introduced a toll on the export of herring and different agricultural products such as grain and horses. 3) As Ribe played a central role in the Danish export of oxen from the 15th century onwards, the toll on oxen was the most important in the late medieval period as well as the early modern era. In the early 16th century the toll was set at 2 shillings (Danish: skilling) per animal.
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Ribe as well as a few other towns (Assens, Kolding and the annual fairs in Skanør and Falsterbo). The stable rights to Ribe were emphasized a couple of times by king Christian II (1513-1523). In the middle of the 16th century Ribe lost its stable privilege.
Harbour_Description: A natural harbour with some man made constructions from the founding of Ribe onwards. According to the German chronicler Adam of Bremen, Ribe was an important harbour in the 11th century. The harbour connected Denmark with Friland, England, Saxony as well as other parts of western Europe. That Ribe continued as one of the most important ports of Denmark in the following period was emphasized by the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus, who finished his Gesta Danorum c. 1208. The harbour lost some of its importance in the later middle ages and early modern period, but was still one of the most important to Danish export and import.

Name: Randers
Alternative_Name: Randrusium; Randrøs; Randrus; Randrosia; Randrusiensis; Randershusen; Rændærs; Ranssner
Settlement_Description: King Canute the Holy (1080-1086) minted coins in Randers, which appear to have had an urban character at the end of the 11th century. The settlement was located in the bottom of Randers Fjord and a relatively easy place to cross the river of Gudenå.
Town_Description: In the end of the 12th century Randers had four paris churches and a urban character. Town council and town seal is known from around 1250. A Franciscan monastery was established already in 1236. Oldest known privileges granted by king Erik VI Menved (1286-1319) in 1302. First mention of  mayors in 1379, and of town hall in 1457. The medieval town fortification was rebuilt in 1535. In the 17th century Randers suffered from the plague, fires and the Dano-Swedish wars.
Fair_Description: Randers held several annual fairs from the early medieval era onwards. A couple of the fairs are well documented from the 16th century onwards, but their dates, age and character is, however, uncertain. In 1634 it was decided that two annual fairs were to be held in Randers, but prior to that the town already had at least two annual fairs. The fairs of Randers played a role in the export of oxen from Jutland.

Settlement_Description: The place name of Odense is a reflection of a sacral status in the pre-Christian era. Presumably, a place of worship and also economical and political center in the Viking Age. The latter is reflected in the ring fortress of Nonnebakken built by king Harald Bluetooth around 980.
Town_Description: Odense was located at a river, Odense Å, that may have been navigable in the Viking Age and early medieval period, but not in the later middle ages. The town was placed at the obvious route used to cross the island of Funen. Odense was first mentioned in a Ottonian charter from 988, issued by emperor Otto III to the bishops of Odense and other Danish towns. Thus, around 1000 AD Odense appears to have had an urban character, but the first time Odense was described as a town was in c. 1075, when the German chronicler Adam of Bremen placed it as the largest town (“civitas … magna”) on the island of Funen. In 1086 the Danish king Canute the Holy (1080-1086) was killed under a rebellion in Odense, and canonized around 1100 as the first royal saint of Denmark. Saint Canute the Holy’s tomb in the town’s cathedral and the status as episcopal sea secured Odense an important religious and political status throughout the medieval period. The town lord was, however, the king of Denmark. The first mention of a royal tax from towns (Danish: Midsommergæld) is from 1137. Townsmen (Danish: bymænd) are documented in 1175, and members of a town council from 1257. The oldest preserved town privileges are from 1335, but Odense was probably granted its first town rights in either the 12th or early 13th century. In 1351 mayors were mentioned for the first time, and a town hall in 1437. During the medieval period several monasteries were established. Three of the town’s monasteries were, a Benedictine Abbey, which may be the first monastery in Denmark, was founded around 1096, and probably in 1239 the Dominicans followed and in 1279 the Franciscians. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era Odense was the largest and dominant town on Funen. The town benefited from the rich agriculture on the island, and its status as the administrative, economical and political center of Funen.
Fair_Description: Due to its central location to both maritime and land-based traffic on the island of Funen Odense was an important market town. This was most likely already the case during the Viking Age, and the town’s status as the trading center of Funen continued throughout the medieval period and early modern era. Apparently, the oldest known annual fair, which also was the most important, was associated with the royal Saint Canute (Danish: Sankt Knudmesse Marked). It was held in the days around July 10th, the day king Canute the Holy was killed in 1086. Around 1600, and maybe also before, three other annual fairs were also held in Odense. In the second half of the 17th century, the number of fairs had been limited to two.

Name: Svendborg
Alternative_Name: Swineburgh; Swineburgensium; Suineborg; Swineburghenses; Suenborre; Kalændæburgh; Kyalteburg
Settlement_Description: There is archaeological evidence of a permanent settlement with an urban character in the first half of the 12th century. Presumably the settlement developed around a castle. Both castle and settlement may have been founded by the Slavic magnate Knud Prislavsøn, who was a vassal of king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182) of Denmark.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by king Valdemar II the Victorious (1202-1241). The castle of Svendborg is first mentioned in 1229, but appears to have been demolished soon after. Perhaps because the town was fortified in the 13th century. Townsmen are documented in 1408, a town hall in 1469 and a town council in 1477. There can be no doubt, however, that these urban institutions were already introduced before the 15th century.
Fair_Description: Svendborg presumably had at least one annual fair. The age and exact character of the fair is unknown. The fair had a local character, and at the end of the 17th century, it was held on the 17th july.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unclear. But clearly Svendborg was an important harbour on the island of Funen, which was often used by foreing merchants. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck used the harbour. A wharf is mentioned several times during the 16th century, and is also shown on the map of Svendborg in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from around 1670.

Name: Weimar
Alternative_Name: Wehmare; Weihmari; Wimares; Wimeri; Wimar; Wymar
Settlement_Description: First mention of a count of Weimar in 975.
Town_Description: Foundation of the town around 1250 by the counts of Orlamünde. In 1254 first mention as civitas. In 1410 acquisition of town rights of Weißensee.
Fair_Description: In 1456 the two three-day fairs were confirmed, so they had existed earlier. Three days before the fairs a cattle market took place. In 1729 a third fair was granted.

Name: Lund
Alternative_Name: Lundona; Lunde; Lundensis; Lundensi; Lundis; Lundh; Lundt; Lunden; Lwnde; Lunndt
Settlement_Description: Founded in the late 10th century by king Swein Forkbeard (c. 987-1014) as a settlement with an urban character. The first archaeological evidence of the settlement is from a graveyard at a wooden church dated to c. 990. The settlement was founded at a central junction in Scania, where several main routes within the province crossed.
Town_Description: In the 11th century Lund became a bishopric, and from 1103/1104 the archbishops of Denmark resided in Lund. Up until the Danish Reformation in 1536 the town was the ecclesiastical center of the Danish kingdom: “Metropolis Daniae”. The cathedral of Saint Laurentius was built in the early 12th century, and by the 13th century the town had 22 churches and four monasteries. The town’s lord was, however, the king of Denmark. A royal mint was established around the year 1000, and a royal official (‘Gælkeren’) is known from the 11th or 12th century. At this time the first town law (‘Birkeretten’) was also introduced, and it later spread to towns across Scania. According to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 Lund was royal institutional property (‘Kongelev’), and an annual town tax (‘Midsommergæld’) was paid to the king from before 1085. Also, the provincial assembly of Scania, Halland and Blekinge was located in Lund. Mayors, a town council and a municipal seal are not documented prior to the 14th century, but there is no reason to doubt that these civic urban institutions were well established already in the 13th century. As a political and religious center Lund remained one of the most important Danish towns, but during the late medieval period and early modern era Lund lost ground to other dynamic urban communities in the region, in particular Copenhagen and Malmö.
Fair_Description: Lund was one of the most important regional market towns in Scania, and the town held several annual fairs. The age, date and character of the earliest fairs are uncertain, but annual fairs were held in Lund before 1400. At a common meeting in 1504 the towns of Scania decided only to allow a limited number of annual fairs in the province. Two of these legal annual fairs of Scania were held in Lund: “Trehøjemarked” and Saint Laurentius fair. In 1540 only two annual fairs were allowed in Scania, one in Lund and the other in Engelholm.

Name: Malmö
Alternative_Name: Malmø; Elbogen; Malmøi Malmoghæ; Malmøghe, Malmøgh; Malmøughe; Malmøye; Malmøghae; Mallmö; Malmøge; Malmöges; Malmogis; Mallmøe
Settlement_Description: In the early 13th century a seasonal herring market at the beach every autumn. A permanent settlement with an urban character began to develop west of the seasonal market.
Town_Description: Archaeological evidence of the development of an urban settlement during the 13th century. Around 1300 the previously market area to the east was covered by permanent structures. At this time Malmö was defined as a town. Throughout the late medieval period Malmö benefited from its central location in the region around the narrow strait of Øresund and the rich fishing of herring in Øresund. Around 1300 construction of the town's enormous parish church began, and in 1419 a Franciscan monastery was founded. Town privileges and a town council are documented from the 14th century onwards. Two town books from the 15th and 16th centuries have been preserved. Malmö belonged to the king of Denmark, and king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) built the castle of Malmöhus. The strong royal castle was rebuilt several times during the following centuries. The castle functioned as a royal residence and home to the royal steward. Malmö was also protected by a palisade and later a town wall. In the 1440ties Malmö became the most important royal mint place, and in the following period the town developed into the largest town in the Danish kingdom. Throughout the middle ages Malmö had strong connections to towns in northern Germany, in particular Stralsund. A German guild is documented from around 1330. The town of Malmö also played a central role in the process leading up to the Danish Reformation in 1536. When Scania was handed over to Sweden after the Dano-Swedish wars in the 1650ties Malmö stagnated up until the 19th century.
Fair_Description: In the 14th century the market activities in Malmö grew in importance, and the town developed into one of the most important of the international markets in Scania. Like the other annual fairs in Scania the fishing market in Malmö probably took place from August 15th to October 9th. As other Scania fairs, the one in Malmö lost its importance during the 16th century. The town also held another annual fair, which apparently took place during spring. This fair appears to have been a cattle market, and was first mentioned in 1360.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Malmö and Copenhagen was most likely founded by the middle of the 13th century.
Harbour_Description: Originally a natural harbour where ships anchored in the shallow water, and barges were used to transport people and goods into the town of Malmö. Later in the medieval period a jetty was constructed. The jetty was around 150 meters long. The harbour was frequently visited by foreign ships, in particular from Germany. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Malmö.

Name: Roskilde
Alternative_Name: Roschild; Roscald; Rosci; Roskildis; Roskyldiæ; Roeskilde
Settlement_Description: Established as a settlement with an urban character in the late 10th century.
Town_Description: The town was home to the diocese of Roskilde, also known as the diocese of Zealand. The diocese was founded around 1020, at a time when the newly founded settlement of Roskilde already had an urban character. Throughout the medieval period and into the early modern era, Roskilde was a religious centre of not only Zealand but the whole of Denmark. At the end of the 12th century, for example, there were at least ten churches within the town. The town also had several monasteries. Two of these were the Dominicans (established c. 1232) and the Franciscans (established c. 1237). In 1554 the bishopric was moved from Roskilde to Copenhagen. The many clerical institutions had a great influence on the town during the middle ages, when various bishops of Roskilde also were among the most powerful political agents of Denmark. The town lord, however, was the king of Denmark. And from an early stage the royal presence was also strong. King Swein Forkbeard (Danish: Svend Tveskæg) minted coins in Roskilde around 995, and royal minting was carried out in the town until the 14th century. A royal official (Danish: bryde) is encountered for the first time in 1145, and by the middle of the following 13th century the town had a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged). A municipal seal is known from 1250, and in 1268 king Eric Glipping (1259-1286) granted Roskilde a town law. Members of the town council (consules) as well as a town hall were mentioned for the first time in the 1270s and 1280s. At this time the town probably also had mayors, but this institution is not documented before 1349. According to a registration of royal taxes from the towns of Zealand and surrounding islands (Danish: “Købstadslisten”) in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1241, Roskilde was the wealthiest town on Zealand. Roskilde remained one of the political and economical centers of Zealand throughout the medieval period and into the early modern era, but during the late medieval period, however, it lost ground to other towns, such as Køge and in particular Copenhagen.
Fair_Description: Roskilde was an important market town on the island of Zealand, and several annual fairs were held in or near the town. However, the date, age and character of the fairs are uncertain. From the 13th century, and probably also before, Roskilde must have held at least one annual fair. In the 15th century, and probably also before, the most important fairs took place at Easter and on the feast of Saint Dionysius (October 1th). In 1516 king Christian II (1513-1523) allowed only four annual fairs on the island of Zealand. A fair in Roskilde was one of these legal fairs. The effect of the king’s initiative is, however, uncertain, as other fairs at least in time continued. In the second part of the 17th century Roskilde had three annual fairs.
Toll_Description: The age and character of the toll in Roskilde is not known. Presumably, a royal toll was collected already in the Viking Age, and most certainly also in the early medieval period. Different tolls are documented from the early 16th century onwards. One of these was a toll (sise) on imported German beer.
Harbour_Description: A natural harbour at Vindeboder near Sankt Jørgensbjerg from the Viking Age onwards. Sailing to Roskilde was, however, difficult, due to the shallow water in Roskilde Fjord, especially for larger medieval and early modern ships. The character of the harbour is not known.

Name: Edam
Alternative_Name: Aedamme; Adam; Yedamme; Yedam; Edamum; Eedam
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Edam is first mentioned in 1342-1343. Cox states that there is an earlier mention dating from 1310. A hospital is first mentioned in 1392.
Town_Description: Edam was granted town privileges on 19 November 1357 by William V, count of Holland.
Fair_Description: The townprivilege of count William V also granted three fairs: 1) starting 8 days before Palm Sunday, 2) 8 days after St. John in the summer (June 24), 3) the third sunday after St. Bavo (Oct. 1), each during 8 days. The municipal account dated 1560/'1 mentions incomes of the autumn-fair and the Easter-fair. In 1585 a meath-hall and a fishmarket were built.
Harbour_Description: In the town privileges of 1357, Edam acquired the right to construct a new harbour, that connected the Purmer lake with the Zuiderzee. It became an important sea harbour for the hinterland of northern Holland. In 1412 (May 1) it obtained toll-exemption at the tolls of Spaarndam and Beverwijk. In the Enqueste dated 1494 they state they had at the time of duke Charles the Bold (before 1477) 40 'maer'ships, of which only six are left over and 30 'reyn'(Rhine)ships for the catch of herring before 1477, of which only two now are left over. They a.o. built ships and trade eastward over water.

Name: Alkmaar
Alternative_Name: Almere; Alcmere; Allecmere; Alkmer; Alcmare; Alcmar; Alcmaer; Alcmair;
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Alkmaar is first mentioned in the first half of the eleventh century. Cox, however, claims that the earliest mention dates from 922-939. A market is mentioned in 1132, and Alkmaar is called an 'oppidum' in 1166. A hospital is first mentioned in 1341.
Town_Description: Alkmaar is granted town rights on 11 June 1254 by William II, count of Holland. However, in 1426, Alkmaar lost its town privileges (and its military defences). The defences were re-established in 1451. In 1456, the town rights were re-granted, but these (and the city gates and walls) were lost again in 1491. The town rigts were again restored in the sixteenth century.
Fair_Description:
A 'forum' (market) in Alkmaar is found between 1132 and 1174 and in 1215, as appears from the Annales Egmundenses, the yearly toll was property of the abbot of Egmond. In 1277 the toll outside the fair is mentioned. In 1339 (Dec. 8) count Willem IV granted three fairs to the citizens, each of 3 weeks: 1) Midlent, 2) St. Jacobsmisse (July 25), 3) Bamis (Oct. 1). Merchants from Flanders, Brabant, Denmark a.o. had to pay toll of cattle and cloth and furthermore the '100e penning' (1%). That year the count also gave a toll for the Oostfriezen on the fairs. In 1365 the fair after Easter was moved to the Monday after the octave of Easter. In 1379 (Sept. 22) duke Albrecht granted a fourth fair starting 3 days before St. Matheusday (Sept. 21) till 4 days after with equal freedom and rights as the fair with Low Sunday (Sunday after Easter).
The comital account dated 1524 mentions tolls of three fairs: 1) Easter fair for 8 days, 2) St. Bartholomeusfair (August 24) for 12 days and 3) St. Mathysfair (Sept. 21) for 8 days. In particular those of 'Overmase' (south of the river Maas) had to pay toll. Tol was levied from cattle and linen cloth. As a result of damage by war and the fact that local lords around the town had raised fairs with lower tolls in 1526 (May 4) emperor Charles V gave permission to levy a lower toll during 12 years. The comital account of 1544 stated that the right of the horse-fair was equal to that in Gouda, Valkenburg, Voorschoten and Vlaardingen. King Philip II granted in 1575 (March 3) two leather fairs. Alkmaar was not as good situated as other towns in West-Friesland and Waterland, which resulted in the fact that artisans as shoemakers did not establish easily because of lack of materials. The decaying trade would improve by the new leather fairs like in Hoorn, Purmerend and Beverwijk. Dates: Monday after Low Sunday and the day after St. Matheus (Sept. 22).
Staple_Description: In 1347 the count prohibited the weekly markets in the villages in  Kennemerland and Westfriesland and ordained that the bailiff would assure that the weekly market at Alkmaar was attended.

Fair_Description:
A 'forum' (market) in Alkmaar is found between 1132 and 1174 and in 1215, as appears from the Annales Egmundenses, the yearly toll was property of the abbot of Egmond. In 1277 the toll outside the fair is mentioned. In 1339 (Dec. 8) count Willem IV granted three fairs to the citizens, each of 3 weeks: 1) Midlent, 2) St. Jacobsmisse (July 25), 3) Bamis (Oct. 1). Merchants from Flanders, Brabant, Denmark a.o. had to pay toll of cattle and cloth and furthermore the '100e penning' (1%). That year the count also gave a toll for the Oostfriezen on the fairs. In 1365 the fair after Easter was moved to the Monday after the octave of Easter. In 1379 (Sept. 22) duke Albrecht granted a fourth fair starting 3 days before St. Matheusday (Sept. 21) till 4 days after with equal freedom and rights as the fair with Low Sunday (Sunday after Easter).
The comital account dated 1524 mentions tolls of three fairs: 1) Easter fair for 8 days, 2) St. Bartholomeusfair (August 24) for 12 days and 3) St. Mathysfair (Sept. 21) for 8 days. Name: Potsdam
Alternative_Name: Potzupimi; Bostam; Postam; Postamp; Potsdamp; Potstam; Potstamb; Poztamp
Settlement_Description: First mention 993 in a donation charte by Otto III to Quedlinburg monastery. A Slavic settlement and a Kietz existed next to each other, the castle warden first took residence in the Slavic fortification in the 12th century. Before 1237 a stone castle was erected at the bank of the Havel river.
Town_Description: Developed into a town in the 14th century: mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1317, as small town ('städeken') in 1323. In 1345 mention as civitas with a town council. The date of acquisition of town rights is unknown. From the 15th century usually called small town or borough. Became residence of the kings of Prussia in the 18th century, then reverted to full town.
Toll_Description: The castle was the seat of the custums office. The toll station is first mentioned in 1370.

Name: Goes
Alternative_Name: Curtagosum; Cortagosum; Curtagosu; Gous; Gos; Goys; Gois
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Goes is first mentioned in 976. Cox seems to consider the subsequent mention in 1216 more trustworthy as a first mention.
Town_Description: From a juridical perspective, Goes became a town on 7 July 1405, via a statement of Willem VI, count of Holland en Zeeland. From a social-economic point of view, Goes may already be considered a town before that date. In 1417, Goes was granted the right to built fortifications.
Fair_Description: Jacoba van Beieren granted in 1417 (August 7) a fair with tariffs, starting 8 days before Lady Day (August 15) and 8 days after (August 8-22). The first showday was on August 14, but that caused problems as nobody showed up the day after the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. In 1441 (Sept. 12) the first showday was replaced to the Monday after August 15. In 1575 the secretary of Goes visited the central government to obtain the fair of Reimerswaal. A result is not known. King Philip II granted Goes a free fair in 1580 (Dec. 24) for all kind of commodities, in particular horses and cattle. Duration: ? CHECK

Name: Zierikzee

Settlement_Description: Zierikzee is first mentioned in a thirteenth-century copy of a document dated 1156. Zierikzee developed into a governmental centre of the count, and became a port and trading place. A meat house exists in 1248. A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1318. A hospital is first mentioned in 1271.  A chapter in the church is found for the years 1378-1573.
Town_Description: Zierikzee was granted town privileges some time around 1220 (before May 1217, or May 1220- February 1222) by William I, count of Holland. The charter, however, has not survived. The earliest surviving charter dates from 11 March 1248. In 1290 it obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. In 1304 Zierikzee was freed from the staple in Dordrecht. In 1368 Zierikzee received from the king of Sweden the rigt to have a 'vitte' (trading-post) on Schonen (southern point of Sweden) with its own guardian.
Fair_Description: In 1389 Zierikzee is supposed to have obtained a fair lasting 14 days by duke Albrecht. In 1421 (August 27) Philip of Burgundy granted a free fair. priv.boek op NA, HS 3e afd. inv.nr. 1436 fol.? DATA? In 1531 the emperor donated a second fair in the Lent and a staple for madder. In 1575 (June 22) the fair with St. Jacob (July 25) which was too early in the harvest as there was little grain, was relocated to the Monday before the Assumption of the Virgin (August 15). In 1583 (July 12) stadtholder William of Orange granted a fair the first Monday in September during six days.
Staple_Description: In 1304 the town obtained the right on the 'korenmaat' (measure for grain) and was ordained that all grain from the Land of Schouwen had to be traded on the market in Zierikzee. One year later all people working in the drapery Beoosten Schelde should only do that in Zierikzee. Emperor Charles V ordained in 1531 that all madder from Schouwen had to be inspected at Zierikzee and all grain had to be sold there. The guild-charter of the fishermen of St. Peter and Paul dated 1553 (August 21) said that alle fresh fish from Vlieland or from the sea transported along the harbour of Zierikzee had to be marketed and sold in the town for a fourth part.

Name: Helmond
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Helmond can be found in a twelfth-century copy of documents dating from 1108. Archaeological evidence indicates that a new settlement came into being east of the river Aa near the castle 't Oude Huys around 1225.
Town_Description: According to Cox, Helmond probably received town rights between 1225 and 28 May 1241. He states that it is most likely that this happened some time around 1232. Around 1400 stone town walls and a castle were built.
Fair_Description:
In 1376 duchess Johanna granted the lord of Helmond three fairs and a weekly markt on Tuesday. Dates fairs: 1) Sunday before Midlent, 2) Tuesday after Pentecost and 3) third Sunday before St. Dionisusday (Oct. 9). In 1382 toll-exemptions of Helmond at Grave, in the Land of Cuyk, Den Bosch, Lith, the Land of Breda and the Land of Turnhout are confirmed. Circa 1400 a cloth/breadhouse and meathouse are mentioned. In 1425 a weigh-house is known. In 1456 inhabitants of Helmond are first seen at the fairs of  Frankfurt. In 1457 (Febr. 7) the start of the three fairs was altered: 1) Tuedsay before Half Lent, 2) Tuesday before Pentecost, 3) Tuesday before St. Dionysius. Safe-conduct for all three fairs remainend three days before and after the days. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Helmont' then still has three fairs: 1) the third Tuesday in the Lent, 2) Tuesday before Sinxten (Pentecost), 3) Sunday before St. Michael (Sept. 29) till the Tuesday after that.
In 1592 (March 20) king Philip granted a fourth fair.

Settlement_Description: NULL
Town_Description: NULL
Fair_Description: A flax-market en a linnen-hall are found in 1265. Market-tolls are found between 1256-86. The count of Hainaut granted in 1290 (April) two fairs: with Pentecost and with Allsaints (de la Toussaint: Nov. 1). The first one lasted eight days. The last one existed already in the 12th century, it started with St. Martin and lasted 11 days. On Nov. 2 St. Waudru was commemorated, foundress of the abbey, this was a day of pilgrimage. In 1331 a weekly horsemarket was granted. These privileges were confirmed in 1337 and 1346. In 1607 (Dec. 7) the fair with Pentecost was relocated to the second Monday after Quasimodo (first Sunday after Eastern).

Name: Poperinge
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a charter of Charles the Fat as property of the abbey of Saint-Omer in 877, but the name indicates an origin in the 5th century.
Town_Description: Thierry of Alsace, count of Flanders, granted town privileges in 1147. His son Philipp granted market privileges and the right to build a canal.
Fair_Description: In 1187 marketrights were obtained. In 1272 (Jan.) the count of Flanders confirmed the right to organise a fair granted by the count of Alsace to the abbey of St. Bertin in Pouperinghe. Emperor Charles granted in 1528 a free fair during 3 days on Tuesday after the Sunday called Quasimodo (first Sunday after Eastern) and a free weekly market on Friday to restore damage caused by pestilence and fire.
Harbour_Description: Although a privilege to build a canal was already granted in 1187, a canal was only dug from 1367. This so-called Poperingevaart connected Poperinge with the Yser river.
